sections.eyebrow: Creep, Yield Stress, and Viscosity Profiling
sections.title: Creep, Yield Stress, and Viscosity Profiling
sections.description: What the three core measurement types cover.

cards.title: The stress at which flow begins
Method flexibility across these tests
cards.description: Both controlled shear rate and shear stress modes

paragraphs: Soft solids raise questions a simple viscosity number doesn't answer — how much a material deforms under sustained load before recovering or failing (creep), the stress at which it starts to flow at all (yield stress), and how its viscosity changes as shear conditions vary. RSX SST names all three as core capabilities rather than treating one as primary and the others as secondary.

Both controlled shear rate and controlled shear stress modes support these measurements, since yield stress testing in particular is often better approached through controlled stress ramps than fixed-rate testing. Running all three measurement types on the vane or cross-hatch geometry means the same sample and the same instrument setup can answer multiple questions about a soft solid's behavior without switching hardware between tests.

body: CTX Texture Analyzer load cell range: soft samples, firm samples, one instrument.
A texture measurement is only as good as the load cell measuring it. Too sensitive, and a firm product saturates the reading instantly. Not sensitive enough, and a soft gel barely registers.

CTX solves this with 8 interchangeable load cells spanning 100g to 100kg. No compromise built into a single fixed sensor — the same instrument tests a soft cosmetic and a firm food product, accurately, both.

3 adjustable base tables extend that same flexibility to the sample itself — different shapes, different sizes, no forcing everything onto one fixed platform. Combine that with 280mm of boom travel, and larger or more complex samples that a shorter-reach tester simply couldn't handle become testable.

paragraphs: Some texture events happen fast. A fracture. A rupture. The instant a firm product's surface breaks. If the data acquisition rate is too slow, that exact peak gets lost — averaged away instead of captured.

CTX runs at 500 Hz, specifically to catch those precise moments of change. That matters most on brittle or fracturing materials, where the peak force at the point of break is often the actual measurement — not an average across the whole test.

faqs.question: What is CAP2000+ used for?
faqs.answer: CAP2000+ is a cone and plate viscometer used for moderate to high shear viscosity testing of materials like paints, inks, adhesives, and resins, particularly where small sample volumes are involved.

faqs.question: What speed range does CAP2000+ operate at?
faqs.answer: It offers variable speed control from 5 to 1000 RPM, suited to both R&D and QC testing scenarios.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the L Series and H Series?
faqs.answer: The L Series covers a temperature range of 5°C to 75°C, while the H Series extends to 50°C to 235°C for higher-temperature material testing.

faqs.question: How is temperature controlled on CAP2000+?
faqs.answer: A built-in Peltier plate delivers precise temperature control across the L or H Series range.

faqs.question: What materials can be tested on CAP2000+?
faqs.answer: It handles medium-viscosity materials like coatings, creams, and inks, as well as high-viscosity materials like adhesives, asphalt, chocolate, and epoxies.

faqs.question: What does Capcalc software add to CAP2000+?
faqs.answer: Capcalc automates data collection and viscometer control, supports scripting and looping for repetitive tasks, and provides math modeling for yield stress and plastic index calculations.

faqs.question: Can I compare multiple test results on CAP2000+?
faqs.answer: Yes, with Capcalc software, up to four data sets can be plotted together for direct comparison and analysis.

faqs.question: Does CAP2000+ require large sample volumes?
faqs.answer: No, it's specifically designed for applications requiring small sample volumes alongside precise temperature control.

body: How CAP2000+'s variable speed range and dual temperature series fit different testing needs.
High-shear viscosity testing rarely happens at a single fixed speed or temperature, and CAP2000+ is built to cover a genuinely wide operating window rather than a narrow one.

Variable speed runs from 5 to 1000 RPM, wide enough to move between exploratory R&D testing and repeatable QC protocols on the same instrument. Temperature control runs through a built-in Peltier plate, split across two model series depending on what a formulation actually needs: the L Series covers 5°C to 75°C for standard ambient-to-moderate testing, while the H Series reaches all the way to 235°C for genuinely high-temperature materials like hot melt adhesives or asphalt. Both series pair that temperature control with the same wide shear rate range, keeping the instrument well suited to small sample volumes where precise, repeatable conditions matter.

paragraphs: Manual viscosity testing works, but it leaves room for operator-to-operator variation, and that's exactly the gap Capcalc is built to close.

With Capcalc, data capture and viscometer control both automate directly, removing the manual steps that introduce inconsistency between operators or between runs. The software supports powerful scripting capabilities and looping functions for repetitive testing tasks, along with math modeling for yield stress calculations and plastic index, calculations that would otherwise need to be done separately. Up to four data sets can be plotted together for direct comparison and analysis, useful when comparing formulations, batches, or test conditions side by side.

body: Accuracy and repeatability across a wide viscosity range.

A viscometer that's accurate on a mid-range fluid but drifts at the extremes isn't actually solving the problem most labs have — they need one instrument covering thin inks through heavy industrial pastes without swapping equipment between them. DV2Plus holds ±1.0% accuracy of range and ±0.2% repeatability across that full span.

That precision is what makes the instrument usable for both R&D exploration and regulated QC release testing on the same platform: a method developed during formulation work carries the same measurement confidence into production release testing, without needing to be re-validated on a different instrument because the viscosity range changed.

body: Most rotational viscometers offer a limited set of discrete test speeds, which forces a compromise between the speed a method calls for and the nearest speed the instrument actually has. DV2Plus's 740-speed range removes that compromise, giving ultra-fine control across the full span of testing applications.

Connectivity follows the same philosophy of removing friction rather than adding features for their own sake. Bluetooth and four USB-A ports plus one USB-B port cover PCs, printers, and barcode scanners without cable management becoming its own task. DV360 software extends that into advanced viscosity testing with optional 21 CFR Part 11 compliance, and DV Create builds up to 25-step test methods, live-monitors tests over Bluetooth or USB, and stays compatible with legacy DV2T method files — so a lab moving from DV2T to DV2Plus doesn't lose its existing validated methods in the transition.

That real-time visibility is what turns a routine test into monitored testing — a torque reading trending toward an out-of-range value shows up while the test is still running, not after the fact in a report. The interface itself is built for that kind of glance-and-check use: a wide viewing angle and a clean, modern layout rather than a menu structure that has to be navigated to find the number that matters.

faqs.question: What is the DVNext Cone/Plate Rheometer used for?
faqs.answer: It's a rheometer for precise absolute viscosity measurement of small sample volumes, used in pharmaceutical, biotechnology, cosmetics, and specialty chemical R&D where sample material is limited or expensive.

faqs.question: How small a sample does it need?
faqs.answer: As small as 0.5–2.0 mL.

faqs.question: How does it calculate viscosity?
faqs.answer: It measures the torque required to rotate a cone spindle immersed in the sample against a plate; that torque is proportional to shear stress and is used to calculate absolute viscosity in centipoise (mPa·s).

faqs.question: What is the torque measurement accuracy and repeatability?
faqs.answer: 1% of full-scale range for accuracy, and 0.2% of full-scale range for repeatability.

faqs.question: How is the spindle attached?
faqs.answer: Via a magnetic coupling attachment, simplifying attachment and removal and minimizing handling errors.

faqs.question: Does the instrument require manual gap adjustment?
faqs.answer: No. Electronic gap adjustment reduces manual intervention and improves repeatability.

faqs.question: What do the auto-zero and auto-range functions do?
faqs.answer: Auto-zero automatically calibrates the instrument for optimal torque accuracy; auto-range automatically defines the full-scale range for every spindle/speed combination.

faqs.question: Why is temperature control faster on this instrument?
faqs.answer: The small sample volume has less thermal mass, so it reaches target temperature faster than larger-volume viscometry, reducing wait time during testing.

faqs.question: Is external gauging needed to set the cone/plate gap?
faqs.answer: No. The relative cone-to-plate position is maintained through simple mechanical setup without external gauges.

faqs.question: Can multiple cone spindles be used?
faqs.answer: Yes, multiple cone spindles are supported and can be calibrated for specific applications.

faqs.question: Is 21 CFR Part 11 compliance available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an optional feature, including electronic signatures, audit trails, and secure data management.

faqs.question: Can the instrument connect to a LIMS?
faqs.answer: Yes, optional Ethernet and LIMS connectivity is available for integration with laboratory management systems.

faqs.question: How is DVNext Cone/Plate different from DV2Plus?
faqs.answer: DVNext Cone/Plate is built specifically for small sample volumes (0.5–2.0 mL) using cone/plate geometry. DV2Plus is a general-purpose rotational spindle viscometer with a 740-speed range and built-in Gel Timer functionality, suited to larger, more readily available sample volumes.

sections.title: Precision at Small Sample Volumes
sections.tabSummary: What 0.5–2.0 mL enables and why it matters
body: What 0.5–2.0 mL enables and why it matters.

Standard rotational viscometry generally assumes sample volume isn't the constraint — there's enough material to fill a beaker and immerse a spindle. Cone/plate geometry doesn't need that assumption. DVNext Cone/Plate measures accurate absolute viscosity from 0.5 to 2.0 mL, which is the difference between testing being possible and testing consuming more of a limited or expensive material than a project can afford.

That small volume carries a second benefit beyond conservation: thermal mass is proportionally small too, so temperature adjustments happen quickly. A test sequence that steps through multiple temperature points doesn't spend most of its time waiting for the sample to equilibrate — it spends that time collecting data instead, directly improving throughput for iterative formulation work.

groups.title: Principle of Operation
groups.summary: How the cone/plate geometry calculates absolute viscosity
groups.description: How the cone/plate geometry calculates absolute viscosity.
body: DVNext Cone/Plate measures the torque required to rotate a cone spindle immersed in a small volume of fluid held against a plate. The fluid resists that rotation, and the resistance is directly proportional to shear stress — which is then used to calculate the fluid's absolute viscosity in centipoise (mPa·s) directly, without an external calibration curve standing between the raw measurement and the result.

The cone-to-plate relative position is what makes the shear rate calculation valid, and that position is maintained through a simple mechanical setup rather than requiring external gauges to verify — one less variable for the operator to manage, and one less source of setup-to-setup variability across a testing programme.

For regulated environments, 21 CFR Part 11 compliance is available as an option, bringing electronic signatures, audit trails, and secure data management into the testing workflow rather than requiring a separate paper-based compliance layer. Optional Ethernet and LIMS connectivity extends that further, feeding results directly into a laboratory management system rather than requiring manual transcription between the instrument and the system of record.

faqs.question: What is the DVNext Rheometer used for?
faqs.answer: It's a rheometer for viscosity and yield stress measurement, available in a Standard version for general R&D use and a 21 CFR Part 11 Compliant version for regulated QC release testing.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the Standard and Compliant versions?
faqs.answer: Standard includes digital leveling, a Start-up Wizard, built-in Gel-Timer functionality, and optional magnetic coupling or barcode scanning. Compliant includes magnetic coupling and hand-held barcode scanning as standard, plus 21 CFR Part 11/GAMP compliance, Ethernet and LIMS connectivity, and non-editable PDF reporting.

faqs.question: What is the accuracy and repeatability?
faqs.answer: ±1.0% of range accuracy and ±0.2% repeatability, on both versions.

faqs.question: What is Gel-Timer functionality?
faqs.answer: A built-in capability on the Standard version for measuring gelation time across various applications.

faqs.question: Is magnetic coupling standard or optional?
faqs.answer: Optional on the Standard version, standard-fit on the Compliant version.

faqs.question: Does the Compliant version include barcode scanning?
faqs.answer: Yes, a hand-held barcode scanner is standard, with automatic accessory detection built in.

faqs.question: Can the instrument connect to a LIMS?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the 21 CFR Part 11 Compliant version, via Ethernet and LIMS connectivity.

faqs.question: What does non-editable PDF reporting protect against?
faqs.answer: It generates secure, tamper-evident reports directly from the device, protecting data integrity for regulated environments.

faqs.question: Is ISO 17025 calibration available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an optional feature on the Standard version.

faqs.question: What is the Start-up Wizard?
faqs.answer: A guided setup tool that simplifies the instrument's initial configuration process, included on the Standard version.

faqs.question: How is DVNext Rheometer different from DVNext Cone/Plate Rheometer?
faqs.answer: DVNext Rheometer is a general viscosity and yield stress instrument available in Standard and Compliant versions. DVNext Cone/Plate Rheometer is purpose-built for small sample volumes (0.5–2.0 mL) using cone/plate geometry.

longForm.heroHook: Standard for the bench. Compliant for the audit trail. Same rheometer underneath.
longForm.heroLead: A rheometer bought for R&D and a rheometer bought for regulated QC release testing don't need the same feature set — one needs speed and simplicity, the other needs electronic signatures and a system of record. DVNext Rheometer ships as two versions built around exactly that distinction. The Standard version covers what most labs need day to day: digital leveling for consistent setup, a Start-up Wizard that guides initial configuration, built-in Gel-Timer functionality for tracking gelation, and ±1.0% accuracy with ±0.2% repeatability as the baseline. Magnetic coupling and a barcode scanner are available as options. The 21 CFR Part 11 Compliant version takes that same measurement core and builds a full regulated workflow around it: magnetic coupling attachment as standard, hand-held barcode scanning with automatic accessory detection, Ethernet and LIMS connectivity, and secure non-editable PDF reporting — all under GAMP-compliant audit trails.

sections.title: Standard vs. Compliant
sections.tabSummary: The exact feature split across the two versions
body: The exact feature split across the two versions.

Buying more compliance capability than a lab actually needs adds cost and complexity without adding value; buying too little means a regulated workflow has to be retrofitted later. DVNext Rheometer avoids that mismatch by offering the choice upfront rather than layering compliance on as an afterthought.

The Standard version is built for straightforward, high-quality measurement: digital leveling and a Start-up Wizard get a test running quickly, Gel-Timer functionality is built in rather than an add-on, and magnetic coupling or a barcode scanner can be added where the workflow calls for them. The Compliant version starts from a different assumption — that every test needs to be traceable, auditable, and connected to a system of record — and builds magnetic coupling, hand-held barcode scanning with automatic accessory detection, Ethernet and LIMS connectivity, and non-editable PDF reporting into the standard configuration rather than treating any of them as optional extras.

paragraphs: Brookfield frames the case for DVNext Rheometer around three things holding together on one platform: precision and repeatability from features like digital leveling and real-time graphing; compliance for labs that need it, through the 21 CFR Part 11 Compliant version's audit trails and secure data management; and versatility through optional accessories and configurable features that adapt the instrument to a wide range of testing needs rather than locking it to one workflow.

That combination is what lets the same underlying measurement platform serve both an R&D bench running exploratory formulation work and a regulated QC lab releasing batches against a specification — without either one carrying capability, or cost, they don't need.

sections.title: Precision at an Entry-Level Price
sections.tabSummary: The accuracy/repeatability figures matched against DV2Plus
body: The accuracy and repeatability figures matched against DV2Plus.

Entry-level instrumentation usually signals a trade-off somewhere in the measurement chain — a wider accuracy band, fewer discrete speeds, a narrower operating range. DVPlus doesn't carry that trade-off into its core specification: ±1.0% of range accuracy and ±0.2% repeatability, identical to what Brookfield states for the DV2Plus, and a full 740-speed range rather than a reduced subset.

What positions DVPlus as the entry-level instrument is everything built around that core measurement, not the measurement itself. A 5-inch display instead of 7 inches, no stated Viscosity Wizard or built-in Gel Timer functionality, and a simpler connectivity story via the DVPlus Connect App rather than DV360's advanced compliance-ready software layer. For a lab whose real requirement is accurate, repeatable viscosity data without needing guided complex-test setup or regulated audit trails, that's the right trade to make.

paragraphs: Some testing protocols care less about a single-point viscosity reading and more about how a material's behaviour changes over time — how long it takes to reach a target torque, how long temperature equilibration actually takes, or when a test sequence should stop based on a defined condition rather than a fixed duration. DVPlus provides direct access to those three time-based functions rather than requiring them to be configured through a more general step-program interface.

Automatic range calculation works alongside that: the Full-Scale Range at 100% and the maximum measurable viscosity for a given spindle/speed combination are calculated automatically, removing a manual lookup step from method setup and reducing the chance of a test running outside its valid measurement range without the operator noticing.

sections.tabSummary: Why tracking gelation on the primary rheometer matters
body: Why tracking gelation on the primary rheometer matters.

Gelation isn't a single point measurement the way a viscosity reading is — it's a transition that happens over time, and catching exactly when it occurs matters directly for resins, epoxies, and other curing systems where working time and cure time are process-critical variables. Running that measurement as a bolt-on to a general viscometer, or on a separate dedicated instrument, adds a step and a potential source of inconsistency between the viscosity data and the gel time data.

DVNext Rheometer with Gel Timer Functionality keeps both on the same measurement platform. Gel-Timer functionality is positioned as a defining capability rather than an incidental feature, so gelation studies and standard viscosity/yield stress testing draw on the same calibration, the same interface, and the same reporting path.

sections.title: Krebs Units and ASTM D562
sections.tabSummary: Why this unit system and standard apply to paints and coatings
body: Why this unit system and standard apply to paints and coatings.

Krebs units are the measurement system the paint and coatings industry has used to specify application consistency, and ASTM D562 is the standard method built around that system. A formulation specified in KU can't be directly verified on an instrument reporting only in centipoise without a conversion step, so KU-3 reports in Krebs units, grams, and centipoise at the same time, letting a lab match whichever unit a specification or customer actually requires.

The stated measurement range — 40 to 141 KU, 32 to 1099 grams, 27 to 5274 cP — covers the consistency range Brookfield associates with standard paint, coating, and ink testing. The optional paste spindle extends that into materials outside the standard range, such as roller mill pastes, without requiring a separate instrument.

sections.tabSummary: How the mechanical measurement principle works
body: How the mechanical measurement principle works.

Unlike Brookfield's touchscreen instruments, Dial Reading Viscometer reads torque off a mechanical dial rather than a digital display. The multi-speed electronic drive behind that dial is a direct drive design, which Brookfield states delivers quiet operation and works reliably across global power sources — a consideration relevant for labs operating across different regions or power infrastructure.

Speed selection uses an ergonomic control knob to move between pre-set speeds directly, rather than navigating a menu. Standard models offer 10 pre-set speeds; LVT models offer 8. Continuous torque sensing keeps the reading live throughout a test, and the underlying accuracy and repeatability figures — 1% and 0.2% of full-scale range — match what Brookfield states for its digital DVNext line, despite the different readout method.

sections.title: Rapid Cooling and Throughput
sections.tabSummary: Why the lid fan is the whole speed story
body: Why the lid fan is the real story behind the 25% figure.
Loss-on-drying testing has a bottleneck most people don't think about: the chamber has to cool before the next sample goes in. Every minute spent cooling is a minute the instrument isn't testing.
MAX 4000XL's built-in lid fan solves that directly. It cools the heating chamber fast, and Brookfield states the result plainly: 25% faster throughput than other rapid loss-on-drying instruments.
That's not a marginal gain. Across a full shift of testing, 25% is the difference between finishing the queue and carrying samples into tomorrow.

paragraphs: Not all moisture behaves the same way. Some evaporates fast and easily — free moisture. Some is chemically bound to the material and needs a different temperature, a different endpoint, to release.

MAX 4000XL links multiple test stages into one sequence. Temperature, ending criteria, and timing can all change between segments — so a single run captures both free and bound moisture without manual intervention between stages.
User-adjustable ending criteria go further: the test stops when your material says it's done, not when a generic default says so.

body: Computrac MAX 5000XL vs thermogravimetric analyzers: why 600°C changes the value proposition.

Thermogravimetric analyzers measure moisture, solids, and ash by precisely tracking mass change as temperature rises. They're the reference standard for this kind of testing. They also carry a price tag that puts them out of reach for many labs that only occasionally need that level of capability.

MAX 5000XL closes that gap. A heater reaching 600°C runs both loss-on-drying and loss-on-ignition tests, which is what lets one sample yield moisture, solids, and ash data without switching equipment. Brookfield states this plainly: features typically found in more expensive thermogravimetric analyzers, delivered in a solution built for a fraction of the cost.

faqs.question: What sample vial sizes are compatible?
faqs.answer: Most crimp top vials from 2R to 60R.

faqs.question: Does the sample get exposed to ambient air during testing?
faqs.answer: No, sealed crimp top vials prevent exposure, protecting hygroscopic samples.

faqs.question: How much data can it store?
faqs.answer: Up to 250 test programs, the last 1,000 test results, and the last 100 test graphs.

faqs.question: Can it be accessed remotely?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the optional web server feature, remote monitoring, result downloads, audit log viewing, and program transfer between solutions.

faqs.question: How is Vapor Pro XL different from MAX 4000XL and MAX 5000XL?
faqs.answer: MAX 4000XL and MAX 5000XL measure moisture via weight loss (LOD/LOI). Vapor Pro XL measures moisture specifically via RH-sensor technology, correlating with Karl Fischer titration rather than weight-loss methods.

sections.title: Moisture-Specific Detection, Not Weight Loss
sections.tabSummary: Why RH-sensor technology changes what gets measured
body: Computrac Vapor Pro XL detection method: why RH-sensor technology changes what gets measured.

Loss-on-drying and loss-on-ignition methods measure how much mass a sample loses when heated, then assume the loss is moisture. That assumption breaks down when a sample contains other volatile compounds. The instrument can't tell the difference, and the result reads high.

Vapor Pro XL sidesteps that problem entirely. RH-sensor technology detects moisture specifically, not total mass loss, which means the result reflects actual water content even in samples where other volatiles are present. Sensitivity reaches 10 micrograms of water, low enough to determine moisture content as low as 10ppm, a level weight-loss methods typically can't resolve reliably.

sections.title: The Nine Measurements
sections.tabSummary: What each output tells you about handling behavior
body: PFT Powder Flow Tester measurement outputs: what each number tells you about handling behavior.

A single flow function number doesn't tell a hopper designer everything they need. PFT's testing produces nine distinct outputs, each answering a different practical question about how a powder will actually behave in equipment.

Bulk density, measured at fill and final states, establishes the baseline the rest of the data builds from. Wall friction predicts how the powder interacts with the specific material a hopper or chute is built from, not a generic assumption. Flow index summarizes overall flowability. Arching dimensions and rat-hole diameter predict the two most common hopper discharge failures before either happens on the production line. Hopper half angle informs the actual geometry a new hopper needs. Carr Index and Hausner Ratio flag compressibility and caking risk. Time consolidation testing, run alongside the full flow function data, captures how flow behavior changes after a powder has sat in storage, a condition standard single-point testing misses entirely.

rows: How dense is the powder, loose and settled?
Will it stick to the hopper wall?
How well does it flow overall?
Will it arch and stop flowing?
Will it rat-hole through the center?
Is it prone to caking or poor compressibility?
Does flow behavior change after storage?

longForm.heroHook: Pressurized coaxial cylinder rheometer, up to 1000 psi, -40°C to +260°C, down to 0.2 sec⁻¹.
longForm.heroLead: PVS Rheometer is a dynamic coaxial cylinder, controlled shear rate rheometer for measuring viscosity under pressure at elevated or reduced temperatures, where sample boil-off could otherwise be a problem. Brookfield describes it as suited to simulating in-process conditions on small fluid samples, in industries including chemicals, oil, food processing, polymers, and paints. Pressure range extends to 1000 psi, with a temperature range of -40°C to +260°C. An RTD temperature sensor on the inner cylinder surface measures sample temperature directly. The outer cylinder rotates at shear rates up to 1700 sec⁻¹, and the instrument measures down to 0.2 sec⁻¹ for low shear rate viscosity (LSRV) work. A robust motor reaches speeds up to 1000 RPM, with a stationary spindle inside the rotating outer cylinder. Standard construction uses Hastelloy cups and bobs. A triple annulus geometry option is available for increased sensitivity on low-viscosity fluids. The instrument is designed to meet API industry standards, and includes a safety relief valve. Rheovision software automates and controls test parameters. The footprint is 1' x 1' x 2', described by Brookfield as compact enough for site-to-site mobility.

sections.title: Pressure and Temperature Control
sections.tabSummary: Why boil-off is the problem this design addresses
body: Why boil-off is the problem this design addresses.

A volatile fluid tested at ambient pressure and elevated temperature can boil off before or during measurement, changing its composition and invalidating the result. PVS Rheometer's coaxial cylinder chamber operates under pressure specifically to prevent that — up to 1000 psi, across a temperature range of -40°C to +260°C, which Brookfield states makes it suitable for elevated or reduced temperature testing where boil-off would otherwise be an issue.

An RTD sensor mounted on the inner cylinder surface measures sample temperature directly at the point of shear, rather than inferring it from the chamber wall or an external probe. A safety relief valve is fitted as standard, addressing the operational risk of running a sealed chamber under both pressure and temperature extremes.

sections.title: Low Shear Rate Measurement and Triple Annulus
sections.description: What 0.2 sec⁻¹ and the annulus option enable.

cards.title: Accurate measurement at very low shear rates
Coverage into higher shear conditions on the same instrument

paragraphs: Many process conditions — down-hole drilling, slow blending, reactor flow — happen at shear rates well below what a standard rotational instrument resolves accurately. PVS Rheometer measures down to 0.2 sec⁻¹ for low shear rate viscosity (LSRV) work, extending the usable range into conditions that matter directly for in-process simulation.

At the other end, the outer cylinder rotates at shear rates up to 1700 sec⁻¹, with a stationary spindle inside, giving the instrument range across both slow and fast shear conditions on the same coaxial cylinder geometry. Where the fluid itself is low-viscosity and the standard geometry doesn't provide enough measurement sensitivity, the optional triple annulus geometry increases sensitivity specifically for that case.

faqs.question: What is the RSO Rheometer used for?

faqs.answer: It provides low friction for oscillatory measurement, enabling precise viscoelastic measurement.

faqs.question: Can it profile viscosity against temperature?

faqs.question: What does Rheo3000 software add?
faqs.answer: PC control, data acquisition, and analysis of multiple test files.

faqs.answer: RSO is an oscillatory rheometer for standard-condition QC and R&D testing across two geometries, operated stand-alone. PVS is a pressurized coaxial cylinder rheometer built for volatile or temperature-extreme samples up to 1000 psi and -40°C to +260°C.

sections.tabSummary: Why cone/plate and concentric cylinder on the same platform matters
body: Why cone/plate and concentric cylinder on the same platform matters.

Different materials and test protocols call for different rheometer geometries — cone/plate suits certain viscosity ranges and sample volumes, concentric cylinder suits others. Buying separate instruments for each geometry means separate footprints, separate calibration routines, and separate operator training. RSO Rheometer supports both configurations on the same instrument, described by Brookfield as instrument flexibility suited to a wide range of material testing applications.

A quick connect coupling system attaches spindles without a lengthy fitting process, and automatic gap setting handles the spindle-to-plate distance that cone/plate geometry depends on for accurate shear rate calculation — a step that's traditionally manual and operator-sensitive on other instruments. Spindle barcode recognition identifies which geometry and spindle configuration is fitted automatically, reducing the chance of a test running against the wrong configuration data.

sections.title: High Torque for Difficult Samples
sections.tabSummary: Why 200 Nm matters against a standard motor
body: Why 200 Nm matters against a standard motor.

Testing high-viscosity or highly structured materials — pastes, gels, filled compounds — requires enough torque to actually shear the sample without the motor stalling or the measurement losing accuracy at the top of its range. RSX Coaxial Cylinder's 200 Nm motor is described by Brookfield specifically as an increase over a standard motor, aimed at testing the toughest samples for comprehensive analysis across a wide range of materials.

That torque capacity pairs with coaxial cylinder geometry, which Brookfield states delivers the most accurate results particularly in low-viscosity ranges — meaning the instrument's usable range extends in both directions, from difficult high-torque materials through to precision measurement at the low-viscosity end, on the same geometry.

paragraphs: Temperature-dependent rheology testing needs the sample held at a controlled temperature throughout the measurement, and different lab setups favor different methods of achieving that. RSX Coaxial Cylinder supports two: direct immersion in a temperature-controlled bath, or external circulation using the FTKY3 water jacket, across a stated range of -20°C to 180°C.

Direct bath immersion suits labs already running a compatible bath as part of the workflow. The FTKY3 water jacket option instead circulates temperature-controlled fluid externally around the sample chamber, which may suit setups where immersing the entire measuring head isn't practical. Both methods cover the same overall temperature range.

sections.title: Controlled Shear Rate vs. Controlled Shear Stress
sections.tabSummary: Why having both modes on one instrument matters
body: Why having both modes on one instrument matters.

Some rheological questions are best answered by fixing the shear rate and observing how stress responds; others need the reverse — fixing shear stress and observing the resulting shear rate, particularly around yield behavior. RSX Cone Plate runs both: controlled shear rate (rpm) and controlled shear stress (torque), named explicitly as distinct operating modes rather than one general controlled-shear description.

That distinction matters for method design. A test protocol built around controlled stress — common for yield stress work — and one built around controlled rate — common for standard flow curve generation — can both run on the same instrument without switching hardware, only the operating mode.

paragraphs: Cone/plate rheometry depends on an accurate, consistent gap between the cone tip and the plate — get it wrong and the shear rate calculation the whole measurement rests on is wrong too. RSX Cone Plate automatically detects and adjusts that gap specifically with standard one-piece spindles, removing a manual step that's traditionally sensitive to operator technique.

Combined with auto spindle recognition via barcode, which automatically sets the correct spindle configuration, and the quick connect coupling system for physical attachment, the setup sequence from spindle selection to test-ready gap is largely automated rather than depending on a trained operator getting each step right by hand.

faqs.question: Why does it use vane and cross-hatch geometry instead of standard spindles?
faqs.answer: Standard smooth cone/plate or cylinder geometry can allow soft-solid or paste-like samples to slip at the measuring surface rather than shear internally, corrupting the measurement. Vane and cross-hatch geometry are used specifically to minimize that slippage.

faqs.question: What operating modes does it support?

faqs.question: How are spindles recognized?
faqs.answer: Via barcode, automatically identifying and setting the correct spindle configuration.

faqs.question: What temperature control options are available?
faqs.answer: Peltier or fluid-heated.

faqs.question: Is it suitable for the production floor?
faqs.answer: Yes, described as rugged and built to withstand production floor demands while maintaining precision.

faqs.question: How much sample does a test require?
faqs.answer: A small sample volume, supporting rapid setup and cleanup.

faqs.question: How is RSX SST different from RSX Cone Plate or RSX Coaxial Cylinder?
faqs.answer: RSX SST uses vane and cross-hatch geometry specifically for soft solids, pastes, and slurries, where slippage is a problem on smooth cone/plate or cylinder geometry. RSX Cone Plate and RSX Coaxial Cylinder are built for standard flowable materials, with torque motors stated at 200 mNm and 200 Nm respectively.

faqs.question: How is RSX SST different from RSO Rheometer?
faqs.answer: RSO supports cone/plate and concentric cylinder geometry with stand-alone touchscreen operation, suited to standard-condition fluids. RSX SST is purpose-built with vane and cross-hatch geometry specifically for materials that slip on those standard geometries.

sections.title: Why Vane and Cross-Hatch Geometry
sections.tabSummary: The slippage problem this design solves
body: The slippage problem this design solves.

Standard cone/plate or smooth cylinder geometry works because the sample shears cleanly against the measuring surface. Pastes, slurries, and soft solids often don't behave that way — instead of shearing internally, the material slips at the surface of a smooth spindle or plate, which corrupts the measurement without necessarily looking wrong to the operator.

RSX SST addresses that specifically with vane and cross-hatch spindle geometries, described by Brookfield as used specifically to minimize slippage in soft-solid and paste-like samples. A vane geometry effectively traps material between its blades so the sample shears against itself rather than against a smooth surface; cross-hatch geometry provides a textured surface with the same intent.

rows: Shear happening within the sample, not at its surface
Purpose-built geometry rather than adapted smooth-surface spindles
Confidence the reading reflects the material, not an artifact

sections.eyebrow: Creep, Yield Stress, and Viscosity Profiling
sections.title: Creep, Yield Stress, and Viscosity Profiling
sections.description: What the three core measurement types cover.

cards.title: The stress at which flow begins
Method flexibility across these tests
cards.description: Both controlled shear rate and shear stress modes

paragraphs: Soft solids raise questions a simple viscosity number doesn't answer — how much a material deforms under sustained load before recovering or failing (creep), the stress at which it starts to flow at all (yield stress), and how its viscosity changes as shear conditions vary. RSX SST names all three as core capabilities rather than treating one as primary and the others as secondary.

Both controlled shear rate and controlled shear stress modes support these measurements, since yield stress testing in particular is often better approached through controlled stress ramps than fixed-rate testing. Running all three measurement types on the vane or cross-hatch geometry means the same sample and the same instrument setup can answer multiple questions about a soft solid's behavior without switching hardware between tests.

body: CTX Texture Analyzer load cell range: soft samples, firm samples, one instrument.
A texture measurement is only as good as the load cell measuring it. Too sensitive, and a firm product saturates the reading instantly. Not sensitive enough, and a soft gel barely registers.

CTX solves this with 8 interchangeable load cells spanning 100g to 100kg. No compromise built into a single fixed sensor — the same instrument tests a soft cosmetic and a firm food product, accurately, both.

3 adjustable base tables extend that same flexibility to the sample itself — different shapes, different sizes, no forcing everything onto one fixed platform. Combine that with 280mm of boom travel, and larger or more complex samples that a shorter-reach tester simply couldn't handle become testable.

paragraphs: Some texture events happen fast. A fracture. A rupture. The instant a firm product's surface breaks. If the data acquisition rate is too slow, that exact peak gets lost — averaged away instead of captured.

CTX runs at 500 Hz, specifically to catch those precise moments of change. That matters most on brittle or fracturing materials, where the peak force at the point of break is often the actual measurement — not an average across the whole test.

sections.title: SweepTec and Degas Explained
sections.description: How SweepTec's standing-wave prevention and the Degas function work together on SONOREX DIGITEC DT.
sections.tabSummary: How standing-wave prevention and degassing work together
body: An ultrasonic bath is only as good as how evenly its cavitation reaches the whole tank, and that's exactly what these two functions are built to solve.

Standing waves form naturally in a fixed-frequency ultrasonic field, creating pockets of intense cavitation next to nearly dead zones in the same tank. SweepTec actively varies the field to prevent that pattern from settling in, so cleaning stays consistent whether an object sits in the center of the tank or against the wall. The Degas function tackles a separate problem: dissolved gas in the cleaning liquid absorbs some of the ultrasound's energy before it ever reaches the object being cleaned. Running Degas at the start of a cycle clears that dissolved gas out first, so the ultrasound works at full effect from the very beginning rather than only reaching peak performance partway through.

body: Choosing between SONOREX DIGITEC DT's heated and unheated ultrasonic bath configurations.
Not every cleaning or degassing process needs temperature control, and the range splits cleanly along that line.

Unheated models, like DT 31, DT 52, DT 510, and DT 514, focus on cleaning time control and the display of remaining time, suited to processes where ambient or unheated liquid temperature is enough. Heated models, marked with an H or CH designation such as DT 31 H, DT 255 H, and DT 1028 CH, add bath temperature setting through the same membrane keypad, with the display showing both the set and actual temperature so you can confirm the bath has genuinely reached target conditions before relying on it for a temperature-sensitive process.

sections.title: SweepTec and Even Cavitation
sections.description: How SweepTec's standing-wave prevention keeps cleaning uniform across the RK 255 H tank.
sections.tabSummary: What standing-wave prevention actually changes
body: A fixed-frequency ultrasonic field naturally develops standing waves, pockets where cavitation runs intense right next to areas where it barely reaches at all. That unevenness is exactly what SweepTec is built to eliminate.

Running fully automatically, SweepTec actively varies the ultrasonic field to prevent those standing-wave patterns from forming, so cleaning stays consistent whether an object sits at the center of the tank or against its walls. That matters directly for anything with recessed surfaces, threaded fittings, or complex geometry, exactly the places a manual wipe-down or simple immersion cleaning would miss.

sections.tabSummary: Baskets, lids, inserts, and cleaning concentrates
body: Baskets, lids, insert cups, and cleaning concentrates matched specifically to the RK 255 H.

For RK 255 H specifically, that includes the D 255 lid, the DE 255 perforated lid for cycles needing airflow, the K 5 C hanging basket, and the EG 1 insert grille for organizing smaller items within a basket. Insert cups like the SD 06, PD 06, and EB 05, each with lid and rubber ring, handle smaller sample volumes separately from the main tank. Mounting brackets across several sizes secure baskets in place during operation, and a range of Tickopur and Stammopur cleaning and disinfection concentrates cover everything from general instrument cleaning to gypsum removal and drill disinfection.

sections.title: SweepTec and Degas Explained
sections.description: How SweepTec's standing-wave prevention and the Degas function work together on SONOREX DIGITEC DT.
sections.tabSummary: How standing-wave prevention and degassing work together
body: An ultrasonic bath is only as good as how evenly its cavitation reaches the whole tank, and that's exactly what these two functions are built to solve.

Standing waves form naturally in a fixed-frequency ultrasonic field, creating pockets of intense cavitation next to nearly dead zones in the same tank. SweepTec actively varies the field to prevent that pattern from settling in, so cleaning stays consistent whether an object sits in the center of the tank or against the wall. The Degas function tackles a separate problem: dissolved gas in the cleaning liquid absorbs some of the ultrasound's energy before it ever reaches the object being cleaned. Running Degas at the start of a cycle clears that dissolved gas out first, so the ultrasound works at full effect from the very beginning rather than only reaching peak performance partway through.

body: Choosing between SONOREX DIGITEC DT's heated and unheated ultrasonic bath configurations.
Not every cleaning or degassing process needs temperature control, and the range splits cleanly along that line.

Unheated models, like DT 31, DT 52, DT 510, and DT 514, focus on cleaning time control and the display of remaining time, suited to processes where ambient or unheated liquid temperature is enough. Heated models, marked with an H or CH designation such as DT 31 H, DT 255 H, and DT 1028 CH, add bath temperature setting through the same membrane keypad, with the display showing both the set and actual temperature so you can confirm the bath has genuinely reached target conditions before relying on it for a temperature-sensitive process.

sections.title: SweepTec and Even Cavitation
sections.description: How SweepTec's standing-wave prevention keeps cleaning uniform across the RK 255 H tank.
sections.tabSummary: What standing-wave prevention actually changes
body: A fixed-frequency ultrasonic field naturally develops standing waves, pockets where cavitation runs intense right next to areas where it barely reaches at all. That unevenness is exactly what SweepTec is built to eliminate.

Running fully automatically, SweepTec actively varies the ultrasonic field to prevent those standing-wave patterns from forming, so cleaning stays consistent whether an object sits at the center of the tank or against its walls. That matters directly for anything with recessed surfaces, threaded fittings, or complex geometry, exactly the places a manual wipe-down or simple immersion cleaning would miss.

sections.tabSummary: Baskets, lids, inserts, and cleaning concentrates
body: Baskets, lids, insert cups, and cleaning concentrates matched specifically to the RK 255 H.
A tank on its own only does half the job. Getting the right basket, lid, and cleaning chemistry matched to that specific tank size is what makes a cleaning cycle actually consistent.

For RK 255 H specifically, that includes the D 255 lid, the DE 255 perforated lid for cycles needing airflow, the K 5 C hanging basket, and the EG 1 insert grille for organizing smaller items within a basket. Insert cups like the SD 06, PD 06, and EB 05, each with lid and rubber ring, handle smaller sample volumes separately from the main tank. Mounting brackets across several sizes secure baskets in place during operation, and a range of Tickopur and Stammopur cleaning and disinfection concentrates cover everything from general instrument cleaning to gypsum removal and drill disinfection.

faqs.question: What makes the INVENIO different from a routine FT-IR spectrometer?

faqs.question: What is the spectral resolution of the INVENIO?
faqs.answer: Below 0.085 cm⁻¹, suited to research requiring fine spectral detail.

faqs.question: Can the INVENIO run two experiments at once?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Transit channel is an independent second measurement channel with its own detector, running alongside the main sample compartment.

faqs.answer: Yes. OPUS software complies with major pharmacopeia requirements and 21 CFR Part 11, with secure data handling for data integrity.

faqs.question: What is EMILIE?
faqs.answer: EMILIE is a nanomechanical infrared analyzer that integrates with the INVENIO for picogram-level sensitivity on nanomaterials, aerosols, and trace-level samples, without cryogenic cooling.

faqs.answer: It supports kinetics studies and reaction monitoring down to the nanosecond timescale, useful for researching catalysts and batteries under real-world conditions.

faqs.question: What is the VERTEX 80/80v FT-IR Research Spectrometer used for?
faqs.answer: It's a peak-performance research FT-IR platform used across semiconductor research, pharmaceutical analysis, physics, and surface science, wherever the highest resolution or sensitivity is required.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the VERTEX 80 and VERTEX 80v?
faqs.answer: The VERTEX 80v adds an evacuated optics bench, removing atmospheric moisture from the beam path. This enables high-resolution work, ultra-fast rapidscan, step-scan, and UV-range measurements that the standard purge-optics VERTEX 80 doesn't reach.

faqs.question: What resolution can the VERTEX 80/80v achieve?
faqs.answer: Standard configuration reaches better than 0.2 cm⁻¹. The PEAK configuration reaches better than 0.06 cm⁻¹, which Bruker states is the highest resolution achieved on a commercial benchtop FT-IR spectrometer.

faqs.question: What spectral range does it cover?
faqs.answer: From 50,000 cm⁻¹ in the UV/VIS region down to 5 cm⁻¹ in the far IR and terahertz range, the broadest range in Bruker's benchtop FT-IR line.

faqs.question: Can external light sources and accessories be connected?
faqs.answer: Yes. Five exit ports and two input ports allow simultaneous connection of accessories such as synchrotron sources, bolometers, FT-IR microscopes, and Raman modules.

faqs.question: Can beamsplitters be changed without opening the instrument?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the VERTEX 80v. The BMS-c option remotely exchanges up to four beamsplitter types automatically, under vacuum, without venting the optics bench.

faqs.question: Is the VERTEX 80/80v suitable for nanoscience research?
faqs.answer: Yes. The evacuated VERTEX 80v reaches sensitivity below 10⁻³ monolayers, suited to demanding surface and nanomaterial studies.

faqs.question: Can it be used for terahertz spectroscopy?
faqs.answer: Yes. A broadband far IR/THz beamsplitter covers approximately 900 down to 5 cm⁻¹ in a single measurement, and an external Hg-arc source with a room-temperature DTGS detector makes the terahertz range accessible.

faqs.question: What is EMILIE, and does it work with this solution?
faqs.answer: EMILIE is a nanomechanical infrared analyzer that adds picogram-level sensitivity for nanomaterials and trace-level samples, without cryogenic cooling. It's compatible with the VERTEX 80/80v.

faqs.answer: The price depends on the configuration, resolution tier, and external accessories your research needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

sections.tabSummary: Choosing between VERTEX 80 and 80v
body: Two decisions shape which VERTEX configuration fits your work: how much resolution you need, and whether atmospheric moisture can be allowed anywhere near your measurement.

The standard VERTEX 80 reaches better than 0.2 cm⁻¹, sufficient for most ambient-pressure gas-phase studies and room-temperature sample work. The PEAK configuration pushes that to better than 0.06 cm⁻¹, useful for low-temperature crystalline semiconductor work or gas-phase measurements at reduced pressure. The VERTEX 80v goes a step further, evacuating the entire optics bench so atmospheric water vapour cannot mask weak spectral features, which is what makes nanoscience work down to below 10⁻³ monolayers possible.

products.overview: A thermal analyzer tells you a sample lost weight, and at what temperature. It doesn't tell you what left. TG-FTIR couples the two techniques together: thermogravimetric analysis quantifies the mass change, and FT-IR spectroscopy identifies the gases released, at the moment they're released. Three coupling methods connect the two systems, chosen for your flexibility, sensitivity, or setup requirements, and one of them, PERSEUS, links directly to the ALPHA II, with no transfer line at all.

faqs.question: What is TG-FTIR?
faqs.answer: TG-FTIR couples thermogravimetric analysis with FT-IR spectroscopy, so the mass change a sample undergoes and the identity of the gases it releases are measured together, also known as Hyphenated FT-IR or Evolved Gas Analysis.

faqs.question: Why can't thermal analysis alone identify the gases released?
faqs.answer: Thermogravimetric analysis measures mass change accurately, but it has no way to identify what left the sample. FT-IR spectroscopy adds that identification, since nearly every substance produces a characteristic infrared spectrum.

faqs.question: What are the three coupling modes?
faqs.answer: External coupling, using an external gas cell and transfer line for maximum FT-IR flexibility; internal coupling, using the FT-IR's own sample chamber; and PERSEUS, a direct connection with no transfer line, pairing the ALPHA II with a NETZSCH Thermoanalyzer.

faqs.question: What is PERSEUS?
faqs.answer: PERSEUS is a patented direct coupling between the compact ALPHA II FT-IR spectrometer and NETZSCH Thermoanalyzers, with no transfer line required.

faqs.question: Which detector should I choose for external coupling?
faqs.answer: A room-temperature DLaTGS detector suits routine sensitivity needs. A liquid-nitrogen-cooled MCT detector offers higher sensitivity for trace-level evolved gases.

faqs.question: What controls detection sensitivity in TG-FTIR?
faqs.answer: Sensitivity follows Beer's law: it depends on the cell's path length, the cell's volume, and the molecule's own absorptivity, which cannot be changed by the experimental setup.

faqs.question: Are there substances FT-IR cannot detect?
faqs.answer: Yes. Homonuclear diatomics and noble gases do not produce an infrared spectrum, since their vibration does not change the molecule's dipole moment.

faqs.question: What applications has TG-FTIR been used for?
faqs.answer: Documented studies include plasticizer analysis, aspirin decomposition, PUR powder coating identification, potassium acetate and HNF decomposition, and PVC cable coating failure analysis.

faqs.question: Does TG-FTIR include the thermal analyzer?
faqs.answer: No. TG-FTIR is a coupling technique; the thermal analyzer and the Bruker FT-IR spectrometer are separate components, and Inkarp confirms the right pairing for your work.

faqs.answer: The price depends on your thermal analyzer, the FT-IR spectrometer chosen, and the coupling mode required. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your configuration is confirmed.

sections.title: Coupling Modes and Detection Sensitivity
sections.tabSummary: Choosing External, Internal, or PERSEUS
body: Choosing a coupling mode is really choosing what you're prepared to trade for flexibility, sensitivity, or simplicity.

External coupling gives the most flexibility, since the FT-IR system stays free to run standalone measurements and switches to combined TG-FT-IR runs on command, with a detector choice of room-temperature DLaTGS or a more sensitive liquid-nitrogen-cooled MCT. Internal coupling uses the FT-IR's own sample chamber, and its sensitivity is governed directly by Beer's law: a longer cell path length passes more molecules at any given moment, while a smaller cell volume concentrates the same evolved gas more strongly, both raising the signal. PERSEUS removes the transfer line entirely, pairing the ALPHA II directly with a NETZSCH Thermoanalyzer.

faqs.question: What is the Hyperion FT-IR Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: Hyperion is a research-grade FT-IR microscope used for chemical imaging and mapping, combining FT-IR and QCL laser imaging in one instrument, across pharma, forensics, semiconductor, and materials research.

faqs.question: What makes Hyperion the first of its kind?
faqs.answer: It's the first instrument to combine FT-IR and Infrared Laser Imaging (QCL) technology in a single device, supporting both in transmission, reflection, and ATR modes.

faqs.question: How much faster is QCL imaging than standard FT-IR imaging?
faqs.answer: QCL imaging at a single wavenumber runs at 6.4 mm² per second, against 0.1 mm² per second for full-spectrum FT-IR imaging, more than 60 times faster, at the cost of narrower spectral information per image.

faqs.question: How do I decide between FT-IR and QCL imaging for my sample?
faqs.answer: Collect a full FT-IR spectrum first to identify the wavelengths that matter for your sample, then switch to QCL imaging at those specific wavelengths to generate a fast chemical image in seconds.

faqs.question: How do I choose between the LN2-cooled and TE-cooled MCT detector?
faqs.answer: Choose the LN2-cooled MCT for maximum sensitivity where liquid nitrogen is available, or the thermoelectrically cooled MCT when you need high spatial resolution and sensitivity without a cryogen supply.

faqs.question: What is spatial coherence reduction, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: It's a patented technology that removes fringe and speckle artifacts from laser-based IR imaging, addressing a physical effect that occurs specifically in QCL microscopy and not in classical FT-IR, solved in hardware without slowing down the measurement.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Hyperion and the LUMOS II?
faqs.answer: Hyperion gives the user full manual control over every measurement parameter, while the LUMOS II automates the measurement process for a more guided workflow. Bruker positions them as different philosophies, not different capability tiers.

faqs.question: What FPA detector resolutions are available?
faqs.answer: 64×64 or 128×128 pixel, for diffraction-limited FT-IR imaging.

faqs.question: Can Hyperion data be correlated with Raman data from the same sample?
faqs.answer: Yes, using Co-Local Measurement, which transfers the same region of interest between Hyperion, LUMOS II, and SENTERRA II for combined IR and Raman analysis.

sections.title: FT-IR and QCL Imaging Modes
sections.tabSummary: When to use full-spectrum FT-IR versus fast QCL imaging
body: The choice between FT-IR and QCL imaging isn't about which is better. It's about what the measurement actually needs.

Full-spectrum FT-IR imaging via the FPA detector gives complete spectral information at every pixel, at 0.1 mm² per second. QCL imaging trades that breadth for speed: once you know which wavelengths matter, ILIM images at a single wavenumber at 6.4 mm² per second, more than 60 times faster. The patented coherence reduction is what makes that laser-based speed usable at all, removing the fringe and speckle artifacts that would otherwise compromise the image.

longForm.heroHook: FT-IR and laser imaging. Combined, for the first time.
heroParagraphs: Most microscopes make you choose: full spectral information, or fast imaging speed. Not both.

The Hyperion FT-IR Microscope is the first instrument to combine FT-IR and Infrared Laser Imaging in a single device. Collect a full FT-IR spectrum, then switch to laser imaging at the wavelengths that matter, and build a chemical image in seconds.
A patented coherence reduction technology solves the artifact problem that normally plagues laser-based imaging, in hardware, without slowing anything down or costing sensitivity.

This is a precision tool, not an automated one. Where some FT-IR microscopes handle the experimental details for you, Hyperion remains under your control at every step, from detector choice to objective to measurement mode.

faqs.question: What is the LUMOS II FT-IR Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: LUMOS II is a stand-alone FT-IR and IR laser imaging microscope used for failure analysis, material research, and life science applications, across pharma, forensics, and environmental testing.

faqs.question: Does the LUMOS II need liquid nitrogen?
faqs.answer: No. TE-MCT is the standard detector, requiring no liquid nitrogen and no dry-air purge, though LN-cooled MCT is available as an option.

faqs.question: Is the LUMOS II suitable for beginners?
faqs.answer: Yes. The LUMOS II Wizard guides new users to correct results quickly, while experienced users retain full instrument control underneath.

faqs.question: How do I decide between single-point FT-IR, FPA, and ILIM imaging?
faqs.answer: Use single-point FT-IR for routine point measurements without cryogen requirements, FPA imaging for full-field chemical imaging at 1.6 mm² per second, and ILIM for the fastest possible imaging at a known wavelength, 4.5 mm² per second.

faqs.question: How do I image a round sample, like a filter, efficiently?
faqs.answer: Use FPA imaging with a circular measurement grid, which measures only the actual region of interest on round samples such as microplastic filters, saving significant time over a square grid.

faqs.question: Can I upgrade a single-point LUMOS II to FPA imaging later?
faqs.answer: Yes. The single-point FT-IR configuration is upgradeable to FPA imaging at any time, without replacing the instrument.

faqs.question: What is PermaSure+?
faqs.answer: PermaSure+ is Bruker's patented imaging calibration technology built into the LUMOS II for reliable, consistent imaging performance.

faqs.question: How large a sample can the LUMOS II accommodate?
faqs.answer: Up to 40 mm in height, with 270° access from three sides for straightforward sample placement.

faqs.question: Is the LUMOS II suitable for a regulated pharmaceutical environment?
faqs.answer: Yes. It's fully compliant with cGMP, GLP, FDA 21 CFR Part 11, and all major pharmacopeias, with automated OQ/PQ qualification testing.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the LUMOS II and the Hyperion?
faqs.answer: LUMOS II is faster at full-field FPA imaging and needs no cryogen, with guided, wizard-based operation. Hyperion is faster at single-wavelength ILIM imaging and gives the user complete manual control over every parameter.

faqs.question: What is the price of the LUMOS II FT-IR Microscope in India?
faqs.answer: The price depends on the detector and imaging configuration your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

faqs.question: Who is the authorized distributor of the LUMOS II FT-IR Microscope in India?
faqs.answer: Inkarp is the authorized distributor and service provider for the Bruker LUMOS II FT-IR Microscope in India, providing demonstration, installation, training, AMC, spare parts, and technical support.

sections.title: Three Imaging Modes, Compared
sections.tabSummary: Single-point, FPA, and ILIM, matched to your task
body: LUMOS II doesn't force a choice at purchase. It offers three genuinely different ways to image a sample, and the right one depends on the question you're asking.

Single-point FT-IR, with TE-MCT as standard, is the starting configuration and needs no cryogen supply at all. FPA imaging adds full-field chemical imaging at 1.6 mm² per second with 1.25 µm spatial resolution in ATR, fast enough to make routine imaging genuinely practical. ILIM laser imaging trades some of that flexibility for raw speed at a single wavenumber, 4.5 mm² per second across a 1,800 to 950 cm⁻¹ range, in transmission and reflection.

faqs.question: What is the ALPHA II Compact FT-IR Spectrometer used for?
faqs.answer: The ALPHA II identifies, quantifies, and verifies materials, from raw ingredients to finished products, across applications including polymers, pharmaceuticals, food, environmental testing, and forensic drug analysis.

faqs.question: How long does a measurement take?
faqs.answer: Bruker states that a full workflow, from selection to result, takes under a minute using OPUS TOUCH.

faqs.question: Is the ALPHA II suitable for a regulated laboratory?
faqs.answer: Yes. It offers full 21 CFR Part 11 compliance, follows the ALCOA+ principle, and includes secure user profiles with complete audit trails. Bruker also offers an ISO 17025 support package for laboratories pursuing accreditation.

faqs.question: Does the ALPHA II require extensive operator training?
faqs.answer: No. Guided workflows and built-in tutorial videos are designed to let a new operator work independently after a short introduction.

faqs.question: What is OPUS TOUCH?
faqs.answer: OPUS TOUCH is the ALPHA II's touch-screen software interface. It guides users through method selection, measurement, and report generation.

faqs.question: Can the ALPHA II monitor a chemical reaction in real time?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the optional INSITU-ATR module, which tracks reaction progress, intermediates, and endpoints directly in the reaction vessel using a diamond crystal probe.

faqs.question: Can the ALPHA II analyze soil samples?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the dedicated Soil Analyzer configuration, which reports organic carbon, texture, pH, carbonates, and other parameters from a single measurement.

faqs.question: What is included with the ALPHA II?

faqs.question: What is the MOBILE-IR II FT-IR Spectrometer used for?
faqs.answer: The MOBILE-IR II is a portable FT-IR spectrometer used for field identification of materials, including forensic drug testing, customs screening, warehouse quality control, and polymer sorting.

faqs.question: How is this different from a benchtop FT-IR spectrometer?
faqs.answer: It's built to work off-grid and in harsh environments, with IP65 enclosure protection and an IP67 carry case, while its TE-MCT detector halves measurement time and doubles signal-to-noise ratio compared to a standard DTGS detector.

faqs.question: Does portability mean a compromise in performance?
faqs.answer: No. Bruker states the TE-MCT detector outperforms a standard DTGS detector on both speed and signal-to-noise ratio, so field use doesn't come at the cost of measurement quality.

faqs.question: How much training does an operator need?
faqs.answer: OPUS TOUCH is stated to require about 10 minutes of training to operate.

faqs.question: How does the MOBILE-IR II connect to other systems?
faqs.answer: Through Wi-Fi, Ethernet, cloud, or USB, with data transfer to LIMS or MES systems via MS SQL.

faqs.question: What sampling accessory does it use?
faqs.answer: A heatable diamond ATR crystal with a sample trough, for rapid liquid evaporation and temperature experiments. A non-heatable flat ATR plate is also available for larger flat samples.

faqs.question: Does it run without mains power?
faqs.answer: Yes. An internal high-capacity battery powers off-grid and in-field operation, with a charge indicator at 100, 75, 50, and 25 percent.

faqs.question: Is the MOBILE-IR II suitable for regulated laboratory use?
faqs.answer: Bruker's documentation for this solution does not state 21 CFR Part 11 or ISO 17025 compliance. For a regulated lab environment, the benchtop ALPHA II is built around that requirement.

body: The detector is what separates a field spectrometer that merely survives outdoors from one that performs there.

A standard DTGS detector works, but it's slower and less sensitive than it needs to be once external conditions start interfering, which is exactly what a warehouse floor or a construction site does. The TE-MCT detector in the MOBILE-IR II is cooled thermoelectrically rather than with liquid nitrogen, and Bruker states it halves measurement time and doubles signal-to-noise ratio against a standard DTGS detector, with the added benefit of greater spectral stability against those external influences.

sections.title: Reflection and Transmission Measurement
sections.tabSummary: Choosing solid or liquid configuration
body: The right TANGO II configuration comes down to one question: is your sample solid or liquid?

Reflection is built for solids and semi-solids. A gold-coated integrating sphere captures diffuse reflection, and sample rotators enlarge the effective measurement area, which matters for a heterogeneous sample where one 10 mm spot wouldn't represent the whole. Transmission is built for liquids, with a heater and cooler built in as standard, holding the sample between +20°C and +80°C while a dedicated sensor tracks vial temperature continuously.

faqs.question: What is the MPA III FT-NIR Spectrometer used for?
faqs.answer: The MPA III is a modular FT-NIR solution used for both sophisticated calibration method development and routine QA/QC, across food, pharmaceutical, chemical, and polymer industries.

faqs.question: What sampling modules does the MPA III support?
faqs.answer: Four: a Sample Compartment for liquids, an Integrating Sphere for solids and semi-solids, Fiber Optic Probes for measuring directly in containers, and an External Transmission Unit for automated vial or tablet analysis.

faqs.question: Can I try different sampling methods before committing to one?
faqs.answer: Yes. The modular design is built for exactly this, since the best sampling method often isn't obvious until you've tested it on your actual sample.

faqs.question: What is the warranty on the MPA III?
faqs.answer: 10 years on the interferometer's moving parts and the solid-state laser.

faqs.question: Is the MPA III suitable for a regulated pharmaceutical environment?
faqs.answer: Yes. OPUS software offers GMP and 21 CFR Part 11 compliance in validated mode, with a complete audit trail and the OPUS Validation Program covering OQ and PQ protocols to USP, JP, and Ph. Eur. guidelines.

faqs.question: Can the MPA III be used outside the lab?
faqs.answer: Yes. Its robustness supports use on the factory floor, and it can be mounted on a utility cart for mobile applications.

faqs.question: What software is available for the MPA III?
faqs.answer: OPUS/LAB for routine analysis, OPUS/IDENT for raw material identification, OPUS/CONFO for conformity checking, OPUS/QUANT2 for multivariate calibration development, and ONET for managing a network of solutions remotely.

faqs.question: Does the MPA III require trained operators?
faqs.answer: No. Customizable workspaces and guided measurement modes in OPUS are designed so untrained personnel can operate the solution from day one.

faqs.question: How is the instrument monitored for accuracy?
faqs.answer: An online diagnostic system continuously monitors all optical components and notifies the user immediately if anything falls out of specification.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the MPA III and TANGO II?
faqs.answer: The MPA III offers four interchangeable sampling modules and a full software suite for method development, while the TANGO II is a simpler, fixed-configuration analyzer built for fast, routine measurement with minimal setup.

faqs.answer: The price depends on the sampling modules and software packages your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

body: The right sampling method depends on the sample and where it sits, and the MPA III is built so you don't have to guess correctly the first time.

Liquids in cuvettes or disposable vials go through the Sample Compartment, with an optional heater and automated background capability. Solids and semi-solids go through the Integrating Sphere by diffuse reflection, with a sample rotator improving reproducibility on heterogeneous material. Samples that can't come to the instrument, like material sitting in a warehouse, are measured directly through Fiber Optic Probes, with two probes running at once for solids and liquids together. Tablets or vials needing automated, repeatable transmission measurements run through the External Transmission Unit with its optional sample wheel.

sections.title: Fluorescence Mitigation and Laser Safety
sections.tabSummary: How SSE and DuoLaser work together
body: Fluorescence is the reason a lot of raw materials never get measured with handheld Raman at all. It swamps the much weaker Raman signal, and most handheld systems have no way around it.

SSE addresses this directly. By shifting the laser's temperature in controlled steps, it separates the fluorescence background from the genuine Raman signal, recovering a usable spectrum from materials that would otherwise be unreadable. DuoLaser's two excitation wavelengths, 785 nm and 852 nm, extend that sensitivity across a broader spectral range than a single-wavelength system reaches. And because BRAVO holds Laser Class 1 in every mode, none of that performance comes with a safety trade-off.

faqs.question: What is the SENTERRA II Raman Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: The SENTERRA II is a confocal Raman microscope used for failure analysis, quality control, and scientific research, across pharmaceuticals, forensics, polymers, and environmental testing.

faqs.question: What is SureCal, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: SureCal is a patented technology that continuously recalibrates the SENTERRA II in the background, holding sub-wavenumber precision without a manual recalibration step interrupting analysis.

faqs.question: How many lasers does the SENTERRA II support?
faqs.answer: Bruker's own materials state one-click switching between 4 built-in lasers as a technical feature, and separately reference up to 3 excitation lasers for material science applications. Inkarp confirms the exact configuration for your application.

faqs.question: Is the SENTERRA II safe for students or first-time operators?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Class 1 laser housing with interlock protects the user from harmful laser radiation at all times, without requiring laser safety training.

faqs.question: Can the SENTERRA II identify unknown substances automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes, using A.I.D., an AI-driven tool that matches spectral data against reference databases in seconds, for pure substances or complex mixtures.

faqs.question: How do I identify an unknown chemical sample step by step with the SENTERRA II?
faqs.answer: Select a built-in laser with one click, place the sample under the microscope, and start the measurement. A.I.D. then runs the identification automatically against reference spectral databases, returning a match with diagnostics and hit-quality graphs in seconds.

faqs.question: Can it generate a chemical image without selecting a Raman peak first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Adaptive K-means Clustering sorts spectra into groups automatically and builds the chemical image on its own.

faqs.question: How do I generate a chemical image of a mixed or heterogeneous sample using the SENTERRA II?
faqs.answer: Run Adaptive K-means Clustering after the measurement, without selecting a specific Raman peak first. The software sorts the spectra into groups automatically and builds the chemical image on its own, showing at a glance whether the sample is homogeneous or structured.

faqs.question: Can the SENTERRA II be configured for live cell or tissue research?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the inverted microscope configuration, which gives open sample access without compromising functionality.

faqs.question: Is the SENTERRA II suitable for a regulated pharmaceutical environment?
faqs.answer: Yes. It's 100% compliant with GMP, major pharmacopoeias, and 21 CFR Part 11, and follows the ALCOA+ principle for data integrity.

faqs.question: Can Raman and infrared data be correlated from the same sample spot?
faqs.answer: Yes, using Co-Local Measurement, which transfers overview images and measurement areas between SENTERRA II, LUMOS II, and HYPERION II.

sections.title: Continuous Calibration and Laser Safety
sections.tabSummary: How SureCal and Class 1 safety work together
body: Every Raman microscope drifts. Heat, component wear, and vibration all shift wavenumber accuracy over time, and most systems handle that with a scheduled recalibration routine that takes the instrument offline.

SureCal removes that step entirely, recalibrating continuously in the background so precision holds without a pause in analysis. That matters whether you're running a quick material identification or collecting a large dataset for PCA or other statistical work, where consistency across hundreds of measurements is the whole point. Laser safety runs on the same always-on principle: the Class 1 housing and interlock protect the user in every operating mode, which is what makes SENTERRA II usable by students and first-time operators without a separate safety program.
