faqs.question: What is the RAMANwalk Raman Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: The RAMANwalk is a confocal Raman microscope used for fast Raman imaging and targeted material identification, across battery research, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, and food quality control.

faqs.question: What is random-walk imaging?
faqs.answer: Random-walk imaging is a search algorithm that finds and follows the Raman signal directly, rather than scanning a sample in a fixed pattern regardless of what's present.

faqs.question: How much faster is RAMANwalk than a conventional Raman microscope?
faqs.answer: More than 5 times faster for obtaining Raman images, and on a targeted question like contamination detection, RAMANwalk can reach a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes where a conventional raster scan is only 10% complete in the same time.

faqs.question: How do I get a fast preview of an unknown sample with the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: Start the random-walk scan and watch the preview build: rough detail appears within seconds to a minute, finer detail within a few minutes, letting you decide whether the sample is worth a full-resolution scan before committing to the full run time.

faqs.question: How do I check a sample for a specific contaminant quickly with the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: Run the random-walk search targeted at the contaminant's Raman signature rather than a full scan. On a comparable real sample, this reached a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes, versus roughly 50 minutes for a complete image.

faqs.question: Can RAMANwalk find signal in low-contrast samples?
faqs.answer: Yes. It locates regions of interest using chemical Raman information, even when the sample gives no useful visual contrast.

faqs.question: What is the spatial resolution of the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: 350 nm in X and Y, and 1 µm in Z.

faqs.question: How many objective lenses does the RAMANwalk offer?
faqs.answer: Five: 5x, 10x, 20x, 50x, and 100x, covering broad overview imaging through fine sub-micron detail.

faqs.question: Does the RAMANwalk need manual calibration?
faqs.answer: No. It auto-calibrates against a standard lamp and sample, and auto-aligns its own optical path.

faqs.question: Is the RAMANwalk safe to use without laser safety training?
faqs.answer: Yes. It has a Class I laser safety housing with an interlocked door, protecting the user at all times.

faqs.answer: The price depends on the objective and grating configuration your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

sections.title: Random Walk Imaging and Scan Speed
sections.tabSummary: How the algorithm finds an answer faster than a scan
body: A conventional Raman microscope treats every point in a sample as equally worth visiting. RAMANwalk doesn't.

The random-walk algorithm finds a distinctive Raman signal, searches the surrounding area for more of it, and moves rapidly elsewhere once the signal runs out. It's a fundamentally different search strategy, not just a faster version of the old one, and it's why RAMANwalk delivers a rough preview in under a minute and finer detail within a few minutes, well before a full scan would even be close to done. On a real contamination question, that difference is the whole point: a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes, against a traditional raster scan that's only 10% complete in the same time, with nothing found yet.

It's dusty, it swings in temperature, and it's often somewhere the safety rules don't let a standard analyzer sit at all. MATRIX-F II solves that with distance: the spectrometer sits in a protected analysis house, and an industry-hardened fiber optic probe reaches into the process itself, with no measurement delay. Ten years of warranty cover the interferometer and the solid-state laser, and Bruker states thousands of these are already installed across chemical, pharmaceutical, and food manufacturing.

sections.eyebrow: Fiber Optic Probes and Contactless Measurement
sections.title: Fiber Optic Probes and Contactless Measurement
sections.tabSummary: Choosing probes, heads, or both
body: Choosing between contact and contactless measurement, or using both, comes down to what your process point actually allows.

Fiber optic probes go into the process directly, as diffuse reflectance, transflectance, or transmission probes, in materials like stainless steel or Hastelloy, or as flow cells for pilot plant assemblies. Contactless heads use tungsten illumination to measure from a distance, with the scattered light carried back to the spectrometer by fiber, useful where physical contact with the process isn't practical or safe. The duplex variant runs both at once, so a single instrument covers a reactor immersion probe and a remote conveyor head simultaneously.

A pipeline needing a flow cell
Fiber optic probe, process flow cell
A conveyor belt or moving web

Up to 6 contactless heads on one spectrometer

longForm.heroHook: The spectrometer stays safe. The probe goes where the process is.
heroParagraphs: A reactor, a pipeline, or a conveyor belt isn't a place for a delicate instrument. It's dusty, it swings in temperature, and it's often somewhere the safety rules don't let a standard analyzer sit at all.
MATRIX-F II solves that with distance. The spectrometer sits in an analysis house, and an industry-hardened fiber optic probe reaches into the process itself, with no measurement delay.

It's the only FT-NIR spectrometer that measures both in contact and contactless with one instrument. Fiber optic probes handle direct immersion measurements; fiber-coupled heads with tungsten sources handle contactless measurement from a distance, up to six connected at once.
Ten years of warranty cover the interferometer and the solid-state laser. Bruker states thousands of these are already installed across chemical, pharmaceutical, and food manufacturing.

faqs.question: What is the MATRIX-MF FT-IR Process Reaction Monitoring solution used for?
faqs.answer: MATRIX-MF monitors chemical and biological reactions in real time, using a direct-contact diamond ATR probe placed in the reaction itself, in the lab or on a process line.

faqs.question: How is MATRIX-MF different from MATRIX-F II?
faqs.answer: MATRIX-MF works the mid-IR region using direct-contact ATR probes, while MATRIX-F II works the near-IR region using fiber optic probes and contactless heads. They suit different measurement needs and are sometimes used together.

faqs.question: How do I choose the right ATR probe for my reaction?
faqs.answer: Match the probe diameter to your vessel scale: IN351 (3.17 mm) for micro-scale reactions, IN355 (6.3 mm) for standard lab vessels, or IN350-T (6 mm) and IN356-EX (12 mm) where ATEX hazardous-area compliance is required.

faqs.question: How do I monitor several reactions at once with MATRIX-MF?
faqs.answer: Connect up to six probes to the built-in automated multiplexer, allowing one instrument to monitor up to six reactions simultaneously.

faqs.question: Can MATRIX-MF be used in a hazardous, ATEX-classified area?
faqs.answer: Yes, either using the IN350-T or IN356-EX ATEX-rated probes, or the fully certified MATRIX-MF exproof variant.

faqs.question: Can MATRIX-MF monitor biological reactions, not just chemical ones?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mid-IR ATR sampling suits biological process monitoring as well as chemical reaction monitoring.

faqs.question: How quickly can probes be swapped on the MATRIX-MF?
faqs.answer: Bruker's proprietary BQC quick-connector design allows fast probe exchange in seconds, without compromising measurement reproducibility.

faqs.question: Can MATRIX-MF move between the lab and the production line?
faqs.answer: Yes. Its small footprint works as a standalone lab system, or mounts in a standard 19-inch rack for process installation.

faqs.question: How is MATRIX-MF validated for regulated use?
faqs.answer: The OPUS Validation Program runs automated performance tests through a built-in filter wheel, tracking hardware and consumable status continuously.

faqs.question: What is the price of the MATRIX-MF FT-IR Process Reaction Monitoring solution in India?
faqs.answer: The price depends on the probe selection, multiplexer configuration, and hazard rating your installation needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

products.overview: Most single-point NIR analyzers give up something to fit on a process line. BEAM doesn't. It's the first dedicated single-point spectrometer to carry full FT-NIR power, mounted directly on a pipeline, a hopper, or over a conveyor belt, monitoring solid and semi-solid material as it moves. It scans at more than 250 times a minute, fast enough to catch process variation as it happens, not after the batch is done. From incoming goods to final product inspection, one instrument covers the whole production chain, tightening control and cutting the waste and rework that come from specs missed too late.

faqs.question: What is the OMEGA 5 FT-IR Gas Analyzer used for?
faqs.answer: OMEGA 5 monitors gas concentrations in real time, quantifying over 350 compounds without calibration, across industrial process monitoring, environmental analysis, and trace impurity detection.

faqs.question: How does calibration-free quantification actually work?
faqs.answer: OPUS GA software continuously records the gas's pressure and temperature during analysis and corrects for both in real time, which is what allows accurate quantification without a calibration curve.

faqs.question: How do I decide between standard and high-resolution configuration?
faqs.answer: Choose standard resolution, better than 2 cm⁻¹, for gas mixtures with clearly separated IR signals, and the high-resolution option, better than 1 cm⁻¹, when your mixture has significant signal overlap that needs to be resolved.

faqs.question: How do I decide if I need the high-pressure option?
faqs.answer: Choose the high-pressure option, up to 15 bar absolute, when you're detecting trace impurities or measuring gas directly at elevated industrial process pressure rather than after depressurizing it.

faqs.question: What is the H2O detection limit on the OMEGA 5?
faqs.answer: As low as 10 ppm, achieved through a sealed, purgeable optics compartment that stabilizes background H2O and CO2 levels.

faqs.question: Does the OMEGA 5 need liquid nitrogen?
faqs.answer: No. The TE-MCT detector runs continuously without a cryogen requirement.

faqs.question: What is DryPath, and when should I use it?
faqs.answer: DryPath is an optional feature that eliminates the need for external purge gas, which is worth adding wherever purge gas supply is inconvenient or unavailable, including mobile applications.

faqs.question: Can the OMEGA 5 be used for mobile gas analysis?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the DryPath option, which removes the external purge gas requirement that would otherwise limit it to fixed installations.

faqs.question: How long is the gas cell, and can it be heated?
faqs.answer: The multi-reflection gas cell is 5 meters, heatable up to 191°C.

faqs.question: What is the price of the OMEGA 5 FT-IR Gas Analyzer in India?
faqs.answer: The price depends on the resolution, pressure, and DryPath options your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your gas mixture and operating conditions are confirmed.

faqs.question: What is the INVENIO FT-IR Research Spectrometer used for?
faqs.answer: The INVENIO is a modular research-grade FT-IR platform, used across pharmaceutical R&D, polymer science, chemistry, materials research, and semiconductor development.

faqs.question: What makes the INVENIO different from a routine FT-IR spectrometer?
faqs.answer: Every core feature can be upgraded in the field at any time, and the solution supports up to seven software-controlled detectors, covering the full spectral range from 28,000 to 15 cm⁻¹ in a single automated measurement.

faqs.question: What is the spectral resolution of the INVENIO?
faqs.answer: Below 0.085 cm⁻¹, suited to research requiring fine spectral detail.

faqs.question: Can the INVENIO run two experiments at once?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Transit channel is an independent second measurement channel with its own detector, running alongside the main sample compartment.

faqs.question: Can the INVENIO be upgraded after purchase?
faqs.answer: Yes. All core features can be added or changed in the field at any time, as research requirements evolve.

faqs.question: What extensions are available for the INVENIO?
faqs.answer: FT-IR microscopy with HYPERION II, FT-Raman with RAM II, thermogravimetric coupling, high-throughput screening with HTS-XT, and EMILIE for picogram-level nanomaterial analysis.

faqs.question: Is the INVENIO suitable for regulated pharmaceutical work?
faqs.answer: Yes. OPUS software complies with major pharmacopeia requirements and 21 CFR Part 11, with secure data handling for data integrity.

faqs.question: What is EMILIE?
faqs.answer: EMILIE is a nanomechanical infrared analyzer that integrates with the INVENIO for picogram-level sensitivity on nanomaterials, aerosols, and trace-level samples, without cryogenic cooling.

faqs.question: What is time-resolved spectroscopy used for on the INVENIO?
faqs.answer: It supports kinetics studies and reaction monitoring down to the nanosecond timescale, useful for researching catalysts and batteries under real-world conditions.

body: The INVENIO isn't sized for one job. It's sized for whichever job you bring to it, and reconfigured when the next one is different.

Detector capacity is built in layers: the DigiTect slot for a detector of choice, such as an LN2-cooled option, the MultiTect unit adding up to five more room-temperature or thermostabilized detectors, and the Transit channel's own independent detector for a second experimental setup. Together, that's up to seven software-controlled detectors on one solution. Pair the MultiTect with the upgraded INTEGRAL interferometer, and the full spectral range, 28,000 down to 15 cm⁻¹, runs as a single automated measurement.

faqs.answer: The VERTEX 80v adds an evacuated optics bench, removing atmospheric moisture from the beam path. This enables high-resolution work, ultra-fast rapidscan, step-scan, and UV-range measurements that the standard purge-optics VERTEX 80 doesn't reach.

faqs.question: What resolution can the VERTEX 80/80v achieve?
faqs.answer: Standard configuration reaches better than 0.2 cm⁻¹. The PEAK configuration reaches better than 0.06 cm⁻¹, which Bruker states is the highest resolution achieved on a commercial benchtop FT-IR spectrometer.

faqs.question: What spectral range does it cover?
faqs.answer: From 50,000 cm⁻¹ in the UV/VIS region down to 5 cm⁻¹ in the far IR and terahertz range, the broadest range in Bruker's benchtop FT-IR line.

faqs.question: Can external light sources and accessories be connected?
faqs.answer: Yes. Five exit ports and two input ports allow simultaneous connection of accessories such as synchrotron sources, bolometers, FT-IR microscopes, and Raman modules.

faqs.question: Can beamsplitters be changed without opening the instrument?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the VERTEX 80v. The BMS-c option remotely exchanges up to four beamsplitter types automatically, under vacuum, without venting the optics bench.

faqs.question: Is the VERTEX 80/80v suitable for nanoscience research?
faqs.answer: Yes. The evacuated VERTEX 80v reaches sensitivity below 10⁻³ monolayers, suited to demanding surface and nanomaterial studies.

faqs.question: Can it be used for terahertz spectroscopy?
faqs.answer: Yes. A broadband far IR/THz beamsplitter covers approximately 900 down to 5 cm⁻¹ in a single measurement, and an external Hg-arc source with a room-temperature DTGS detector makes the terahertz range accessible.

faqs.question: What is EMILIE, and does it work with this solution?
faqs.answer: EMILIE is a nanomechanical infrared analyzer that adds picogram-level sensitivity for nanomaterials and trace-level samples, without cryogenic cooling. It's compatible with the VERTEX 80/80v.

faqs.question: What is TG-FTIR?
faqs.answer: TG-FTIR couples thermogravimetric analysis with FT-IR spectroscopy, so the mass change a sample undergoes and the identity of the gases it releases are measured together, also known as Hyphenated FT-IR or Evolved Gas Analysis.

faqs.question: Why can't thermal analysis alone identify the gases released?
faqs.answer: Thermogravimetric analysis measures mass change accurately, but it has no way to identify what left the sample. FT-IR spectroscopy adds that identification, since nearly every substance produces a characteristic infrared spectrum.

faqs.question: What are the three coupling modes?
faqs.answer: External coupling, using an external gas cell and transfer line for maximum FT-IR flexibility; internal coupling, using the FT-IR's own sample chamber; and PERSEUS, a direct connection with no transfer line, pairing the ALPHA II with a NETZSCH Thermoanalyzer.

faqs.question: What is PERSEUS?
faqs.answer: PERSEUS is a patented direct coupling between the compact ALPHA II FT-IR spectrometer and NETZSCH Thermoanalyzers, with no transfer line required.

faqs.question: Which detector should I choose for external coupling?
faqs.answer: A room-temperature DLaTGS detector suits routine sensitivity needs. A liquid-nitrogen-cooled MCT detector offers higher sensitivity for trace-level evolved gases.

faqs.question: What controls detection sensitivity in TG-FTIR?
faqs.answer: Sensitivity follows Beer's law: it depends on the cell's path length, the cell's volume, and the molecule's own absorptivity, which cannot be changed by the experimental setup.

faqs.question: Are there substances FT-IR cannot detect?
faqs.answer: Yes. Homonuclear diatomics and noble gases do not produce an infrared spectrum, since their vibration does not change the molecule's dipole moment.

faqs.question: What applications has TG-FTIR been used for?
faqs.answer: Documented studies include plasticizer analysis, aspirin decomposition, PUR powder coating identification, potassium acetate and HNF decomposition, and PVC cable coating failure analysis.

faqs.question: Does TG-FTIR include the thermal analyzer?
faqs.answer: No. TG-FTIR is a coupling technique; the thermal analyzer and the Bruker FT-IR spectrometer are separate components, and Inkarp confirms the right pairing for your work.

sections.title: Coupling Modes and Detection Sensitivity
sections.tabSummary: Choosing External, Internal, or PERSEUS
body: Choosing a coupling mode is really choosing what you're prepared to trade for flexibility, sensitivity, or simplicity.

External coupling gives the most flexibility, since the FT-IR system stays free to run standalone measurements and switches to combined TG-FT-IR runs on command, with a detector choice of room-temperature DLaTGS or a more sensitive liquid-nitrogen-cooled MCT. Internal coupling uses the FT-IR's own sample chamber, and its sensitivity is governed directly by Beer's law: a longer cell path length passes more molecules at any given moment, while a smaller cell volume concentrates the same evolved gas more strongly, both raising the signal. PERSEUS removes the transfer line entirely, pairing the ALPHA II directly with a NETZSCH Thermoanalyzer.

longForm.heroHook: Thermogravimetric analysis shows the mass loss. FT-IR identifies what came off.
heroParagraphs: A thermal analyzer tells you a sample lost weight, and at what temperature. It doesn't tell you what left.
TG-FTIR couples the two techniques together. Thermogravimetric analysis quantifies the mass change. FT-IR spectroscopy identifies the gases released, at the moment they're released.
Every substance except homonuclear diatomics and noble gases gives a characteristic infrared spectrum. That's what makes the identification possible.
Three coupling methods connect the two systems, chosen for your flexibility, sensitivity, or setup requirements. One of them, PERSEUS, links directly to the ALPHA II, with no transfer line at all.

faqs.question: What is the Hyperion FT-IR Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: Hyperion is a research-grade FT-IR microscope used for chemical imaging and mapping, combining FT-IR and QCL laser imaging in one instrument, across pharma, forensics, semiconductor, and materials research.

faqs.question: What makes Hyperion the first of its kind?
faqs.answer: It's the first instrument to combine FT-IR and Infrared Laser Imaging (QCL) technology in a single device, supporting both in transmission, reflection, and ATR modes.

faqs.question: How much faster is QCL imaging than standard FT-IR imaging?
faqs.answer: QCL imaging at a single wavenumber runs at 6.4 mm² per second, against 0.1 mm² per second for full-spectrum FT-IR imaging, more than 60 times faster, at the cost of narrower spectral information per image.

faqs.question: How do I decide between FT-IR and QCL imaging for my sample?
faqs.answer: Collect a full FT-IR spectrum first to identify the wavelengths that matter for your sample, then switch to QCL imaging at those specific wavelengths to generate a fast chemical image in seconds.

faqs.question: How do I choose between the LN2-cooled and TE-cooled MCT detector?
faqs.answer: Choose the LN2-cooled MCT for maximum sensitivity where liquid nitrogen is available, or the thermoelectrically cooled MCT when you need high spatial resolution and sensitivity without a cryogen supply.

faqs.question: What is spatial coherence reduction, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: It's a patented technology that removes fringe and speckle artifacts from laser-based IR imaging, addressing a physical effect that occurs specifically in QCL microscopy and not in classical FT-IR, solved in hardware without slowing down the measurement.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Hyperion and the LUMOS II?
faqs.answer: Hyperion gives the user full manual control over every measurement parameter, while the LUMOS II automates the measurement process for a more guided workflow. Bruker positions them as different philosophies, not different capability tiers.

faqs.question: What FPA detector resolutions are available?
faqs.answer: 64×64 or 128×128 pixel, for diffraction-limited FT-IR imaging.

faqs.question: Can Hyperion data be correlated with Raman data from the same sample?
faqs.answer: Yes, using Co-Local Measurement, which transfers the same region of interest between Hyperion, LUMOS II, and SENTERRA II for combined IR and Raman analysis.

faqs.answer: The price depends on the detector, objective, and QCL module configuration your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

sections.tabSummary: When to use full-spectrum FT-IR versus fast QCL imaging
body: The choice between FT-IR and QCL imaging isn't about which is better. It's about what the measurement actually needs.

Full-spectrum FT-IR imaging via the FPA detector gives complete spectral information at every pixel, at 0.1 mm² per second. QCL imaging trades that breadth for speed: once you know which wavelengths matter, ILIM images at a single wavenumber at 6.4 mm² per second, more than 60 times faster. The patented coherence reduction is what makes that laser-based speed usable at all, removing the fringe and speckle artifacts that would otherwise compromise the image.

faqs.question: What is the LUMOS II FT-IR Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: LUMOS II is a stand-alone FT-IR and IR laser imaging microscope used for failure analysis, material research, and life science applications, across pharma, forensics, and environmental testing.

faqs.question: Does the LUMOS II need liquid nitrogen?
faqs.answer: No. TE-MCT is the standard detector, requiring no liquid nitrogen and no dry-air purge, though LN-cooled MCT is available as an option.

faqs.question: Is the LUMOS II suitable for beginners?
faqs.answer: Yes. The LUMOS II Wizard guides new users to correct results quickly, while experienced users retain full instrument control underneath.

faqs.question: How do I decide between single-point FT-IR, FPA, and ILIM imaging?
faqs.answer: Use single-point FT-IR for routine point measurements without cryogen requirements, FPA imaging for full-field chemical imaging at 1.6 mm² per second, and ILIM for the fastest possible imaging at a known wavelength, 4.5 mm² per second.

faqs.question: How do I image a round sample, like a filter, efficiently?
faqs.answer: Use FPA imaging with a circular measurement grid, which measures only the actual region of interest on round samples such as microplastic filters, saving significant time over a square grid.

faqs.question: Can I upgrade a single-point LUMOS II to FPA imaging later?
faqs.answer: Yes. The single-point FT-IR configuration is upgradeable to FPA imaging at any time, without replacing the instrument.

faqs.question: What is PermaSure+?
faqs.answer: PermaSure+ is Bruker's patented imaging calibration technology built into the LUMOS II for reliable, consistent imaging performance.

faqs.question: How large a sample can the LUMOS II accommodate?
faqs.answer: Up to 40 mm in height, with 270° access from three sides for straightforward sample placement.

faqs.question: Is the LUMOS II suitable for a regulated pharmaceutical environment?
faqs.answer: Yes. It's fully compliant with cGMP, GLP, FDA 21 CFR Part 11, and all major pharmacopeias, with automated OQ/PQ qualification testing.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the LUMOS II and the Hyperion?
faqs.answer: LUMOS II is faster at full-field FPA imaging and needs no cryogen, with guided, wizard-based operation. Hyperion is faster at single-wavelength ILIM imaging and gives the user complete manual control over every parameter.

faqs.question: What is the price of the LUMOS II FT-IR Microscope in India?
faqs.answer: The price depends on the detector and imaging configuration your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

faqs.question: Who is the authorized distributor of the LUMOS II FT-IR Microscope in India?
faqs.answer: Inkarp is the authorized distributor and service provider for the Bruker LUMOS II FT-IR Microscope in India, providing demonstration, installation, training, AMC, spare parts, and technical support.

body: LUMOS II doesn't force a choice at purchase. It offers three genuinely different ways to image a sample, and the right one depends on the question you're asking.

Single-point FT-IR, with TE-MCT as standard, is the starting configuration and needs no cryogen supply at all. FPA imaging adds full-field chemical imaging at 1.6 mm² per second with 1.25 µm spatial resolution in ATR, fast enough to make routine imaging genuinely practical. ILIM laser imaging trades some of that flexibility for raw speed at a single wavenumber, 4.5 mm² per second across a 1,800 to 950 cm⁻¹ range, in transmission and reflection.

faqs.question: What is the MOBILE-IR II FT-IR Spectrometer used for?
faqs.answer: The MOBILE-IR II is a portable FT-IR spectrometer used for field identification of materials, including forensic drug testing, customs screening, warehouse quality control, and polymer sorting.

faqs.question: How is this different from a benchtop FT-IR spectrometer?
faqs.answer: It's built to work off-grid and in harsh environments, with IP65 enclosure protection and an IP67 carry case, while its TE-MCT detector halves measurement time and doubles signal-to-noise ratio compared to a standard DTGS detector.

faqs.question: Does portability mean a compromise in performance?
faqs.answer: No. Bruker states the TE-MCT detector outperforms a standard DTGS detector on both speed and signal-to-noise ratio, so field use doesn't come at the cost of measurement quality.

faqs.question: How much training does an operator need?
faqs.answer: OPUS TOUCH is stated to require about 10 minutes of training to operate.

faqs.question: How does the MOBILE-IR II connect to other systems?
faqs.answer: Through Wi-Fi, Ethernet, cloud, or USB, with data transfer to LIMS or MES systems via MS SQL.

faqs.question: What sampling accessory does it use?
faqs.answer: A heatable diamond ATR crystal with a sample trough, for rapid liquid evaporation and temperature experiments. A non-heatable flat ATR plate is also available for larger flat samples.

faqs.question: Does it run without mains power?
faqs.answer: Yes. An internal high-capacity battery powers off-grid and in-field operation, with a charge indicator at 100, 75, 50, and 25 percent.

faqs.question: Is the MOBILE-IR II suitable for regulated laboratory use?
faqs.answer: Bruker's documentation for this solution does not state 21 CFR Part 11 or ISO 17025 compliance. For a regulated lab environment, the benchtop ALPHA II is built around that requirement.

sections.title: Field Performance and Detector Advantage
sections.tabSummary: What the TE-MCT detector actually buys you
body: The detector is what separates a field spectrometer that merely survives outdoors from one that performs there.

A standard DTGS detector works, but it's slower and less sensitive than it needs to be once external conditions start interfering, which is exactly what a warehouse floor or a construction site does. The TE-MCT detector in the MOBILE-IR II is cooled thermoelectrically rather than with liquid nitrogen, and Bruker states it halves measurement time and doubles signal-to-noise ratio against a standard DTGS detector, with the added benefit of greater spectral stability against those external influences.

sections.tabSummary: Choosing solid or liquid configuration
body: The right TANGO II configuration comes down to one question: is your sample solid or liquid?

Reflection is built for solids and semi-solids. A gold-coated integrating sphere captures diffuse reflection, and sample rotators enlarge the effective measurement area, which matters for a heterogeneous sample where one 10 mm spot wouldn't represent the whole. Transmission is built for liquids, with a heater and cooler built in as standard, holding the sample between +20°C and +80°C while a dedicated sensor tracks vial temperature continuously.

faqs.question: What is the MPA III FT-NIR Spectrometer used for?
faqs.answer: The MPA III is a modular FT-NIR solution used for both sophisticated calibration method development and routine QA/QC, across food, pharmaceutical, chemical, and polymer industries.

faqs.question: What sampling modules does the MPA III support?
faqs.answer: Four: a Sample Compartment for liquids, an Integrating Sphere for solids and semi-solids, Fiber Optic Probes for measuring directly in containers, and an External Transmission Unit for automated vial or tablet analysis.

faqs.question: Can I try different sampling methods before committing to one?
faqs.answer: Yes. The modular design is built for exactly this, since the best sampling method often isn't obvious until you've tested it on your actual sample.

faqs.question: What is the warranty on the MPA III?
faqs.answer: 10 years on the interferometer's moving parts and the solid-state laser.

faqs.question: Is the MPA III suitable for a regulated pharmaceutical environment?
faqs.answer: Yes. OPUS software offers GMP and 21 CFR Part 11 compliance in validated mode, with a complete audit trail and the OPUS Validation Program covering OQ and PQ protocols to USP, JP, and Ph. Eur. guidelines.

faqs.question: Can the MPA III be used outside the lab?
faqs.answer: Yes. Its robustness supports use on the factory floor, and it can be mounted on a utility cart for mobile applications.

faqs.question: What software is available for the MPA III?
faqs.answer: OPUS/LAB for routine analysis, OPUS/IDENT for raw material identification, OPUS/CONFO for conformity checking, OPUS/QUANT2 for multivariate calibration development, and ONET for managing a network of solutions remotely.

faqs.question: Does the MPA III require trained operators?
faqs.answer: No. Customizable workspaces and guided measurement modes in OPUS are designed so untrained personnel can operate the solution from day one.

faqs.question: How is the instrument monitored for accuracy?
faqs.answer: An online diagnostic system continuously monitors all optical components and notifies the user immediately if anything falls out of specification.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the MPA III and TANGO II?
faqs.answer: The MPA III offers four interchangeable sampling modules and a full software suite for method development, while the TANGO II is a simpler, fixed-configuration analyzer built for fast, routine measurement with minimal setup.

body: The right sampling method depends on the sample and where it sits, and the MPA III is built so you don't have to guess correctly the first time.

Liquids in cuvettes or disposable vials go through the Sample Compartment, with an optional heater and automated background capability. Solids and semi-solids go through the Integrating Sphere by diffuse reflection, with a sample rotator improving reproducibility on heterogeneous material. Samples that can't come to the instrument, like material sitting in a warehouse, are measured directly through Fiber Optic Probes, with two probes running at once for solids and liquids together. Tablets or vials needing automated, repeatable transmission measurements run through the External Transmission Unit with its optional sample wheel.

Liquids in cuvettes or vials, solids and semi-solids by diffuse reflection, samples measured directly in a warehouse container, or automated tablets and vials in transmission. Swap the module, not the solution.
It's built for both jobs at once: sophisticated calibration method development, and routine QA/QC simple enough for untrained staff to run from day one.
And it's built to last. Ten years of warranty cover the interferometer's moving parts and the solid-state laser.

sections.title: Fluorescence Mitigation and Laser Safety
sections.tabSummary: How SSE and DuoLaser work together
body: Fluorescence is the reason a lot of raw materials never get measured with handheld Raman at all. It swamps the much weaker Raman signal, and most handheld systems have no way around it.

SSE addresses this directly. By shifting the laser's temperature in controlled steps, it separates the fluorescence background from the genuine Raman signal, recovering a usable spectrum from materials that would otherwise be unreadable. DuoLaser's two excitation wavelengths, 785 nm and 852 nm, extend that sensitivity across a broader spectral range than a single-wavelength system reaches. And because BRAVO holds Laser Class 1 in every mode, none of that performance comes with a safety trade-off.

faqs.question: What is the SENTERRA II Raman Microscope used for?

faqs.question: What is SureCal, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: SureCal is a patented technology that continuously recalibrates the SENTERRA II in the background, holding sub-wavenumber precision without a manual recalibration step interrupting analysis.

faqs.question: How many lasers does the SENTERRA II support?

faqs.question: Is the SENTERRA II safe for students or first-time operators?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Class 1 laser housing with interlock protects the user from harmful laser radiation at all times, without requiring laser safety training.

faqs.question: Can the SENTERRA II identify unknown substances automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes, using A.I.D., an AI-driven tool that matches spectral data against reference databases in seconds, for pure substances or complex mixtures.

faqs.question: How do I identify an unknown chemical sample step by step with the SENTERRA II?
faqs.answer: Select a built-in laser with one click, place the sample under the microscope, and start the measurement. A.I.D. then runs the identification automatically against reference spectral databases, returning a match with diagnostics and hit-quality graphs in seconds.

faqs.question: Can it generate a chemical image without selecting a Raman peak first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Adaptive K-means Clustering sorts spectra into groups automatically and builds the chemical image on its own.

faqs.question: How do I generate a chemical image of a mixed or heterogeneous sample using the SENTERRA II?
faqs.answer: Run Adaptive K-means Clustering after the measurement, without selecting a specific Raman peak first. The software sorts the spectra into groups automatically and builds the chemical image on its own, showing at a glance whether the sample is homogeneous or structured.

faqs.question: Can the SENTERRA II be configured for live cell or tissue research?

faqs.question: Is the SENTERRA II suitable for a regulated pharmaceutical environment?

body: Every Raman microscope drifts. Heat, component wear, and vibration all shift wavenumber accuracy over time, and most systems handle that with a scheduled recalibration routine that takes the instrument offline.

SureCal removes that step entirely, recalibrating continuously in the background so precision holds without a pause in analysis. That matters whether you're running a quick material identification or collecting a large dataset for PCA or other statistical work, where consistency across hundreds of measurements is the whole point. Laser safety runs on the same always-on principle: the Class 1 housing and interlock protect the user in every operating mode, which is what makes SENTERRA II usable by students and first-time operators without a separate safety program.

faqs.question: What is random-walk imaging?
faqs.answer: Random-walk imaging is a search algorithm that finds and follows the Raman signal directly, rather than scanning a sample in a fixed pattern regardless of what's present.

faqs.question: How much faster is RAMANwalk than a conventional Raman microscope?
faqs.answer: More than 5 times faster for obtaining Raman images, and on a targeted question like contamination detection, RAMANwalk can reach a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes where a conventional raster scan is only 10% complete in the same time.

faqs.question: How do I get a fast preview of an unknown sample with the RAMANwalk?

faqs.question: How do I check a sample for a specific contaminant quickly with the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: Run the random-walk search targeted at the contaminant's Raman signature rather than a full scan. On a comparable real sample, this reached a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes, versus roughly 50 minutes for a complete image.

faqs.question: Can RAMANwalk find signal in low-contrast samples?
faqs.answer: Yes. It locates regions of interest using chemical Raman information, even when the sample gives no useful visual contrast.

faqs.question: What is the spatial resolution of the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: 350 nm in X and Y, and 1 µm in Z.

faqs.question: How many objective lenses does the RAMANwalk offer?
faqs.answer: Five: 5x, 10x, 20x, 50x, and 100x, covering broad overview imaging through fine sub-micron detail.

faqs.question: Does the RAMANwalk need manual calibration?
faqs.answer: No. It auto-calibrates against a standard lamp and sample, and auto-aligns its own optical path.

faqs.question: Is the RAMANwalk safe to use without laser safety training?
faqs.answer: Yes. It has a Class I laser safety housing with an interlocked door, protecting the user at all times.

sections.tabSummary: How the algorithm finds an answer faster than a scan
body: A conventional Raman microscope treats every point in a sample as equally worth visiting. RAMANwalk doesn't.

The random-walk algorithm finds a distinctive Raman signal, searches the surrounding area for more of it, and moves rapidly elsewhere once the signal runs out. It's a fundamentally different search strategy, not just a faster version of the old one, and it's why RAMANwalk delivers a rough preview in under a minute and finer detail within a few minutes, well before a full scan would even be close to done. On a real contamination question, that difference is the whole point: a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes, against a traditional raster scan that's only 10% complete in the same time, with nothing found yet.

The result isn't just faster, it's faster at the question that matters. Looking for a contaminant in a sample where the full scan takes 50 minutes, RAMANwalk reaches a conclusive answer in about 5. In that same 5 minutes, a traditional raster scan is only 10% through the sample, with nothing found yet.
Galvanic mirrors steer the beam instead of moving the stage, spatial resolution runs to 350 nm, and the whole system calibrates and aligns itself automatically.

faqs.question: What is the MATRIX-F II FT-NIR Process Spectrometer used for?
faqs.answer: MATRIX-F II is used for direct, real-time monitoring of chemical processes in reactors, pipelines, and conveyor belts, across chemical, pharmaceutical, and food manufacturing.

faqs.question: What makes MATRIX-F II different from a standard FT-NIR spectrometer?
faqs.answer: It's the only FT-NIR spectrometer that measures both in contact and contactless with one instrument, using fiber optic probes for direct measurement and fiber-coupled heads for remote measurement.

faqs.question: How do I choose between contact and contactless measurement for my process?
faqs.answer: Use a fiber optic probe wherever direct immersion into the process is possible, and a contactless head where physical contact isn't practical, such as a moving conveyor belt or web; the duplex variant supports both at once.

faqs.question: How do I set up monitoring for multiple points on one production line?
faqs.answer: Connect up to six contactless heads to a single MATRIX-F II emission or duplex spectrometer, allowing simultaneous monitoring across multiple points from one instrument.

faqs.question: Can MATRIX-F II be installed in a hazardous or ATEX-classified area?

faqs.question: Can a method developed in the lab be used directly in the process?
faqs.answer: Yes. MATRIX-F II can run as a stand-alone laboratory system during method development, then transfer directly into the process application without redevelopment.

faqs.question: What is the warranty on the MATRIX-F II?
faqs.answer: 10 years on the interferometer's moving parts and the solid-state laser.

faqs.question: Is MATRIX-F II suitable for pharmaceutical manufacturing?

faqs.question: How does MATRIX-F II connect to existing plant control systems?

sections.eyebrow: Fiber Optic Probes and Contactless Measurement
sections.title: Fiber Optic Probes and Contactless Measurement
sections.tabSummary: Choosing probes, heads, or both
body: Choosing between contact and contactless measurement, or using both, comes down to what your process point actually allows.

Fiber optic probes go into the process directly, as diffuse reflectance, transflectance, or transmission probes, in materials like stainless steel or Hastelloy, or as flow cells for pilot plant assemblies. Contactless heads use tungsten illumination to measure from a distance, with the scattered light carried back to the spectrometer by fiber, useful where physical contact with the process isn't practical or safe. The duplex variant runs both at once, so a single instrument covers a reactor immersion probe and a remote conveyor head simultaneously.

faqs.question: What is the MATRIX-MF FT-IR Process Reaction Monitoring solution used for?
faqs.answer: MATRIX-MF monitors chemical and biological reactions in real time, using a direct-contact diamond ATR probe placed in the reaction itself, in the lab or on a process line.

faqs.question: How is MATRIX-MF different from MATRIX-F II?
faqs.answer: MATRIX-MF works the mid-IR region using direct-contact ATR probes, while MATRIX-F II works the near-IR region using fiber optic probes and contactless heads. They suit different measurement needs and are sometimes used together.

faqs.question: How do I choose the right ATR probe for my reaction?
faqs.answer: Match the probe diameter to your vessel scale: IN351 (3.17 mm) for micro-scale reactions, IN355 (6.3 mm) for standard lab vessels, or IN350-T (6 mm) and IN356-EX (12 mm) where ATEX hazardous-area compliance is required.

faqs.question: How do I monitor several reactions at once with MATRIX-MF?
faqs.answer: Connect up to six probes to the built-in automated multiplexer, allowing one instrument to monitor up to six reactions simultaneously.

faqs.question: Can MATRIX-MF be used in a hazardous, ATEX-classified area?
faqs.answer: Yes, either using the IN350-T or IN356-EX ATEX-rated probes, or the fully certified MATRIX-MF exproof variant.

faqs.question: Can MATRIX-MF monitor biological reactions, not just chemical ones?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mid-IR ATR sampling suits biological process monitoring as well as chemical reaction monitoring.

faqs.question: How quickly can probes be swapped on the MATRIX-MF?
faqs.answer: Bruker's proprietary BQC quick-connector design allows fast probe exchange in seconds, without compromising measurement reproducibility.

faqs.question: Can MATRIX-MF move between the lab and the production line?
faqs.answer: Yes. Its small footprint works as a standalone lab system, or mounts in a standard 19-inch rack for process installation.

faqs.question: How is MATRIX-MF validated for regulated use?
faqs.answer: The OPUS Validation Program runs automated performance tests through a built-in filter wheel, tracking hardware and consumable status continuously.

faqs.question: What is the price of the MATRIX-MF FT-IR Process Reaction Monitoring solution in India?
faqs.answer: The price depends on the probe selection, multiplexer configuration, and hazard rating your installation needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

faqs.answer: BEAM monitors solid and semi-solid material in real time, mounted directly on pipelines, hoppers, or conveyor belts, across food, feed, polymer, and pharmaceutical manufacturing.

faqs.question: What makes BEAM different from a conventional single-point NIR analyzer?
faqs.answer: It's the first dedicated single-point spectrometer to carry the full spectral range and resolution of FT-NIR spectroscopy, handling applications conventional single-point analyzers can't reach.

faqs.question: How fast does BEAM measure?

faqs.question: How do I choose the right mounting hardware for my installation?
faqs.answer: Use Tri-Clamp flanges for hygienic pipeline or sight-glass connections, mounting brackets for flexible orientation on conveyors or hoppers, and the laboratory stand for method development before transferring to production.

faqs.question: How do I keep monitoring running if a light source fails?
faqs.answer: Dual source mode switches automatically to a backup light source when the primary fails, so measurement continues without waiting for a service visit.

faqs.question: Can I develop a method in the lab before installing BEAM on the line?
faqs.answer: Yes. The laboratory stand provides the correct measurement distance using a Petri dish turntable or the supplied holder, so a method developed in the lab transfers directly to production.

faqs.question: What feed parameters can BEAM measure?
faqs.answer: Moisture, oil, protein, fiber, and ash, plus more specialized parameters including ADF, NDF, and amino acids, in both raw materials and finished feed.

faqs.question: Is BEAM suitable for pharmaceutical process monitoring?
faqs.answer: Yes. Typical applications include monitoring mixing processes and determining the endpoint of API drying.

faqs.question: What is dual source mode?
faqs.answer: A redundancy feature that automatically switches to a second light source if the primary one fails, doubling system availability and avoiding unplanned downtime.

faqs.question: What is the OMEGA 5 FT-IR Gas Analyzer used for?
faqs.answer: OMEGA 5 monitors gas concentrations in real time, quantifying over 350 compounds without calibration, across industrial process monitoring, environmental analysis, and trace impurity detection.

faqs.question: How does calibration-free quantification actually work?
faqs.answer: OPUS GA software continuously records the gas's pressure and temperature during analysis and corrects for both in real time, which is what allows accurate quantification without a calibration curve.

faqs.question: How do I decide between standard and high-resolution configuration?
faqs.answer: Choose standard resolution, better than 2 cm⁻¹, for gas mixtures with clearly separated IR signals, and the high-resolution option, better than 1 cm⁻¹, when your mixture has significant signal overlap that needs to be resolved.

faqs.question: How do I decide if I need the high-pressure option?
faqs.answer: Choose the high-pressure option, up to 15 bar absolute, when you're detecting trace impurities or measuring gas directly at elevated industrial process pressure rather than after depressurizing it.

faqs.question: What is the H2O detection limit on the OMEGA 5?
faqs.answer: As low as 10 ppm, achieved through a sealed, purgeable optics compartment that stabilizes background H2O and CO2 levels.

faqs.question: Does the OMEGA 5 need liquid nitrogen?
faqs.answer: No. The TE-MCT detector runs continuously without a cryogen requirement.

faqs.question: What is DryPath, and when should I use it?
faqs.answer: DryPath is an optional feature that eliminates the need for external purge gas, which is worth adding wherever purge gas supply is inconvenient or unavailable, including mobile applications.

faqs.question: Can the OMEGA 5 be used for mobile gas analysis?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the DryPath option, which removes the external purge gas requirement that would otherwise limit it to fixed installations.

faqs.question: How long is the gas cell, and can it be heated?
faqs.answer: The multi-reflection gas cell is 5 meters, heatable up to 191°C.

faqs.question: What is the price of the OMEGA 5 FT-IR Gas Analyzer in India?
faqs.answer: The price depends on the resolution, pressure, and DryPath options your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your gas mixture and operating conditions are confirmed.

body: Two configuration choices decide what OMEGA 5 can actually see in a gas sample: how finely it resolves overlapping signals, and how much pressure it can measure under.

Standard resolution, better than 2 cm⁻¹, handles most routine gas analysis cleanly. Where compounds share closely overlapping IR signals, the high-resolution option pushes past 1 cm⁻¹, separating what the standard configuration would blur together. Pressure works the same way: standard operation covers up to 2 bar absolute, while the high-pressure option reaches 15 bar, which matters both for trace impurity detection and for measuring gas directly at real industrial process pressure rather than after it's been stepped down.

faqs.question: What is Lyovapor L-210 used for?

faqs.question: How cold does the condenser get?
faqs.answer: The lowest condenser temperature is -55°C, reached rapidly through EcoStream cooling technology.

faqs.question: What is the condenser capacity?
faqs.answer: Condenser and condensing capacity are both rated up to 6 kg, with condensing capacity at up to 6 kg per 24 hours.

faqs.question: What's the environmental impact of Lyovapor L-210?
faqs.answer: It carries a GWP index of 3, achieved through natural coolants used in the EcoStream cooling system.

faqs.question: What's the difference between Basic and Pro configurations?
faqs.answer: Pro configurations add heatable shelves up to 60 ± 1°C and temperature-based endpoint determination, while Basic configurations use unheatable shelves and pressure-based endpoint determination.

faqs.question: Can I upgrade from Basic to Pro later?
faqs.answer: Yes, Lyovapor L-210 supports upgrading from a Basic to a Pro instrument as application needs change.

faqs.question: Does Lyovapor L-210 support automated, unattended runs?
faqs.answer: Yes, method programming combined with a sample protective state enables fully automated freeze-drying runs.

faqs.question: What does the hot gas defrosting feature do?

sections.title: Time-Saving Automation
body: Watching a freeze-drying run manually, guessing at when primary drying ends and secondary drying begins, wastes both time and confidence in the result. Infinite-Control removes that guesswork directly.

A live graphical display on the 4.6-inch touch screen keeps process parameters visible throughout the run, while advanced process analytics pin down precise endpoint determination across both primary and secondary drying phases. Method programming combined with a sample protective state means a run can proceed fully automated once it's started, without needing constant supervision. Where hot gas defrosting is included, melting the ice layer that builds up on the condenser coil happens faster too, cutting downtime between cycles.

faqs.question: What is the BWB XP used for?
faqs.answer: It's a 5-channel flame photometer used for simultaneous measurement of sodium, potassium, lithium, calcium, and caesium, applied across clinical, pharmaceutical, environmental, and industrial elemental analysis.

faqs.question: How is BWB XP different from other flame photometers?
faqs.answer: It's the first and only flame photometer offering simultaneous detection and display of all five elements from a single dilution, removing the filter-change-and-recalibrate cycle every other flame photometer design has required since 1951.

faqs.question: Does each element need a separate sample dilution?
faqs.answer: No. All five elements are measured from a single dilution.

faqs.question: What gas does the instrument require?
faqs.answer: Propane, LPG, or butane.

faqs.question: Does it need a separate air supply?
faqs.answer: No. A built-in air compressor is included, so connecting gas is the only requirement.

faqs.question: What's included with the instrument?
faqs.answer: Solutions and labware ship as standard, along with the built-in compressor — accessories BWB notes other manufacturers often sell separately.

faqs.question: How does data leave the instrument?
faqs.answer: Via USB to a connected PC, with support for intranet or internet-linked distributed reporting across multiple sites.

faqs.question: Does BWB XP correct for interference between elements?
faqs.answer: Yes. Calcium readings are automatically corrected for interference from high sodium levels.

faqs.question: Is IQ/OQ/PQ certification available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as a web-based standard offering, which BWB describes as unique in the analytical instrumentation market.

faqs.question: Can results be reported in different units?
faqs.answer: Yes. Five user-selectable units of measure are available, with selectable decimal places.

faqs.question: Is a printer available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an integrated option using readily available standard paper.

faqs.question: How is the instrument constructed?
faqs.answer: Metal casework using RoHS-compliant components and materials wherever possible, designed to be portable and recyclable.

faqs.question: How long has BWB XP been in production?
faqs.answer: Since 2006, as BWB Technologies' flagship flame photometer model.

paragraphs: Every flame photometer design from 1951 onward has shared the same workflow: measure one element, change the filter, recalibrate, measure the next. Across five elements, that's five setups per sample. BWB XP was built from the ground up specifically to remove that repetition, detecting and displaying all five elements — sodium, potassium, lithium, calcium, and caesium — from one dilution and one flame simultaneously.

The practical effect compounds across a batch. A lab running fifty samples for a five-element panel isn't running two hundred and fifty sequential measurements; it's running fifty. Operator-independent result determination means the output doesn't drift with who's running the instrument that day, and the step-by-step interface keeps a less experienced analyst on the correct procedure without hand-holding.

IQ/OQ/PQ certification is available web-based, which BWB positions as unique in the analytical instrumentation space — relevant wherever qualification documentation is a purchasing requirement rather than a nice-to-have.

faqs.question: What is the BWB XP Plus used for?
faqs.answer: It's a 4-channel flame photometer used for simultaneous measurement of sodium, potassium, lithium, and calcium, with an internal reference standard for calibration stability, applied across clinical, pharmaceutical, environmental, and industrial elemental analysis.

faqs.question: What is the Internal Reference Standard (IRS)?
faqs.answer: An option to use either caesium or lithium as an internal standard that adjusts for small changes occurring during calibration and measurement, correcting drift inline rather than requiring periodic manual recalibration.

faqs.question: How is XP Plus different from the standard BWB XP?
faqs.answer: XP measures 5 elements simultaneously (Na, K, Li, Ca, Cs) with no internal reference. XP Plus measures 4 simultaneously (Na, K, Li, Ca) and uses caesium or lithium as an internal reference standard for drift correction instead of reporting it as a fifth result.

faqs.question: Can caesium still be measured as a result on XP Plus?
faqs.answer: On XP Plus, caesium (or lithium) is used as the IRS reference rather than reported as a measured result. Where caesium needs to be a reported analyte, the BWB XP is the appropriate instrument.

faqs.question: Does each element need a separate sample dilution?
faqs.answer: No. All four elements, plus the IRS channel, are measured from a single dilution.

faqs.question: What gas does the instrument require?
faqs.answer: Propane, LPG, or butane.

faqs.question: Does it need a separate air supply?
faqs.answer: No. A built-in air compressor is included, so connecting gas is the only requirement.

faqs.question: What's included with the instrument?
faqs.answer: Solutions and labware ship as standard, along with the built-in compressor.

faqs.question: How does data leave the instrument?
faqs.answer: Via USB to a connected PC, with support for intranet or internet-linked distributed reporting across multiple sites.

faqs.question: Is IQ/OQ/PQ certification available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as a web-based standard offering, which BWB describes as unique in the analytical instrumentation market.

faqs.question: Can results be reported in different units?
faqs.answer: Yes. Four user-selectable units of measure are available, with selectable decimal places.

faqs.question: Is a printer available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an integrated option using readily available standard paper.

faqs.question: How is the instrument constructed?
faqs.answer: Metal casework using RoHS-compliant components and materials wherever possible, designed to be portable and recyclable.

paragraphs: Any flame photometer's calibration can drift over a long session — small changes in flame conditions, aspiration rate, or sample delivery accumulate quietly and show up as error in later readings. XP Plus addresses that directly rather than relying on periodic manual recalibration: an Internal Reference Standard, set to either caesium or lithium, runs alongside the four primary channels and acts as an internal standard, adjusting for those small changes as they occur.

The choice between caesium and lithium as the reference matters in practice. If lithium is one of the elements actually being measured in the sample, caesium is the sensible reference so the two don't interfere. Where lithium isn't a target analyte, it becomes available as the reference instead. Either way, the correction happens inline, during calibration and measurement, rather than being caught only when a check standard is re-run.

sections.eyebrow: Choosing Between XP and XP Plus
sections.title: Choosing Between XP and XP Plus
sections.tabSummary: Five raw channels versus four with drift correction
body: Five raw channels against four with drift correction.

The two instruments share the same underlying platform, the same removal of the filter-change cycle, and the same standard inclusions. The difference is what they're built to prioritize. BWB XP measures five elements simultaneously — sodium, potassium, lithium, calcium, and caesium — with no internal reference; caesium is a full measurement channel, not a correction mechanism. XP Plus trades that fifth channel for the IRS: four elements measured simultaneously, with caesium or lithium held back specifically to monitor and correct calibration drift.

Which one fits depends on what the panel actually needs. A lab that routinely reports caesium as a result wants XP. A lab running long batch sessions where calibration stability matters more than a fifth data point, or one that values the internal check IRS provides, wants XP Plus.

paragraphs: Most flame photometers measure whatever solution is presented to them, with calibration standards the lab has to source and prepare separately. BWB BIO ships with 5-point calibration standards for urine and 6-point standards for serum included as standard — matched to the two sample types clinical and renal research labs actually run, rather than generic multi-element standards adapted after the fact.

The Automatic Fluid Handling System extends that same logic to sample handling itself. It was originally designed specifically to work with the BIO unit, and it's configured through the same FP-PC software that manages calibration curves and generates reports, rather than as a bolt-on accessory with its own separate control layer. Together with an IRS option — caesium or lithium — correcting drift during calibration and measurement, the instrument is built around the realities of running blood and urine samples at volume rather than adapted to them.

body: How results move from instrument to record, with or without a PC.

FP-PC software is the connected route: results become .pdf files, .csv files, data presentations, and full reports, with calibration curves viewable and editable directly rather than locked behind a fixed factory setting. For labs where PCs and data acquisition aren't permitted inside the test lab itself, an integrated printer provides the hard-copy record QA and QC processes require, using environmentally friendly ink rated for a minimum 10-year character capture life — long enough to outlast most regulatory retention requirements — and compatible with standard, readily available paper rather than a proprietary cartridge.

IQ/OQ/PQ web-based certification comes standard on BIO specifically, and is available across the wider BWB flame emission spectrometer range. For a clinical or pharma lab, that qualification documentation is often the deciding factor between an instrument that's simply accurate and one that can actually be validated for regulated use.

faqs.question: What is the BWB Flash used for?
faqs.answer: It's a fully configurable flame photometer available in seven models, used for single-element through four-element (Na, K, Li, Ca) simultaneous measurement across routine QC, environmental, agricultural, and teaching applications.

faqs.question: What models are available?
faqs.answer: FL-C (Ca), FL-K (K), FL-L (Li), FL-N (Na), FL-2 (Na & K), FL-3 (Na, K & Li), and FL-4 (Na, K, Li & Ca).

faqs.question: Can I buy a single-element version?
faqs.answer: Yes. FL-C, FL-K, FL-L, and FL-N each measure only one element, avoiding the cost of unused channels.

faqs.question: How is Flash different from BWB XP?
faqs.answer: XP is a fixed 5-channel instrument (Na, K, Li, Ca, Cs). Flash is configurable across seven models from one to four channels, sharing XP's core no-filter-change engineering at a lower entry cost, but without a caesium channel or IRS option.

faqs.question: Does Flash include an Internal Reference Standard?
faqs.answer: No. IRS (caesium or lithium reference) is available on XP Plus and BIO, not on Flash.

faqs.question: What display does it use?
faqs.answer: A 5-inch touchscreen, compatible with most disposable laboratory gloves.

faqs.question: Does it need a separate air supply?
faqs.answer: No. A built-in air compressor and gas regulator are included.

faqs.question: What gas does it require?
faqs.answer: Propane, LPG, or butane.

faqs.question: Are calibration standards included?
faqs.answer: Yes, supplied as standard at 10,000ppm concentration.

faqs.question: How does auto-read technology work?
faqs.answer: It enables operator-independent determination of results, reducing variability between different users running the same measurement.

faqs.question: Is Flash more efficient than previous BWB models?
faqs.answer: Yes. BWB states 13% lower gas consumption and 26% lower electricity consumption (kWh) compared to previous model generations.

faqs.question: Is IQ/OQ/PQ certification available?
faqs.answer: Yes, web-based, and BWB positions this as unique in the analytical instrumentation arena.

faqs.question: What's included with the instrument?
faqs.answer: Complete basic labware, calibration standards at 10,000ppm, and the built-in compressor and regulator.

faqs.question: How does data leave the instrument?
faqs.answer: Via USB to a connected PC as standard, with support for intranet or internet-linked distributed reporting.

faqs.question: Can I upgrade to a higher-channel model later?
faqs.answer: The source material doesn't specify a field-upgrade path between models; confirm with Inkarp whether moving from a lower to a higher-channel Flash model requires a new unit.

faqs.answer: Detection limits, linear range, precision, sample throughput, and physical dimensions were not available on the source page reviewed — Inkarp can request the full datasheet from BWB Technologies.

longForm.heroLead: Most flame photometers sell every channel whether the lab needs it or not. BWB Flash asks the opposite question first: how many elements does the work actually require? It's the first and only fully configurable flame photometer, up to four channels, detecting and displaying all calibrated ions simultaneously — available across seven models, from single-element units (FL-C, FL-K, FL-L, FL-N) through two-, three-, and four-element configurations (FL-2, FL-3, FL-4). A lab measuring only calcium buys FL-C. A lab needing the full sodium, potassium, lithium, and calcium panel buys FL-4. No unused channels, no paying for capability that sits idle. It carries the XP platform's core advantage forward: no filter changes, no recalibration between elements, on whichever model is chosen. And it's genuinely more efficient than what came before it — 13% lower gas consumption and 26% lower electricity consumption compared to previous BWB model generations. A 5-inch touchscreen, compatible with most disposable lab gloves, and calibration standards supplied at 10,000ppm concentration round out a unit that, like the rest of the range, ships with everything needed to start measuring.

sections.title: Seven Models, One Platform
sections.description: How the range maps configuration to actual measurement need.
paragraphs: Buying a four-channel instrument to measure one element is a common but unnecessary cost, and it's exactly what the Flash range is built to avoid. Four single-element models — FL-C, FL-K, FL-L, and FL-N — cover labs whose routine work is genuinely one ion. From there, FL-2 adds sodium and potassium together, FL-3 extends to lithium, and FL-4 completes the panel with calcium, matching BWB XP's core element set but on a lower-cost, purpose-configured platform.

Every model in the range shares the same underlying engineering: the touchscreen, the built-in compressor, auto-read technology, and the removal of the filter-change-and-recalibrate cycle. The configuration decision is purely about which ions the lab needs measured, not a trade-off in build quality between models.

sections.title: Efficiency Gains Over Previous Generations
sections.tabSummary: What the 13% and 26% figures mean in practice
body: What the 13% and 26% figures mean for day-to-day running cost.

Flame photometers run on gas and electricity continuously through a working shift, so small percentage reductions compound into real operating savings across a year. BWB states Flash uses 13% less gas and 26% less electricity than previous BWB model generations — a stated, generation-over-generation comparison rather than a claim against unnamed competitors.

That reduction sits alongside BWB's wider stated objective of an exceptionally low carbon footprint as a responsible manufacturer, and it's engineered into the platform rather than achieved by running the instrument differently. For a lab weighing Flash against an older BWB unit already in service, or budgeting gas cylinder and electricity costs for a new installation, those two figures translate directly into lower recurring cost.

faqs.question: What is the BWB BIO AV used for?
faqs.answer: It's a flame photometer specialized for biological samples, measuring sodium, potassium, and lithium simultaneously from a single dilution, with a particular strength in lithium therapeutic monitoring and renal electrolyte panels.

faqs.question: How is BIO AV different from BIO?
faqs.answer: BIO measures four elements (Na, K, Li, Ca) with matrix-specific 5-/6-point calibration standards for urine and serum. BIO AV measures three (Na, K, Li) from a single dilution range with enhanced lithium detection and a simplified menu, trading the calcium channel for speed and sensitivity.

faqs.question: What is the dilution range?
faqs.answer: 1:6 to 1:100, with all three elements calibrated and measured from the same dilution.

faqs.question: Is lithium detection improved on BIO AV?
faqs.answer: Yes. Lithium detection is enhanced compared to the standard BIO platform.

faqs.question: How many calibration curves can be stored?
faqs.answer: Two, user-defined, allowing quick switching between two distinct sample types.

faqs.question: What is the Internal Reference Standard (IRS)?
faqs.answer: An option to use caesium or lithium as an internal standard that adjusts for small changes during calibration and measurement.

faqs.question: What calibration standards are supplied?
faqs.answer: 10,000ppm standards for each of the three measured elements.

faqs.question: What is the AFHS?
faqs.answer: The Automatic Fluid Handling System, originally designed to work specifically with the BIO range of instrumentation, configured through the FP-PC software. Detailed mechanical specifications are available on request.

faqs.question: How does data leave the instrument?
faqs.answer: Via FP-PC software, generating .pdf files, .csv files, data presentations, and reports containing all key analysis data.

faqs.question: Is there a printer option for labs without PC access?
faqs.answer: Yes. An integrated printer with environmentally friendly ink, rated for a minimum 10-year character capture life, provides hard-copy output for QA/QC.

faqs.question: Is IQ/OQ/PQ certification included?
faqs.answer: Yes, as standard on the BIO AV model, and available web-based across the wider BWB flame emission spectrometer range.

faqs.question: Is calcium measurable on BIO AV?
faqs.answer: No. BIO AV measures sodium, potassium, and lithium only. Where calcium is a required result, the standard BIO is the appropriate instrument.

faqs.question: Is the interface simpler than BIO?
faqs.answer: Yes. BIO AV uses a simplified menu structure compared to the standard BIO interface.

longForm.heroHook: One dilution, three elements, a menu built to get out of the way.
longForm.heroLead: BIO AV is an offshoot of the BWB BIO, purpose-built around a narrower, sharper question: sodium, potassium, and lithium, calibrated and measured together from a single dilution, with a simplified menu structure and enhanced lithium detection. The dilution range runs from 1:6 to 1:100, covering the span most biological sample types actually need without switching prep protocols between them. Two user-defined calibration curves can be entered and stored, so a lab running two distinct sample types can move between them without rebuilding the calibration each time. Everything that makes the BIO platform work for clinical throughput carries over: the Automatic Fluid Handling System (AFHS), built specifically for the BIO range and configured through FP-PC software; .pdf, .csv, and report export; an integrated printer with 10-year-rated ink for labs that don't permit PCs in the test area; and an IRS option — caesium or lithium — for calibration drift correction.

paragraphs: Where BIO measures four elements including calcium, BIO AV narrows to three — sodium, potassium, and lithium — and uses that narrower scope to sharpen everything else. All three calibrate and measure from the same dilution, across a range of 1:6 to 1:100, so sample prep is one step rather than a decision tree depending on which element is being targeted.

Lithium detection is specifically enhanced over the standard BIO platform, which matters directly wherever lithium therapeutic monitoring is the primary reason for the panel rather than an incidental fourth channel. The simplified menu structure removes steps that BIO's broader four-element configuration carries, and two user-defined calibration curves can be stored, so a lab running two distinct sample types — say, two different biological matrices — switches between them without rebuilding calibration from scratch each time.

sections.title: BIO or BIO AV
sections.tabSummary: Four elements against three, and when each fits
body: Four elements against three, and when each fits.

Both instruments share the AFHS, FP-PC software, IRS option, and long-life printer — the difference is scope and speed. BIO measures four elements (Na, K, Li, Ca) with calibration standards specifically built around urine and serum matrices via 5- and 6-point multi-ion standards. BIO AV drops calcium, measures three (Na, K, Li) from a single dilution range, and sharpens lithium detection specifically, trading the fourth channel for a faster, simpler workflow.

The choice comes down to whether calcium needs to be a reported result. If it does, BIO is the instrument. If the work centres on sodium, potassium, and lithium — particularly where lithium monitoring is the clinical priority — BIO AV's narrower, enhanced panel and simplified menu are built specifically for that.

paragraphs: A multi-element instrument divides its detection design across every channel it supports. BWB LI doesn't — every part of its optical array and every detection channel is concentrated on lithium alone, which is what BWB positions as the reason it's the most accurate lithium flame photometer they've built.

That focus came from a specific development path rather than a general engineering exercise: adaptation and optimisation of BWB's proprietary optical array detection systems, refined with input from Dr. Richard Roman at the University of Mississippi, and a final configuration set exclusively to specifications laid out through consultation with BWB's own customers. The result is described as the first instrument of its kind — not a lithium channel bolted onto a broader panel, but an instrument engineered around lithium from the ground up.

sections.tabSummary: When lithium alone is the right answer
body: When lithium alone is the right answer.

Most flame photometry work needs a panel, sodium and potassium alongside lithium, or the full electrolyte set including calcium. BWB LI is the exception: it exists for the specific case where lithium accuracy is the entire requirement, and where any other element would be a distraction from the one measurement that actually matters.

That's a narrower use case than BIO AV (which measures Na, K, and Li together with enhanced lithium detection) or the standard BIO and XP Plus panels. Where the work genuinely never needs sodium or potassium as a reported result — a dedicated lithium QC line, a research programme built entirely around lithium pharmacokinetics — BWB LI's concentrated design has no panel-instrument equivalent in accuracy terms. Where sodium or potassium are needed even occasionally, one of BWB's multi-element instruments is the better fit.

faqs.question: What is the BWB SOIL used for?
faqs.answer: It's a flame photometer purpose-built for agriculture, measuring sodium, potassium, and calcium in soil substrates and fertilisers, usable in either a laboratory or field setting.

faqs.question: Why was BWB SOIL developed?
faqs.answer: It builds on 2017 research by Professor Akiharu Sasaki establishing the specific case for flame photometry in agricultural analysis, developed further in conjunction with field requests and operational requirements from agricultural users.

faqs.question: Which elements does it measure?
faqs.answer: Sodium, potassium, and calcium, simultaneously, with enhanced calcium detection optimised for soil and fertiliser matrices.

faqs.question: Can it be used outside a laboratory?
faqs.answer: Yes. It's designed for genuine field portability, including setup in the back of a van, and can conduct on-site analysis at various geographical locations.

faqs.question: What does "just add gas" mean for field use?
faqs.answer: The instrument requires minimal setup infrastructure at the sample site, needing only a gas connection to run.

faqs.question: Does it produce a record of field results?
faqs.answer: Yes. A thermal printer is fitted as standard, maintaining traceability for sample analysis throughout field work.

faqs.question: What is the Internal Reference Standard (IRS) option?
faqs.answer: Lithium can be used as an internal reference standard, correcting small changes during calibration and measurement.

faqs.question: How is sample handling configured?
faqs.answer: Either through the BWB collection cup feature for manual introduction, or the AFHS automated sample handling system for higher-volume operation.

faqs.question: How is BWB SOIL different from BWB XP or XP Plus?
faqs.answer: XP and XP Plus are general-purpose bench instruments optimised for lab throughput across broader element panels. SOIL trades some of that panel breadth (no caesium channel, lithium available only as IRS) for enhanced calcium detection and genuine field portability specific to agricultural work.

faqs.question: Does it correct for interference between elements?
faqs.answer: Yes. Calcium readings are automatically corrected for interference from high sodium levels.

faqs.question: Is IQ/OQ/PQ certification available?
faqs.answer: Yes, web-based.

faqs.question: Can results be reported in different units?
faqs.answer: Yes. Four user-selectable units of measure are available, with selectable decimal places.

faqs.question: What platform is BWB SOIL built on?
faqs.answer: The footprint of the award-winning BWB XP, optimised beyond the original design specifically for agricultural analysis.

paragraphs: Every other instrument in BWB's range is a bench device. BWB SOIL is built to leave the bench entirely: a "just add gas" configuration and physical portability that allows the instrument to be set up in the back of a van and run field analysis on-site at various geographical locations.

That matters directly for agricultural sampling programmes, where the alternative is bagging soil samples, transporting them back to a lab, and waiting for results before a fertilisation or amendment decision can be made. Running the analysis at the point of sampling collapses that gap. A thermal printer fitted as standard keeps traceability intact throughout — every sample analysed in the field produces a physical record, which matters for advisory work, research documentation, and any context where field results need to be defensible after the fact.
