sections.tabSummary: Why capacity, not top speed, defines this centrifuge
body: Learn why capacity, not top speed, defines the Kubota Model 8730.

Blood bank and clinical laboratory work rarely needs the 15,000-22,000 rpm range that Kubota's research centrifuges reach, it needs enough capacity to process real batches of blood bags and large bottles at a controlled temperature, reliably, run after run. Model 8730 is built around exactly that priority: a maximum capacity of 4,000 mL, blood bag compatibility built directly into the rotor design, and a temperature range wide enough to protect clinical samples throughout.

The rotor set reflects the same focus. 1 high capacity swinging bucket rotor handles the largest batches, and 2 multi-purpose swinging bucket rotors cover the routine tube and bottle work that fills the rest of a clinical lab's day.

sections.title: Twelve Bags, One Spin
sections.tabSummary: Why batch capacity defines this centrifuge entirely
body: Learn why batch capacity defines the Kubota Model 9945 entirely.

A blood bank doesn't process one bag at a time, it processes donations in batches, and every centrifuge cycle that handles fewer bags means more cycles, more time, and more staff hours spent loading and unloading. Model 9945 is built specifically to remove that bottleneck: 12 blood bags in a single run, on a rotor purpose-built for the 200 mL to 500 mL bag sizes standard blood collection actually uses.
There's no rotor decision to make here, no swapping between tube and plate configurations. One dedicated rotor, one job, done at the batch size a real blood bank actually needs.

sections.title: The HD-5000 Pump System
body: The HD-5000 sits at the center of every Labomatic Industrial LC system, and its flexibility is what allows the same core platform to scale across very different production needs.

Its three-piston design, built around primary and secondary pistons, delivers a nearly pulsation-free flow across a wide range, from 5 mL/min at the low end up to 4920 mL/min, at pressures reaching 600 bar. Five different pump heads are available, and they can be combined with one another rather than locking you into a single fixed configuration. Gradient elution goes all the way up to quaternary, in either high-pressure or low-pressure form, with an active mixing system supporting the low-pressure side specifically. Active piston back-flushing keeps buffer eluents genuinely usable, avoiding the fouling issues they can otherwise cause. From a single system controller, the HD-5000 can manage 12 or more pump mechanisms and up to 20 valves, static or pulsed, while also supporting microliter-precision dosing for additives like DEA or TFA.

sections.title: The LH-5000 Modular Platform
body: Most liquid handling platforms come in a handful of fixed sizes. The LH-5000 takes a different approach, building the entire base unit out of combinable X and Y elements.

That building-block construction is what gets the platform to over 1000 different size and configuration variations, with practically no limitation on dimensions, sample number, or sample volume. Effective travel reaches up to 2800mm on the X-axis, 800mm on the Y-axis, and 500mm on the Z-axis, and axis height itself can be adapted to fit the customer's specific application. sections.title: Application Modules Explained
body: The base LH-5000 platform is the movement system. The modules are what turn that movement into an actual workflow, and they're designed to be combined rather than chosen one at a time.

The LABOCOL fraction collector module automates collection directly off the platform, while the LABOCOL data storage module keeps run data logged and accessible. A LABOCOL cleaning module supports consistent cleanup between runs. On the LABOPORT side, the autosampler module automates sample introduction, the aliquot removal module handles precise sub-sampling, and the pooling module combines fractions or samples as your method requires. Because the platform is freely programmable and modules are combinable, several of these functions can run together on a single system rather than requiring separate instruments for each step.
Product expert note: Tell our team which steps in your current workflow are still manual, and Inkarp will confirm which modules close that gap.

faqs.question: What is Labomatic's Industrial Liquid Chromatography system used for?
faqs.answer: Labomatic's Industrial Liquid Chromatography systems are used for industrial-scale process and production purification. They're engineered for high-throughput, continuous separation in pharmaceutical and chemical industry settings.

faqs.question: What is the HD-5000 pump and why does it anchor the system?
faqs.answer: The HD-5000 is Labomatic's three-piston HPLC gradient pump, and it anchors the platform because it includes an integrated system controller for method programming and control of the complete HPLC system.

faqs.question: What flow rate and pressure does the HD-5000 support?
faqs.answer: The HD-5000 pump system supports flow rates from 5 to 4920 mL/min, with pressures up to 600 bar (8700 psi).

faqs.question: Can the HD-5000 run complex gradients?
faqs.answer: Yes, the HD-5000 supports binary through quaternary gradient formation, in both high-pressure and low-pressure configurations, with an active mixing system for low-pressure gradients.

faqs.question: How many pumps and valves can one system controller manage?
faqs.answer: A single HD-5000 system controller can manage 12 or more pump mechanisms and up to 20 valves, whether static or pulsed.

faqs.question: What other components make up a full Labomatic system?
faqs.answer: A complete system typically includes LABOPORT valves and sample injection systems, LABOCORD detectors (UV/VIS, DAD, RI, or MS), the LABOCOL Vario 4000 fraction collector series, and LABOCHROM 5 software.

faqs.question: Is an ATEX-compliant or GMP version available?
faqs.answer: Yes, Labomatic offers fully custom system configurations, including ATEX-compliant GMP system solutions for hazardous-area or regulated production environments.

faqs.question: Can the HD-5000 handle buffer eluents?
faqs.answer: Yes, active piston back-flushing is built into the HD-5000, allowing buffer eluents to be used without the typical complications they can introduce.

sections.title: The HD-5000 Pump System
body: The HD-5000 sits at the center of every Labomatic Industrial LC system, and its flexibility is what allows the same core platform to scale across very different production needs.

Its three-piston design, built around primary and secondary pistons, delivers a nearly pulsation-free flow across a wide range, from 5 mL/min at the low end up to 4920 mL/min, at pressures reaching 600 bar. Five different pump heads are available, and they can be combined with one another rather than locking you into a single fixed configuration. Gradient elution goes all the way up to quaternary, in either high-pressure or low-pressure form, with an active mixing system supporting the low-pressure side specifically. Active piston back-flushing keeps buffer eluents genuinely usable, avoiding the fouling issues they can otherwise cause. From a single system controller, the HD-5000 can manage 12 or more pump mechanisms and up to 20 valves, static or pulsed, while also supporting microliter-precision dosing for additives like DEA or TFA.

sections.title: The LH-5000 Modular Platform
body: Most liquid handling platforms come in a handful of fixed sizes. The LH-5000 takes a different approach, building the entire base unit out of combinable X and Y elements.

That building-block construction is what gets the platform to over 1000 different size and configuration variations, with practically no limitation on dimensions, sample number, or sample volume. Effective travel reaches up to 2800mm on the X-axis, 800mm on the Y-axis, and 500mm on the Z-axis, and axis height itself can be adapted to fit the customer's specific application. On the largest configurations, that scales up to 3000mm in width and 1200mm in depth, with up to 4 Z-axes and 2 Y-axes supporting as many as 5 applications running at the same time.

sections.title: Application Modules Explained
body: The base LH-5000 platform is the movement system. The modules are what turn that movement into an actual workflow, and they're designed to be combined rather than chosen one at a time.

The LABOCOL fraction collector module automates collection directly off the platform, while the LABOCOL data storage module keeps run data logged and accessible. A LABOCOL cleaning module supports consistent cleanup between runs. On the LABOPORT side, the autosampler module automates sample introduction, the aliquot removal module handles precise sub-sampling, and the pooling module combines fractions or samples as your method requires. Because the platform is freely programmable and modules are combinable, several of these functions can run together on a single system rather than requiring separate instruments for each step.
Product expert note: Tell our team which steps in your current workflow are still manual, and Inkarp will confirm which modules close that gap.

faqs.question: What purity level can Labstation I maintain?
faqs.answer: Below 1 ppm for both oxygen and moisture, held automatically through closed loop recirculation.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the main and mini-antechamber?
faqs.answer: The main antechamber runs its vacuum and refill cycle automatically under PLC control. The mini-antechamber uses a manual valve for fast, simple transfers.

faqs.question: Can I upgrade my Labstation I later?
faqs.answer: Yes, the modular design supports adding a second purifier column, a dry pump, remote monitoring, a vacuum oven, and several other upgrades without replacing the base system.

faqs.question: What gases can I use?
faqs.answer: Nitrogen, argon, or helium as your working gas, with an N₂/H₂ or Ar/H₂ mix at 5 to 10% hydrogen for regeneration.

faqs.question: What does my facility need to supply for installation?
faqs.answer: 220V single phase power at 1.5 kW, working gas at 5-6 bar, regeneration gas at 0.3-0.4 bar, and cooling water under 25°C at 1 atm.

faqs.question: How do I choose between the two vacuum pump options?
faqs.answer: RV12 delivers 12 cubic meters per hour, DRV10Y delivers 10, with DRV10Y typically the dry pump option; tell us your process requirements and we'll confirm which fits.

faqs.question: Which glove material should I choose?
faqs.answer: Butyl comes standard at 0.4mm thickness, with Hypalon and Neoprene available depending on your chemical exposure.

body: We built Labstation i SPS around a simple substitution: pressurized inert gas and two filter columns doing what a still used to do, without the heat, the glassware, or the standing watch. Nitrogen or argon at 99.999% purity pushes your solvent through, and both columns work in series so nothing slips through a single pass.

Purity holds below 10 ppm moisture depending on your starting solvent, and every column ships pre-activated. When one runs out after roughly 800 liters, you swap it yourself with a fresh one, no in-house regeneration step.

The modular multi-solvent unit handles up to five solvents from a confirmed list of eight compatible types, so you configure your five around what your lab actually runs. If your needs are simpler, the single-solvent benchtop unit delivers the same 800-liter capacity in a fraction of the footprint, with its own circulation pump for repeated purification cycles.

sections.title: How Solvent Purification Works
body: Getting a solvent below 10 ppm moisture comes down to two things: consistent gas pressure and enough filtration to catch what a single pass would miss.

Nitrogen or argon at 99.999% purity pressurizes your solvent reservoir, driving the solvent through two filter columns in series. That serial arrangement is what pulls both oxygen and moisture out reliably, rather than relying on a single column to catch everything at once. From there, purified solvent goes straight into an evacuated vessel or directly into a connected glovebox, ready to use without an extra transfer step exposing it to air.

body: We built Labstation i SPS around a simple substitution: pressurized inert gas and two filter columns doing what a still used to do, without the heat, the glassware, or the standing watch. Nitrogen or argon at 99.999% purity pushes your solvent through, and both columns work in series so nothing slips through a single pass.

Purity holds below 10 ppm moisture depending on your starting solvent, and every column ships pre-activated. When one runs out after roughly 800 liters, you swap it yourself with a fresh one, no in-house regeneration step.

The modular multi-solvent unit handles up to five solvents from a confirmed list of eight compatible types, so you configure your five around what your lab actually runs. If your needs are simpler, the single-solvent benchtop unit delivers the same 800-liter capacity in a fraction of the footprint, with its own circulation pump for repeated purification cycles.

sections.title: How Solvent Purification Works
body: Getting a solvent below 10 ppm moisture comes down to two things: consistent gas pressure and enough filtration to catch what a single pass would miss.

Nitrogen or argon at 99.999% purity pressurizes your solvent reservoir, driving the solvent through two filter columns in series. That serial arrangement is what pulls both oxygen and moisture out reliably, rather than relying on a single column to catch everything at once. From there, purified solvent goes straight into an evacuated vessel or directly into a connected glovebox, ready to use without an extra transfer step exposing it to air.

sections.intro: WPI is built around a problem every high-throughput photochemistry screen runs into: getting the same light to land on well 1 and well 24 equally. A single light source spread across a plate almost never manages it. Twenty-four individual LEDs, one per well, each with its own optical guide and lens, does.
paragraphs: Illumination comes from below rather than above, running straight through a transparent plate or vial bottom. That same bottom-up design lets 4 mL auto-sampler vials drop directly into the plate format when the workflow calls for it, without switching to a different instrument.

Heat management runs on two fronts at once: the anodized aluminum body dissipates heat passively, and an integrated cooling fan keeps operating temperature stable through longer experiments, important with 24 LEDs running simultaneously rather than one.

sections.title: Wavelength Selection and PWM Intensity Control
sections.tabSummary: Choosing wavelength and dialing in intensity
body: Getting the right wavelength is only half the job in a screening experiment. The other half is controlling intensity without accidentally changing the wavelength that was just selected.

Nine wavelength options cover near UV through far red, plus lime and cool white as broad-spectrum choices, all fully characterized so exactly what's being delivered is never a guess. The optional PWM dimmer module solves the intensity problem specifically: instead of reducing current to dim the LED, which can shift its emission wavelength, PWM adjusts the duty cycle, how long the LED stays on during each rapid switching cycle, so spectral output stays exactly where it started even as irradiance changes.

body: Photoreactor XL automation: multi-stage program sequences and standard safety interlock.

A reaction that needs light for twenty minutes, then heat for ten, then both together, shouldn't require standing at the unit managing each transition manually. Photoreactor XL's onboard automation sets and recalls exactly that kind of sequence, so the same multi-stage protocol runs identically every time it's called up.

Safety and usability run alongside that automation rather than working against it. The door safety interlock stops operation the moment the chamber opens, the spacious window lets a run be checked visually without interrupting it, and the removable sample carousel makes loading and unloading between runs straightforward rather than fiddly.

faqs.question: What is the LZC Photoreactor used for?
faqs.answer: It's a closed-chamber benchtop irradiation system built for photochemistry, photobiology, organic synthesis, materials science, and teaching applications requiring uniform light exposure across multiple samples.

faqs.question: How do I change the wavelength on my LZC Photoreactor?
faqs.answer: Lamps pull out and swap in without tools, so switching between UVA, UVC, or another wavelength in the LZC-Series range takes seconds, not a system rebuild.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the four LZC packages?
faqs.answer: They differ mainly in lamp geometry: LZC-4V combines top and side illumination, LZC-1 runs top lamps only, LZC-ORG runs side lamps only, and LZC-4X offers a fourth confirmed configuration.

faqs.question: Can I use lamps from a Rayonet reactor in my LZC Photoreactor?
faqs.answer: Many Rayonet-compatible lamps work with LZC hardware, since both platforms share compatibility across much of the same lamp range.

faqs.question: What comes standard with the LZC-4V package?
faqs.answer: Six top lamps and eight side lamps, two complete lamp sets (14 UVA at 367nm and 14 UVC at 254nm), a carousel and turntable, magnetic stirrer, timer, gas inlet, hour meter, safety interlock, UVA power meter, exhaust kit, and safety glasses.

faqs.question: How does the carousel and turntable work?
faqs.answer: Both run off the same integrated motor drive, with the carousel handling test tubes and the turntable handling solid samples.

faqs.question: What safety features are standard across all packages?
faqs.answer: A safety interlock, integrated timer, hour meter, bulkhead gas connector, safe exhaust system, and safety glasses ship with every LZC package.

faqs.question: What power supply does the LZC Photoreactor need?
faqs.answer: It runs on 120/240V, suited to benchtop use without a separate power converter.

sections.title: Chamber Design and Package Configurations
sections.description: LZC Photoreactor chamber design: uniform 12x12x8.5 inch chamber across four package configurations.
paragraphs: Getting uniform light across multiple samples starts with chamber geometry, and LZC solves it with a spacious, air-cooled 12 x 12 x 8.5 inch chamber that keeps every sample under consistent irradiation rather than a hot spot at the center.

Where the four packages differ is lamp placement. LZC-4V combines top and side illumination for full-coverage work and doubles as a two-wavelength platform with its included UVA and UVC lamp sets. LZC-1 concentrates eight lamps overhead for applications that call for top-down exposure specifically, and LZC-ORG runs ten side lamps for a different geometry entirely. LZC-4X offers a fourth configuration, and a related LZC-ICH2 unit shows up in the broader product lineup for specialized needs.

body: LZC Photoreactor lamp flexibility: tool-free wavelength changes and standard safety features.

A reactor that locks you into one wavelength stops being useful the moment your research changes direction. LZC lamps pull and swap without tools, so a new experiment with a different wavelength requirement doesn't mean a new reactor purchase.

That flexibility extends beyond Luzchem's own lamp range. The same hardware accepts the complete LZC-Series UV and visible fluorescent and LED lamp lineup, and much of that range is also compatible with many Rayonet reactors, useful if your lab already has lamps on hand from elsewhere. Every package backs that flexibility with the same safety foundation: an interlock that stops irradiation when the chamber opens, an integrated timer and hour meter for tracking exposure and lamp life, and a safe exhaust system for managing fumes during longer runs.

faqs.question: What is the Solar Simulator used for?
faqs.answer: It's a xenon-based light source built to match the ASTM G173 AM1.5 solar spectrum, used for sunscreen testing, photobiology, photodegradation studies, and pharmaceutical photostability testing.

faqs.question: How do I know my simulator is actually matching the AM1.5 spectrum?
faqs.answer: The included calibrated Sunmeter measures and confirms the AM1.5 match directly, rather than relying on the filter set alone.

faqs.question: Does this system need ventilation?
faqs.answer: No, the ozone-free xenon design removes that requirement for the lamp itself; ventilation is only needed if your own experimental byproducts call for it.

faqs.question: What's the difference between SolSim2, LZCX-ICH1, and LZCX-Xe?
faqs.answer: SolSim2 handles general AM1.5 solar simulation, LZCX-ICH1 carries ICH Option 1 certification for pharmaceutical photostability testing, and LZCX-Xe opens the same platform to your own custom filters.

faqs.question: How do I choose between a xenon-based system and LED-SOL?
faqs.answer: Choose a Xenon Series configuration if your work needs UV coverage; choose LED-SOL if your application stays in the visible and near-infrared range, such as photovoltaic or energy research.

faqs.question: Is this system certified for pharmaceutical stability testing?
faqs.answer: The LZCX-ICH1 configuration is certified for ICH Option 1 photostability testing specifically; confirm this configuration if your protocol requires that certification.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does the Solar Simulator cover?
faqs.answer: 300 to 800nm is the confirmed spectral interval for standard AM1.5 matching; the underlying xenon platform can extend further depending on configuration and filters chosen.

faqs.question: What power does the xenon lamp run at?

sections.glanceDescription: Solar Simulator overview: spectral matching, ozone-free design, and Xenon Series configuration options.
paragraphs: Solar Simulator overview: xenon-based AM1.5 solar spectrum matching for photostability and solar research.

Simulating sunlight well means being able to say exactly which reference standard your output matches, and SolSim2 is built to match ASTM G173, the AM1.5 solar spectrum most commonly cited in photostability and solar-driven research, across the 300 to 800 nm range.

The design runs ozone-free, which removes the mandatory ventilation requirement that standard ozone-generating xenon lamps carry, useful in labs without dedicated exhaust infrastructure already in place. A 300W xenon lamp with variable output power sits at the core, paired with the complete filter set needed to hold that AM1.5 match and a calibrated Sunmeter for confirming it's holding.

The same Xenon Series platform underneath SolSim2 also configures two other ways. LZCX-ICH1 carries certification for ICH Option 1 pharmaceutical photostability testing specifically, and LZCX-Xe opens the system up to your own custom filters for general photochemical research.

paragraphs: Matching a named standard rather than an approximate "sunlight-like" output is what separates a real solar simulator from a bright broadband lamp. ASTM G173 defines the AM1.5 solar spectrum, and the filter set included with every Xenon Series unit is what holds output to that spectrum across the confirmed 300-800nm interval.

The ozone-free build removes a real practical burden most xenon-based systems carry. Standard ozone-generating xenon lamps require dedicated ventilation because of the ozone they produce as a byproduct; this design doesn't generate that ozone in the first place, so ventilation only becomes necessary if your own experiment's byproducts require it, not because of the light source itself.

sections.tabSummary: Choosing SolSim2, LZCX-ICH1, LZCX-Xe, or LED-SOL
body: Solar Simulator configurations: SolSim2, LZCX-ICH1, LZCX-Xe, and the LED-based LED-SOL.

One xenon platform underneath three configurations means the right choice depends entirely on what you're testing against, not the hardware itself. SolSim2 is built for general controlled sunlight simulation. LZCX-ICH1 carries ICH Option 1 certification specifically, relevant if your photostability testing needs to meet that pharmaceutical standard directly rather than approximate it. LZCX-Xe opens the same core system to your own custom filters, useful when your research needs a spectral profile the standard AM1.5 filter set doesn't provide.

A separate LED-based system, LED-SOL, sits in the broader Solar range alongside the Xenon Series. It's AAA compliant and meets IEC60904-9 spectral, spatial, and temporal requirements, but covers visible and near-infrared only, not the UV range the xenon-based systems reach, making it suited specifically to energy and photovoltaic research rather than UV-dependent photostability work.

paragraphs: Two decisions shape how this system performs in your setup: which spectral range the lamp covers, and how the beam itself is delivered.

A full-spectrum UV lamp reaches down to 200 nm, suited to work that genuinely needs UV coverage at the shorter end of the range. An ozone-free lamp starts at 320 nm instead, removing UV-driven ozone generation from the equation for labs where that matters. On the beam side, a focused geometry concentrates light for applications like laser flash photolysis monitoring, while a parallel beam spreads illumination evenly across a wider field, useful for photovoltaic testing or broader sample exposure.

body: Cooling, status monitoring, and optional accessories on the Xenon Illuminator.
Running a high-intensity xenon lamp safely and reliably comes down to managing heat and keeping the operator informed, and both are built into the system directly.

The air-cooled housing, with its built-in fan and exhaust system, keeps lamp-generated heat under control during operation. Two indicator lights handle status communication: a Lamp-On indicator confirms the system is active, and a Replace-Lamp warning alerts you before declining lamp performance becomes a problem in your data. Beyond the base system, optional accessories extend what the illuminator can connect to and how operators stay protected, fiber optic adapters for coupling into spectroscopic instruments, filter clips for spectral control, and UV shielding for added operator safety.

sections.intro: WPI is built around a problem every high-throughput photochemistry screen runs into: getting the same light to land on well 1 and well 24 equally. A single light source spread across a plate almost never manages it. Twenty-four individual LEDs, one per well, each with its own optical guide and lens, does.
paragraphs: Illumination comes from below rather than above, running straight through a transparent plate or vial bottom. That same bottom-up design lets 4 mL auto-sampler vials drop directly into the plate format when the workflow calls for it, without switching to a different instrument.

Heat management runs on two fronts at once: the anodized aluminum body dissipates heat passively, and an integrated cooling fan keeps operating temperature stable through longer experiments, important with 24 LEDs running simultaneously rather than one.

sections.title: Wavelength Selection and PWM Intensity Control
sections.tabSummary: Choosing wavelength and dialing in intensity
body: Getting the right wavelength is only half the job in a screening experiment. The other half is controlling intensity without accidentally changing the wavelength that was just selected.

Nine wavelength options cover near UV through far red, plus lime and cool white as broad-spectrum choices, all fully characterized so exactly what's being delivered is never a guess. The optional PWM dimmer module solves the intensity problem specifically: instead of reducing current to dim the LED, which can shift its emission wavelength, PWM adjusts the duty cycle, how long the LED stays on during each rapid switching cycle, so spectral output stays exactly where it started even as irradiance changes.

Temperature ceiling depends on what else is running. Heat-only mode reaches up to 60°C, useful for straightforward thermal steps. body: Photoreactor XL automation: multi-stage program sequences and standard safety interlock.

A reaction that needs light for twenty minutes, then heat for ten, then both together, shouldn't require standing at the unit managing each transition manually. Photoreactor XL's onboard automation sets and recalls exactly that kind of sequence, so the same multi-stage protocol runs identically every time it's called up.

Safety and usability run alongside that automation rather than working against it. The door safety interlock stops operation the moment the chamber opens, the spacious window lets a run be checked visually without interrupting it, and the removable sample carousel makes loading and unloading between runs straightforward rather than fiddly.

sections.title: Chamber Design and Package Configurations
sections.description: LZC Photoreactor chamber design: uniform 12x12x8.5 inch chamber across four package configurations.
paragraphs: Getting uniform light across multiple samples starts with chamber geometry, and LZC solves it with a spacious, air-cooled 12 x 12 x 8.5 inch chamber that keeps every sample under consistent irradiation rather than a hot spot at the center.

Where the four packages differ is lamp placement. LZC-4V combines top and side illumination for full-coverage work and doubles as a two-wavelength platform with its included UVA and UVC lamp sets. LZC-1 concentrates eight lamps overhead for applications that call for top-down exposure specifically, and LZC-ORG runs ten side lamps for a different geometry entirely. LZC-4X offers a fourth configuration, and a related LZC-ICH2 unit shows up in the broader product lineup for specialized needs.

sections.title: Tool-Free Lamp Swapping and Safety Features
sections.tabSummary: Changing wavelengths and what ships standard
body: LZC Photoreactor lamp flexibility: tool-free wavelength changes and standard safety features.

A reactor that locks you into one wavelength stops being useful the moment your research changes direction. LZC lamps pull and swap without tools, so a new experiment with a different wavelength requirement doesn't mean a new reactor purchase.

That flexibility extends beyond Luzchem's own lamp range. The same hardware accepts the complete LZC-Series UV and visible fluorescent and LED lamp lineup, and much of that range is also compatible with many Rayonet reactors, useful if your lab already has lamps on hand from elsewhere. Every package backs that flexibility with the same safety foundation: an interlock that stops irradiation when the chamber opens, an integrated timer and hour meter for tracking exposure and lamp life, and a safe exhaust system for managing fumes during longer runs.

paragraphs: Solar Simulator overview: xenon-based AM1.5 solar spectrum matching for photostability and solar research.

Simulating sunlight well means being able to say exactly which reference standard your output matches, and SolSim2 is built to match ASTM G173, the AM1.5 solar spectrum most commonly cited in photostability and solar-driven research, across the 300 to 800 nm range.

The design runs ozone-free, which removes the mandatory ventilation requirement that standard ozone-generating xenon lamps carry, useful in labs without dedicated exhaust infrastructure already in place. A 300W xenon lamp with variable output power sits at the core, paired with the complete filter set needed to hold that AM1.5 match and a calibrated Sunmeter for confirming it's holding.

The same Xenon Series platform underneath SolSim2 also configures two other ways. LZCX-ICH1 carries certification for ICH Option 1 pharmaceutical photostability testing specifically, and LZCX-Xe opens the system up to your own custom filters for general photochemical research.

paragraphs: Matching a named standard rather than an approximate "sunlight-like" output is what separates a real solar simulator from a bright broadband lamp. ASTM G173 defines the AM1.5 solar spectrum, and the filter set included with every Xenon Series unit is what holds output to that spectrum across the confirmed 300-800nm interval.

The ozone-free build removes a real practical burden most xenon-based systems carry. Standard ozone-generating xenon lamps require dedicated ventilation because of the ozone they produce as a byproduct; this design doesn't generate that ozone in the first place, so ventilation only becomes necessary if your own experiment's byproducts require it, not because of the light source itself.

body: Solar Simulator configurations: SolSim2, LZCX-ICH1, LZCX-Xe, and the LED-based LED-SOL.

One xenon platform underneath three configurations means the right choice depends entirely on what you're testing against, not the hardware itself. SolSim2 is built for general controlled sunlight simulation. LZCX-ICH1 carries ICH Option 1 certification specifically, relevant if your photostability testing needs to meet that pharmaceutical standard directly rather than approximate it. LZCX-Xe opens the same core system to your own custom filters, useful when your research needs a spectral profile the standard AM1.5 filter set doesn't provide.

A separate LED-based system, LED-SOL, sits in the broader Solar range alongside the Xenon Series. It's AAA compliant and meets IEC60904-9 spectral, spatial, and temporal requirements, but covers visible and near-infrared only, not the UV range the xenon-based systems reach, making it suited specifically to energy and photovoltaic research rather than UV-dependent photostability work.

paragraphs: Two decisions shape how this system performs in your setup: which spectral range the lamp covers, and how the beam itself is delivered.

A full-spectrum UV lamp reaches down to 200 nm, suited to work that genuinely needs UV coverage at the shorter end of the range. An ozone-free lamp starts at 320 nm instead, removing UV-driven ozone generation from the equation for labs where that matters. body: Cooling, status monitoring, and optional accessories on the Xenon Illuminator.
Running a high-intensity xenon lamp safely and reliably comes down to managing heat and keeping the operator informed, and both are built into the system directly.

The air-cooled housing, with its built-in fan and exhaust system, keeps lamp-generated heat under control during operation. Two indicator lights handle status communication: a Lamp-On indicator confirms the system is active, and a Replace-Lamp warning alerts you before declining lamp performance becomes a problem in your data. Beyond the base system, optional accessories extend what the illuminator can connect to and how operators stay protected, fiber optic adapters for coupling into spectroscopic instruments, filter clips for spectral control, and UV shielding for added operator safety.

Series 4000 is built to scale with that journey rather than force a new system at every stage. It's a fully automated, computerized battery and cell test system built for batteries, supercapacitors, fuel cells, and other electrochemical devices, supporting virtually any battery chemistry. Configurations range from 1 to 192 test positions, each operating independently, and every system is custom manufactured to your specific requirements as a complete turnkey package, test cabinet, PC, tester software, and data analysis software, all connected and ready to run.

body: Every test position operates independently, so a fault or change on one channel doesn't affect testing running elsewhere in the system.
Systems scale from 1 to 192 test positions, and each one is custom manufactured according to your specific requirements rather than built to a single fixed configuration.

Multiple current ranges are supported, from a 150 µA full-scale range down to ±0.03 µA accuracy, up to a 5000 mA full-scale range, giving precise control across very different cell sizes and chemistries.
A single current range option is also available, supporting up to 2000 A at ±0.05% full-scale accuracy for high-current applications.
Voltage measurement runs from -2V to +8V or 0V to +10V, at ±0.02% full-scale accuracy with 16-bit resolution.

Testing supports multi-step and pulse profiles, programmable across Constant Current, Constant Power, Constant Voltage, Constant Resistance, 1 kHz AC impedance measurement, and Voltage Ramp for cyclic voltammetry.
Data can be recorded at user-defined intervals, with a minimum step time of 10 ms as standard, and 5 ms or 1 ms available as options for faster testing needs.
Calibration is NIST-traceable and only needs to happen once per year, reducing the ongoing maintenance burden on your lab.

The complete system is turnkey: a test cabinet, PC computer, tester software, and data analysis software, all connected over a 10 Base-T LAN network and controlled by embedded microprocessors that handle test control and data collection independently at each position.

sections.title: Testing Modes and Precision
body: A single test system rarely needs to handle only one kind of cell, and the Series 4000 is built around that reality with both flexible test modes and a genuinely wide precision range.

Six programmable modes cover the core of most testing protocols: Constant Current and Constant Power for standard charge and discharge cycling, Constant Voltage and Constant Resistance for specific hold or load conditions, 1 kHz AC Impedance Measurement for internal resistance characterization, and Voltage Ramp for cyclic voltammetry work. Underpinning all of these, four selectable current ranges, from a sensitive 150 µA full-scale range down to ±0.03 µA accuracy, up to a 5000 mA full-scale range, let the same system handle small research cells and larger production cells without losing measurement precision at either end. For applications needing even higher current, a single current range option extends up to 2000 A at ±0.05% full-scale accuracy.

sections.title: Available Options and Expandability
body: A test system's usefulness often depends on what it can connect to, not just what it measures on its own, and the Series 4000's option list reflects that.

Multiplexer support enables EIS integration across more channels, while telecom pulsing profiles cover GSM, CDMA, and GPRS testing scenarios. For labs working with sensor-rich test setups, thermocouple, thermistor, RTD (PT100/PT1000), pressure, reference electrode, auxiliary voltage, and pH inputs are all available, alongside digital inputs and outputs for broader lab integration. External charge and load controllers extend current handling from 5 to 200 A, and environmental chamber control, cell holders, and UPS support round out a genuinely complete test environment. Maccor also offers ongoing calibration and maintenance services to keep the system running at spec.
Product expert note: Tell our team which sensors, controllers, or environmental conditions your protocols require, and Inkarp will confirm the right set of options for your system.

sections.title: 3-Electrode Measurements and Thermal Data
body: Some research questions can't be answered with a simple two-terminal cell measurement, and that's exactly where this system's additional capabilities come in.

3-electrode measurement support lets researchers isolate the behavior of a working electrode against a separate reference electrode, with a counter electrode completing the circuit, a setup that matters for detailed electrochemical characterization work rather than just overall cell performance. Alongside that, an optional thermocouple input allows temperature to be recorded directly alongside electrical measurements, useful when a research question depends on understanding how performance shifts with thermal conditions rather than assuming a constant temperature throughout testing.

sections.title: Channel Configurations and Research Fit
body: Research testing rarely needs the same channel count as production QC, and the Model 4300's configuration options reflect that difference directly.

A single-channel setup suits focused, one-off characterization work, while 2 or 4-channel configurations fit small research groups running a handful of parallel studies. The 8-channel option scales further for labs running broader comparative studies across multiple cell variants or formulations at once. Because every configuration runs on the same underlying Series 4000 technology, moving between channel counts as a research program grows doesn't mean giving up precision or test mode flexibility.

sections.title: Telecom Pulse Testing Explained
body: A phone battery doesn't discharge smoothly. It's hit with short, sharp current demands every time the device transmits, and that pulse behavior is exactly what telecom protocols are built to reproduce.

GSM, CDMA, and iDEN each define their own specific pulse timing and current characteristics, shaped by how those network technologies actually communicate. Testing a cell against those exact profiles, rather than a generic charge-discharge cycle, is what reveals how a battery will genuinely perform in telecom or mobile device use. The Model 4304's dedicated Pulse Testing mode, combined with its wide current range down to 300 nA, gives it the sensitivity to capture that rapid, variable current behavior accurately.

sections.title: Test Mode Range and Software
body: Telecom pulse testing is the specialty here, but it isn't the whole story. Seven distinct test modes make this a genuinely capable general-purpose research tool as well.

Standard Constant Current, Constant Voltage, Constant Power, and Constant Resistance modes cover typical cycling and characterization work. AC Impedance measurement supports internal resistance and material studies, while Cyclic Voltammetry opens up electrochemical characterization beyond simple charge-discharge behavior. Pulse Testing rounds out the set, purpose-built for the telecom protocols the system is named for. All of this runs through Maccor's MacTest32 software, handling test control and data management across every mode.

sections.title: 3-Electrode Measurements and Thermal Data
body: Some research questions can't be answered with a simple two-terminal cell measurement, and that's exactly where this system's additional capabilities come in.

3-electrode measurement support lets researchers isolate the behavior of a working electrode against a separate reference electrode, with a counter electrode completing the circuit, a setup that matters for detailed electrochemical characterization work rather than just overall cell performance. Alongside that, an optional thermocouple input allows temperature to be recorded directly alongside electrical measurements, useful when a research question depends on understanding how performance shifts with thermal conditions rather than assuming a constant temperature throughout testing.
sections.disclaimer: Product expert note: Tell our team whether your protocols require 3-electrode setups or temperature correlation, and Inkarp will confirm the right configuration.

sections.title: Channel Configurations and Research Fit
body: Research testing rarely needs the same channel count as production QC, and the Model 4300's configuration options reflect that difference directly.

A single-channel setup suits focused, one-off characterization work, while 2 or 4-channel configurations fit small research groups running a handful of parallel studies. The 8-channel option scales further for labs running broader comparative studies across multiple cell variants or formulations at once. Because every configuration runs on the same underlying Series 4000 technology, moving between channel counts as a research program grows doesn't mean giving up precision or test mode flexibility.

sections.title: Telecom Pulse Testing Explained
body: A phone battery doesn't discharge smoothly. It's hit with short, sharp current demands every time the device transmits, and that pulse behavior is exactly what telecom protocols are built to reproduce.

GSM, CDMA, and iDEN each define their own specific pulse timing and current characteristics, shaped by how those network technologies actually communicate. Testing a cell against those exact profiles, rather than a generic charge-discharge cycle, is what reveals how a battery will genuinely perform in telecom or mobile device use. The Model 4304's dedicated Pulse Testing mode, combined with its wide current range down to 300 nA, gives it the sensitivity to capture that rapid, variable current behavior accurately.

sections.title: Test Mode Range and Software

Standard Constant Current, Constant Voltage, Constant Power, and Constant Resistance modes cover typical cycling and characterization work. AC Impedance measurement supports internal resistance and material studies, while Cyclic Voltammetry opens up electrochemical characterization beyond simple charge-discharge behavior. Pulse Testing rounds out the set, purpose-built for the telecom protocols the system is named for. All of this runs through Maccor's MacTest32 software, handling test control and data management across every mode.

sections.description: Learn what barcode-driven method loading actually removes from routine water testing on the Mettler Toledo Easy UV.
body: Running a Spectroquant® water test kit normally means finding the right method in a menu, matching it to the specific kit and parameter being tested, and setting it up correctly before the actual measurement can happen. ScanStart™, paired with the handheld barcode scanner, removes it. Scan the 2D barcode printed on the test kit, and Easy UV loads the correct method automatically, no menu search, no manual matching. The SQKitReader™ option extends this further, reading the barcode with an internal reader built into the instrument itself.

longForm.heroHook: 3 samples at once. Up to 300°C. One click to a recorded result.
longForm.heroLead: MP30 is Mettler Toledo's starter melting point system, and it doesn't compromise on the fundamentals. It determines melting point and melting range for up to 3 capillaries simultaneously, across a temperature range from room temperature to 300°C, with a heating rate adjustable from 0.1°C to 20°C per minute. A color video of the transition is recorded automatically, one video stored per run, so the actual melt is visible, not just inferred from a temperature reading. Results export as PDF reports or to a USB stick. The 7" color touchscreen and support for multiple users make it straightforward to operate across a shared lab bench.

sections.title: One Click™ to a Recorded Result
sections.description: Learn what video capture actually adds to melting point determination on the Mettler Toledo MP30.
body: Traditional melting point determination relies on an operator watching a capillary and noting when melting starts and ends, a process that's inherently subjective and hard to verify after the fact. MP30 records a color video of the transition automatically, so the actual melt is captured and stored, not just summarized as a number.

That matters for two reasons: a stored video gives a second reviewer something concrete to check a borderline result against, and it gives a lab a genuine record of what was observed, not just what was concluded. Combined with 4 One Clicks™ that streamline the operational steps, MP30 turns a subjective, manual process into a documented, repeatable one.

sections.eyebrow: Temperature Compensation and Output Units Explained
sections.title: Temperature Compensation and Output Units Explained
sections.description: What automatic compensation and multi-format output actually solve for a portable density meter.
body: Density readings change with temperature, so a measurement taken on a warm sample in production and one taken later on a cooled sample in the lab can genuinely disagree, even if nothing about the sample itself has changed. That's a real problem for a handheld meter meant to be used wherever the sample happens to be, not just in a temperature-controlled lab.

Densito compensates for temperature automatically, so the reading reflects the sample's actual density rather than the temperature it happened to be measured at. Pairing that with output in specific gravity, Brix, API units, or other formats means the result comes out in whatever unit the process already works in, rather than requiring a manual conversion afterward.

body: Manual density testing depends on the operator to load each sample, correct for viscosity, and record the result correctly, and a lab running many samples a day repeats that dependency every single time. A bubble trapped in the measuring cell or an uncorrected viscous sample can quietly skew a result without ever being obvious to the operator.

Excellence D4 automates both problems: BubbleCheck™ catches trapped air before it affects the reading, automatic viscosity correction removes the manual adjustment, and the optional autosampler runs up to 303 samples without an operator loading each one by hand. LabX connectivity then carries that same automation into the compliance side, capturing results with a full audit trail rather than depending on manual transcription.

sections.title: Loss-on-Drying and Switch-Off Criteria Explained
sections.description: How HE53 actually decides when a sample has finished drying, rather than just running a fixed timer.
body: Loss-on-drying moisture testing works by heating a sample and tracking how much weight it loses as moisture evaporates, but knowing when to stop matters as much as the heating itself. Stop too early and the reading understates moisture content; run too long and the result can drift as the sample begins to degrade rather than simply dry.

HE53's automatic switch-off (SOC 3) monitors the rate of weight loss and ends the test once the sample has genuinely stopped losing moisture, rather than running to a fixed time regardless of the sample. A timed switch-off is also available for sample types where a fixed drying duration is the better fit.

body: Setting up a moisture test correctly, choosing the right temperature, drying program, and switch-off criteria for a given sample, normally depends on the operator's experience with that specific material, and getting it wrong means either an inaccurate result or wasted time re-running the test. HX204's QuickPredict™ analyzes the drying curve as it develops and estimates the final moisture value before the test physically finishes, giving an early, reliable read without cutting the actual test short.

HX204's full 21 CFR Part 11 compliance, control charts, and automatic centralized result collection with LabX mean every test is captured, timestamped, and tied to an auditable record from the moment it runs, not reconstructed from a printout afterward.

performance.title: Automatic Sample Weight Transfer Explained
performance.description: What removing a manual data-entry step actually prevents in a routine titration workflow.
body: A titration result is only as accurate as the sample weight it's calculated against, and manually typing that weight into the titrator introduces a genuine risk: a transposed digit, a missed decimal point, or simply the wrong sample's weight entered against the wrong run. That error doesn't show up as an obviously wrong result, it just quietly skews the calculation.
EasyPlus Easy pH's automatic sample weight transfer removes that step entirely, taking the weight directly from a connected balance rather than depending on the operator to type it in correctly.

performance.title: Acid/Base, Precipitation, and Redox Titration Explained
performance.description: What each of Easy Pro's three titration types actually determines, and why covering all three in one instrument matters.
body: Different sample parameters need fundamentally different titration chemistry: acid/base titration measures acidity or alkalinity, precipitation titration determines ions that form an insoluble compound with the titrant, such as chloride, and redox titration measures oxidation-reduction based parameters. A lab testing a varied product range often needs all three at different times, and running three separate single-method instruments for that is both more expensive and more bench space than the testing volume usually justifies.

Easy Pro consolidates all three into one instrument, so a food or chemical lab covering acidity, precipitation-based, and redox-based parameters doesn't need to own, calibrate, and maintain three separate titrators to do it.

performance.title: Volumetric Karl Fischer Titration Explained
performance.description: What Easy KF V actually measures, and why the 100 ppm to 100% range matters.
body: Water content is one of the most common things a lab needs to verify, whether that's confirming a chemical is dry enough to use, checking a food product's moisture level, or verifying a raw material meets spec. Karl Fischer titration measures that directly and precisely, reacting the sample's water content with Karl Fischer reagent and calculating the exact amount present.

Easy KF V's 100 ppm to 100% range means the same instrument covers both trace-level moisture checks and samples that are mostly water, without needing a different method or instrument for each end of that range. Volumetric KF, as opposed to coulometric, is generally the right fit for the higher end of that range, where enough water is present to titrate directly.

InMotion or Rondolino automation layers on top of that, taking the same instrument from manual sample loading to running up to 303 samples per analysis without an operator present for each one.

performance.title: Burette Dispensing Resolution and LOQ Explained
performance.description: What 120,000 dispensing steps and a 0.2 mg limit of quantification actually mean for the accuracy of a result.
body: A titrator's burette resolution determines how finely it can add reagent, and a coarser burette means a coarser titration curve, which shows up as noise in the final result, especially at low water levels where every increment matters. EVA V1's 120,000-step resolution gives it a genuinely fine dispensing curve, tested to DIN/ISO 8655-3 for accuracy and precision rather than just stated.

The limit of quantification, 0.2 mg water per sample at 1% RSD, is the practical consequence of that resolution: it's the smallest water content EVA V1 can reliably report with confidence, not just detect. For a lab testing genuinely low-moisture samples, that number matters more than almost any other spec on the sheet.

performance.title: Coulometric vs Volumetric Karl Fischer Explained
performance.description: Why EVA C1 reaches micrograms of water where EVA V1's volumetric method works in milligrams.
body: Volumetric Karl Fischer titration adds a KF reagent of known concentration until the reaction with water completes, and the amount added tells you how much water was present, a method well suited to samples with a reasonable amount of water. Coulometric KF titration works differently: it generates the reactive iodine electrochemically, in situ, and measures the electric charge needed to do it, which lets it detect and quantify far smaller amounts of water with far greater sensitivity.

That's the difference between EVA V1's 100 ppm to 100% volumetric range and EVA C1's 0.01 to 200 mg coulometric range with a 2 µg detection limit: coulometric titration is built for exactly the trace end that volumetric titration isn't precise enough to reach reliably.

performance.title: ISM Sensor Recognition Explained
performance.description: What automatic sensor recognition actually removes from routine pH calibration.
body: Every pH sensor has its own calibration history and characteristics, and manually re-entering that information every time a sensor is connected, or worse, using the wrong calibration data with the wrong sensor, is a genuine source of measurement error. That risk grows in a shared lab where sensors get swapped between meters or operators.

SD20's Intelligent Sensor Management (ISM) reads the sensor's own stored data the moment it's connected, calibration history included, so the meter recognizes exactly which sensor is attached and configures itself accordingly, without the operator entering anything manually.

performance.title: Wide-Range Conductivity Measurement Explained

body: Conductivity spans an enormous range in practice, from ultra-pure water at a few μS/cm to concentrated process solutions in the mS/cm range, and a sensor built for only one end of that scale either loses accuracy or can't measure at all outside its designed band. performance.title: Ion-Selective Electrode Measurement Explained
performance.description: What pX and ppm actually tell you, and why SD50 reports both.
body: Ion-selective electrodes measure the concentration of one specific ion in a sample, chloride, fluoride, sodium, and others, but the unit that concentration gets reported in depends on who's reading it. Chemists often work in pX, the negative logarithm of the ion's activity, the same style of unit as pH itself, while a QC report or regulatory spec is more likely to want a direct concentration in mg/L or ppm.
SD50 reports both, with auto-ranging 3- or 4-digit resolution, so a result doesn't need converting by hand to match whichever unit the lab's paperwork actually uses.

performance.title: Modular Measurement and DES Sensor Diagnostics Explained
performance.description: What upgrading for more parameters, and a newer digital sensor platform, actually solve for a growing lab.
body: Buying a fixed, single-parameter meter is a fine choice on day one, but a lab's testing needs rarely stay fixed. Adding a second parameter later usually means buying a second meter entirely, doubling the calibration routines, the bench space, and the instruments to maintain. NF2000's base module is built to be upgraded instead, adding parameters to the same unit rather than replacing it.

performance.title: Pure-Water Conductivity Sensors Explained
performance.description: Why a generalist conductivity probe isn't the right tool at the pure-water end of the scale.
body: A generalist conductivity sensor is built to handle a wide range reasonably well, but "reasonably well" at both ends of a range spanning 0.001 μS/cm to 2000 mS/cm usually means genuine compromises at the extremes. At the low end, in purified or ultra-pure water, a sensor not specifically designed for it can struggle to hold accuracy where the conductivity signal itself is faint.

NF3000's InLab 741 Pro-DES sensor is built specifically for pure water, rather than adapted from a generalist design, which matters most for pharmaceutical water systems, semiconductor rinse water, and any lab where the samples sit consistently at the low, sensitive end of the conductivity scale.

performance.title: Two Measurement Modules Explained
performance.description: What running two DES sensors on one modular base actually means, versus a fixed dual-parameter instrument.
body: A fixed dual-parameter meter measures exactly two parameters, permanently, and adding a third means buying a different instrument entirely. NF2300 works differently: it ships with two measurement modules, one for pH and one for conductivity, but sits on the same modular NineFocus base as NF2000 and NF3000, which is built to accept further modules later.

That distinction matters for a lab whose testing needs might grow past pH and conductivity. Rather than replacing NF2300 outright, the base module can be upgraded, the same pattern that runs through the whole NineFocus line, where SevenDirect's fixed-parameter meters would need a full replacement instead.

performance.title: LE703 Sensor Range Explained
performance.description: What "medium to high conductivities" actually means for choosing the right sensor.
body: Conductivity spans several orders of magnitude in practice, and no single sensor design covers the entire range equally well. LE703, the probe included with FP30-Std, is built specifically for the 10 μS/cm to 200 mS/cm range, medium to high conductivities, which covers most process solutions, buffers, and general laboratory samples.

For genuinely low-conductivity samples, purified or ultra-pure water in the low μS/cm range, a different sensor, such as the LE740 built for 0.01 μS/cm to 500 μS/cm, is the better fit. Choosing the right sensor for the sample's actual conductivity range matters more than the meter itself once the sample sits outside a probe's designed band.

performance.title: Piece Counting and Dynamic Weighing Explained
performance.description: What LA204's two built-in apps take off a routine lab's plate.
body: Counting small components by hand is slow and error-prone past a handful of pieces, and weighing anything that shifts, settles, or breathes on the pan, powders, granules, or restless small samples, makes the reading drift before it stabilizes. LA204's two built-in apps are built around exactly those two everyday problems.

The piece counting app establishes an average unit weight from a reference sample, then converts any weighed batch into a piece count automatically. The dynamic weighing app takes repeated readings over a short window and calculates a stable average, so an unsettled sample still returns a trustworthy result instead of a fluctuating one.

performance.title: Guided Leveling and Automatic Adjustment Explained
performance.description: What FACT adjustment and leveling guidance actually remove from getting MR204 set up correctly.
body: An analytical balance that isn't level reads wrong before a single sample even touches the pan, and getting it level by eye, watching a bubble indicator and adjusting feet by feel, is easy to get slightly wrong without noticing. MR204's guided leveling walks the operator through the process on-screen, step by step, until the instrument confirms it's actually level.

Calibration drift is the same problem in a different form. FACT, MR204's automatic internal adjustment, monitors conditions and triggers a self-calibration using a built-in reference mass whenever it's needed, rather than waiting for a scheduled manual check or an operator who remembers to run one.

faqs.question: What is the MX205DU used for?
faqs.answer: Dual-range analytical weighing for pharma labs that need both micro-scale precision and everyday weighing capacity in one instrument.

faqs.question: What does dual-range mean on this balance?
faqs.answer: MX205DU switches automatically between two working ranges: 0.01 mg readability up to 82 g for micro-scale samples, and 0.1 mg readability up to 220 g for everyday capacity, without recalibrating or changing instruments.

faqs.question: What is the repeatability?
faqs.answer: 0.0125 mg, typical.

faqs.question: What is the minimum weight?
faqs.answer: 25 mg (USP, 0.1%, typical); 2.5 mg (U=1%, k=2, typical).

faqs.question: Does it need external weights for calibration?
faqs.answer: No, MX205DU uses internal automatic (FACT) adjustment, calibrating itself using a built-in reference mass without external weights.

faqs.question: What connectivity options are available?
faqs.answer: Ethernet (LAN), USB-A, USB-C, and an optional Bluetooth interface.

faqs.question: How do I switch between the fine and coarse weighing ranges?
faqs.answer: SmartPan technology handles the switch automatically based on the sample weight, moving from 0.01 mg readability up to 82 g to 0.1 mg readability up to 220 g without manual reconfiguration.

faqs.question: Is it a legal-for-trade approved balance?
faqs.answer: No, MX205DU is not an approved balance.

faqs.question: What is the difference between MX205DU and MX204?
faqs.answer: MX204 is a single-range balance with 0.05 mg repeatability up to 220 g, while MX205DU adds a second, finer range, 0.01 mg readability up to 82 g, for labs that need micro-scale precision as well as everyday capacity.

performance.title: GxP Compliance and LabX Connectivity Explained
performance.description: What a regulated lab actually needs from a balance, and where MX204 delivers it.
body: A weighing result in a GxP-regulated environment has to survive an audit, not just be accurate in the moment. That means the data trail matters as much as the number on the display: who weighed it, when, on what instrument, and whether the record can be tampered with after the fact. A balance that isn't built for that leaves the audit trail to manual logbooks and printouts, both easy to lose and easy to challenge.

MX204 is built GxP-compliant from the ground up, and connects directly to Mettler Toledo's LabX software, so weighing results move into a controlled, traceable record automatically rather than depending on someone transcribing a number correctly.

performance.title: IP43 and Passcode Protection Explained
performance.description: What durability and access control actually add in a lab that isn't a clean, controlled analytical bench.
body: A precision balance handling larger, everyday samples usually lives in a busier corner of the lab than an analytical balance: more dust in the air, more chance of a splash, more hands using it across a shift. Neither of those risks stops accurate weighing on their own, but together they wear down an instrument that isn't built for the environment, and they open the door to settings being changed by whoever's standing there.

MA1002's IP43 rating protects against dust ingress and splashing water, and passcode protection restricts who can access or change balance settings, so the instrument holds up physically and the configuration stays under control, regardless of how busy or shared the bench gets.

performance.title: Solid Base and Overload Protection Explained
performance.description: What a metal base and overload guard actually protect against on a busy bench.
body: A precision balance handling larger, heavier samples faces two everyday risks a lighter analytical balance rarely sees: the instrument itself shifting or tipping under an off-center load, and a sample or vessel accidentally set down too hard or too heavy for the pan. Either one can throw off a reading or damage the mechanism over time.

LA2002's solid metal base keeps the instrument planted regardless of how a sample is placed, and its overload protection guards the internal mechanism against a load beyond the 2.2 kg rating, absorbing the impact rather than passing it through.

performance.title: Capacity Without Compromise Explained
performance.description: Why MA6002 can weigh more than five times MA1002's capacity without losing a digit of readability.
body: A common assumption with weighing instruments is that capacity and precision trade off against each other, a bigger balance reads coarser, because that's often true across a manufacturer's full range. It's not true within this specific MA precision line: MA1002 and MA6002 share the identical 0.01 g readability, 7 mg repeatability, and 1-second settling time, on the same 180 x 180 mm pan and the same chassis dimensions.

The difference sits entirely in the internal load cell and calibration range, engineered to handle up to 6.2 kg while holding the same measurement resolution MA1002 delivers at 1,200 g. For a lab choosing between the two, the decision comes down to sample size, not a precision trade-off.

performance.description: What automation actually removes from a routine that repeats trace-level weighing many times a day.
body: Trace-level weighing at 1 µg readability is precise enough on a single measurement, but a routine that repeats the same weighing steps dozens of times a day introduces its own risk: a skipped step, an inconsistent sequence, or a small variation in how each sample is handled compounds across a batch. XPR3's automated workflows guide the operator through a fixed, repeatable sequence, so every sample in a batch goes through the same steps in the same order, with the balance itself enforcing the routine rather than relying on the operator's memory of the process.

sections.title: One Click™ to a Recorded Result
sections.description: Learn what video capture actually adds to melting point determination on the Mettler Toledo MP30.
body: Traditional melting point determination relies on an operator watching a capillary and noting when melting starts and ends, a process that's inherently subjective and hard to verify after the fact. MP30 records a color video of the transition automatically, so the actual melt is captured and stored, not just summarized as a number.

That matters for two reasons: a stored video gives a second reviewer something concrete to check a borderline result against, and it gives a lab a genuine record of what was observed, not just what was concluded. Combined with 4 One Clicks™ that streamline the operational steps, MP30 turns a subjective, manual process into a documented, repeatable one.

sections.eyebrow: Temperature Compensation and Output Units Explained
sections.title: Temperature Compensation and Output Units Explained
sections.description: What automatic compensation and multi-format output actually solve for a portable density meter.
body: Density readings change with temperature, so a measurement taken on a warm sample in production and one taken later on a cooled sample in the lab can genuinely disagree, even if nothing about the sample itself has changed. That's a real problem for a handheld meter meant to be used wherever the sample happens to be, not just in a temperature-controlled lab.

Densito compensates for temperature automatically, so the reading reflects the sample's actual density rather than the temperature it happened to be measured at. Pairing that with output in specific gravity, Brix, API units, or other formats means the result comes out in whatever unit the process already works in, rather than requiring a manual conversion afterward.

sections.title: Loss-on-Drying and Switch-Off Criteria Explained
sections.description: How HE53 actually decides when a sample has finished drying, rather than just running a fixed timer.
body: Loss-on-drying moisture testing works by heating a sample and tracking how much weight it loses as moisture evaporates, but knowing when to stop matters as much as the heating itself. Stop too early and the reading understates moisture content; run too long and the result can drift as the sample begins to degrade rather than simply dry.

HE53's automatic switch-off (SOC 3) monitors the rate of weight loss and ends the test once the sample has genuinely stopped losing moisture, rather than running to a fixed time regardless of the sample. A timed switch-off is also available for sample types where a fixed drying duration is the better fit.

sections.description: What guided method setup and live drying visibility actually remove from testing a new sample type.
body: Setting up a moisture test correctly, choosing the right temperature, drying program, and switch-off criteria for a given sample, normally depends on the operator's experience with that specific material, and getting it wrong means either an inaccurate result or wasted time re-running the test. That's a bigger problem in a lab handling many different sample types than in one running the same method every day.

HC103's Method Wizard walks the operator through parameter selection step by step, and the Temperature Assistant helps identify the right drying temperature for materials the operator hasn't tested before. Once a test is running, the real-time drying curve on the touchscreen shows exactly how the sample is losing weight over time, so an unusual drying pattern is visible as it happens, not just in the final result.

sections.description: What real multi-operator governance and long-term trend tracking add to an instrument multiple people rely on.
body: A moisture analyzer shared across a shift, or across a whole lab, faces two risks a single-operator instrument doesn't: someone changing a setting they shouldn't, and no one noticing a slow drift in performance until a result finally looks wrong. Neither is a single bad reading, both are slower, harder-to-catch problems.

HS153's 10 customizable user groups and up to 30 user profiles let a lab define exactly who can access what, backed by auto-lock and password protection. Control charts address the second problem directly, plotting instrument performance over time so drift shows up as a trend on a chart, not as a surprise result months later.

performance.title: Automatic Sample Weight Transfer Explained
performance.description: What removing a manual data-entry step actually prevents in a routine titration workflow.
body: A titration result is only as accurate as the sample weight it's calculated against, and manually typing that weight into the titrator introduces a genuine risk: a transposed digit, a missed decimal point, or simply the wrong sample's weight entered against the wrong run. That error doesn't show up as an obviously wrong result, it just quietly skews the calculation.
EasyPlus Easy pH's automatic sample weight transfer removes that step entirely, taking the weight directly from a connected balance rather than depending on the operator to type it in correctly.

performance.title: Acid/Base, Precipitation, and Redox Titration Explained
performance.description: What each of Easy Pro's three titration types actually determines, and why covering all three in one instrument matters.
body: Different sample parameters need fundamentally different titration chemistry: acid/base titration measures acidity or alkalinity, precipitation titration determines ions that form an insoluble compound with the titrant, such as chloride, and redox titration measures oxidation-reduction based parameters. A lab testing a varied product range often needs all three at different times, and running three separate single-method instruments for that is both more expensive and more bench space than the testing volume usually justifies.

Easy Pro consolidates all three into one instrument, so a food or chemical lab covering acidity, precipitation-based, and redox-based parameters doesn't need to own, calibrate, and maintain three separate titrators to do it.

performance.title: Volumetric Karl Fischer Titration Explained
performance.description: What Easy KF V actually measures, and why the 100 ppm to 100% range matters.
body: Water content is one of the most common things a lab needs to verify, whether that's confirming a chemical is dry enough to use, checking a food product's moisture level, or verifying a raw material meets spec. Karl Fischer titration measures that directly and precisely, reacting the sample's water content with Karl Fischer reagent and calculating the exact amount present.

Easy KF V's 100 ppm to 100% range means the same instrument covers both trace-level moisture checks and samples that are mostly water, without needing a different method or instrument for each end of that range. Volumetric KF, as opposed to coulometric, is generally the right fit for the higher end of that range, where enough water is present to titrate directly.

performance.title: Burette Dispensing Resolution and LOQ Explained
performance.description: What 120,000 dispensing steps and a 0.2 mg limit of quantification actually mean for the accuracy of a result.
body: A titrator's burette resolution determines how finely it can add reagent, and a coarser burette means a coarser titration curve, which shows up as noise in the final result, especially at low water levels where every increment matters. EVA V1's 120,000-step resolution gives it a genuinely fine dispensing curve, tested to DIN/ISO 8655-3 for accuracy and precision rather than just stated.

The limit of quantification, 0.2 mg water per sample at 1% RSD, is the practical consequence of that resolution: it's the smallest water content EVA V1 can reliably report with confidence, not just detect. For a lab testing genuinely low-moisture samples, that number matters more than almost any other spec on the sheet.

performance.title: Coulometric vs Volumetric Karl Fischer Explained
performance.description: Why EVA C1 reaches micrograms of water where EVA V1's volumetric method works in milligrams.
body: Volumetric Karl Fischer titration adds a KF reagent of known concentration until the reaction with water completes, and the amount added tells you how much water was present, a method well suited to samples with a reasonable amount of water. Coulometric KF titration works differently: it generates the reactive iodine electrochemically, in situ, and measures the electric charge needed to do it, which lets it detect and quantify far smaller amounts of water with far greater sensitivity.

That's the difference between EVA V1's 100 ppm to 100% volumetric range and EVA C1's 0.01 to 200 mg coulometric range with a 2 µg detection limit: coulometric titration is built for exactly the trace end that volumetric titration isn't precise enough to reach reliably.

faqs.question: What is the EVA C1 used for?
faqs.answer: Trace-level coulometric Karl Fischer titration, for water-content determination in liquids, soluble solids, and insoluble solids at the microgram level.

faqs.question: What is the limit of detection?
faqs.answer: 2 µg.

faqs.question: What is the measurement range?
faqs.answer: 0.01 to 200 mg water, at ±0.3% precision.

faqs.question: What is the difference between coulometric and volumetric Karl Fischer?
faqs.answer: Coulometric titration generates the reactive iodine electrochemically and measures the charge needed, allowing detection of far smaller water quantities than volumetric titration, which adds a reagent of known concentration and suits higher water content.

faqs.question: What is the difference between EVA C1 and EVA V1?
faqs.answer: EVA C1 is coulometric, built for trace water content down to 2 µg, while EVA V1 is volumetric, built for the higher 100 ppm to 100% range; they cover opposite ends of the water-content scale.

faqs.question: Does it support insoluble solid samples?
faqs.answer: Yes, alongside liquids and soluble solids, a broader sample range than EVA V1 supports.

faqs.question: Does it include an automated solvent exchange system?
faqs.answer: Yes, it's included as part of the standard package for safer, more efficient day-to-day operation.

performance.title: ISM Sensor Recognition Explained
performance.description: What automatic sensor recognition actually removes from routine pH calibration.
body: Every pH sensor has its own calibration history and characteristics, and manually re-entering that information every time a sensor is connected, or worse, using the wrong calibration data with the wrong sensor, is a genuine source of measurement error. That risk grows in a shared lab where sensors get swapped between meters or operators.

SD20's Intelligent Sensor Management (ISM) reads the sensor's own stored data the moment it's connected, calibration history included, so the meter recognizes exactly which sensor is attached and configures itself accordingly, without the operator entering anything manually.

performance.title: Wide-Range Conductivity Measurement Explained
performance.description: What one sensor covering 0.001 μS/cm to 2000 mS/cm actually removes from routine testing.
body: Conductivity spans an enormous range in practice, from ultra-pure water at a few μS/cm to concentrated process solutions in the mS/cm range, and a sensor built for only one end of that scale either loses accuracy or can't measure at all outside its designed band.
