longForm.heroHook: 45 kg on the stage, 300 × 300 mm of sample, and a standard system you can order today.
longForm.heroLead: Large-sample AFM usually means one of two things: a scan head that needs a stage designed around it, or a full bespoke engineering project with a scoping phase before anything is quoted. Alphacen 300 Flex is neither. It's a complete, standard system — Flex-Mount scan head, CX controller, dedicated acoustic enclosure — that handles samples up to 300 × 300 mm and 45 kg out of the box, with a 50 mm z approach stage so thick samples mount without difficulty. The performance comes from proven parts. The tip-scanner design means imaging quality holds regardless of sample size or weight, because the tip moves and the sample doesn't. The flexure-based scanner from Nanosurf's FlexAFM delivers flat, linear scanning at 100 µm range. The CX controller is Nanosurf's most advanced, giving fast and precise control over the scan process. The acoustic enclosure handles external noise and vibration as part of the system. And when the requirement outgrows it, the same system becomes the basis for a custom solution — additional translation or rotation axes on the sample positioning system and the scan head alike.

heroParagraphs: Large-sample AFM usually means one of two things: a scan head that needs a stage designed around it, or a full bespoke engineering project with a scoping phase before anything is quoted.

Alphacen 300 Flex is neither. It's a complete, standard system — Flex-Mount scan head, CX controller, dedicated acoustic enclosure — that handles samples up to 300 × 300 mm and 45 kg out of the box, with a 50 mm z approach stage so thick samples mount without difficulty.

The performance comes from proven parts. The tip-scanner design means imaging quality holds regardless of sample size or weight, because the tip moves and the sample doesn't. The flexure-based scanner from Nanosurf's FlexAFM delivers flat, linear scanning at 100 µm range. The CX controller is Nanosurf's most advanced, giving fast and precise control over the scan process. The acoustic enclosure handles external noise and vibration as part of the system.
And when the requirement outgrows it, the same system becomes the basis for a custom solution — additional translation or rotation axes on the sample positioning system and the scan head alike.

faqs.question: What is LensAFM used for?
faqs.answer: It's an atomic force microscope that mounts on an optical microscope or profilometer turret, extending resolution and measurement capability beyond the optical limit for surface inspection, defect analysis, and material property characterization.

faqs.question: How does LensAFM mount to a microscope?
faqs.answer: It mounts like a normal objective lens on the turret, using a quick-release kinematic mechanism, so switching to AFM is a matter of rotating the turret.

faqs.question: How accurately does it remount?
faqs.answer: Kinematic mounting guarantees replacement to better than 10 µm accuracy.

faqs.question: Can the same feature be found again after a cantilever change?
faqs.answer: Yes. Alignment grooves on the chip mount place the next cantilever's tip within 4 µm of the same position.

faqs.question: Does the cantilever need laser alignment?
faqs.answer: No. The alignment grooves remove the laser alignment step entirely, saving time on every cantilever change.

faqs.question: Which microscopes is LensAFM compatible with?
faqs.answer: Virtually any optical microscope or 3D optical profilometer, with eight mounting adapters covering Zeiss, Olympus, Leica, Nikon, and Mitutoyo thread standards and working distances.

faqs.question: How is the sample positioned?
faqs.answer: Using the optical microscope's own position manipulators, so no separate stage is required or needs learning.

faqs.question: Does LensAFM have its own optics?
faqs.answer: Yes. An integrated 8x objective lens provides a clear view of both the sample and the cantilever, and is used to relocate areas of interest before scanning.

faqs.question: How does the cantilever approach the sample?
faqs.answer: Automatically — bringing the sample into optical focus is all that's required, and the LensAFM completes the approach.

faqs.question: Can it measure tall surface structures?
faqs.answer: Yes. A large Z-range allows measurement of high structures.

faqs.question: Which properties can LensAFM measure beyond topography?
faqs.answer: Surface roughness, hardness variations, magnetism, and electrical conductance and resistance.

faqs.question: Which electrical modes are available?
faqs.answer: C-AFM, EFM, and MFM.

faqs.question: Can LensAFM characterize transparent samples?
faqs.answer: Yes. AFM overcomes the difficulty of characterizing transparent samples and others hard to assess optically.

faqs.question: How does LensAFM differ from a standalone Nanosurf AFM?
faqs.answer: LensAFM integrates natively with an existing optical microscope and is engineered for repositioning accuracy. Standalone systems like CoreAFM and FlexAFM offer a wider mode set including SMM, SThM, EC-AFM, and FluidFM, along with their own sample stages and vibration isolation.

faqs.question: Can instrument control be scripted?
faqs.answer: Yes. Nanosurf C3000 software offers fully scriptable instrument control, with a Python API available.

faqs.question: Where can I find detailed technical specifications?
faqs.answer: Numeric system specifications are published in the LensAFM brochure rather than on the product page — Inkarp can provide it on request.

faqs.question: What is the price of LensAFM in India?
faqs.answer: Get in touch and Inkarp will put together a quote based on the mounting adapter, modes, and accessories required.

faqs.answer: Inkarp is the authorized distributor and service provider for the Nanosurf LensAFM in India, providing demonstration, installation, training, AMC, spare parts, and technical support.

heroParagraphs: Optical microscopy stops at the wavelength of light. Everything smaller than that limit is a feature you know is there and cannot resolve — and the usual answer is a second instrument, a second bench, and a sample transferred between them with no certainty of finding the same spot twice.

LensAFM mounts on the objective turret like a normal lens. Screen the sample optically, find the area of interest, rotate to the LensAFM position, and scan. The workflow doesn't change; the resolution does.

The numbers behind it are what make that workflow trustworthy. Kinematic mounting guarantees remounting to better than 10 µm accuracy. Alignment grooves on the chip mount place the next cantilever's tip within 4 µm of the same position — so the feature found before a cantilever change is still findable after one. Those same grooves remove laser alignment from the process entirely.
Beyond topography, it reads surface roughness, hardness variation, magnetism, and electrical conductance — and it characterizes transparent samples that defeat optical assessment altogether.

faqs.question: What is NaniteAFM used for?
faqs.answer: It's a compact, integratable atomic force microscope used for nanoscale surface analysis of workpieces of all shapes and sizes, across nanotechnology, data storage, precision optics, and industrial quality and process control.

faqs.question: How small is the scan head?
faqs.answer: Less than 48 × 87 × 61 mm — small enough to integrate into virtually any imaginable environment.

faqs.question: Is there a limit on sample size?
faqs.answer: No inherent limit. Large pieces and components that cannot be divided into smaller segments are measured as they are.

faqs.question: Does measurement damage or alter the sample?
faqs.answer: No. Samples remain intact and unaltered throughout the analysis process.

faqs.question: Can NaniteAFM measure curved surfaces?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is suited for concave surfaces and handles intricate curves.

faqs.question: What surface detail can it resolve?
faqs.answer: Features as small as a few nanometres, and surface roughness below one nanometre.

faqs.question: Can it be integrated into an existing system?
faqs.answer: Yes. It integrates into existing user systems or custom stages, often without significant modification.

faqs.question: What if no existing stage fits the application?
faqs.answer: Nanosurf's engineers design custom stages, along with automation features, around the specific application.

faqs.question: Is a stand-alone configuration available?
faqs.answer: Yes. Stand-alone solutions are offered alongside the integration configurations.

faqs.question: Can AFM control be built into an existing setup?
faqs.answer: Yes. The scripting interface allows AFM control to be integrated into existing system architectures.

faqs.question: Which programming environments are supported?
faqs.answer: LabVIEW, Python, MATLAB, C++, Java, and most other programming environments.

faqs.question: Which imaging modes are available?
faqs.answer: Static force, dynamic force (tapping), and phase imaging, plus C-AFM, EFM, and MFM for electrical properties and force modulation, spectroscopy, and mapping for mechanical properties.

faqs.question: Does the system include a camera?
faqs.answer: Yes. An integrated top and side view camera provides sample observation.

faqs.question: How is the cantilever set up before measurement?
faqs.answer: Select the cantilever in the software and the system automatically performs the frequency sweep before approach, with no manual parameter setting required.

faqs.question: How does NaniteAFM differ from LensAFM?
faqs.answer: LensAFM mounts on an optical microscope turret to extend an existing optical workflow. NaniteAFM is a scan head built to embed into systems or custom stages, with no inherent sample size limit and concave surface capability. LensAFM additionally offers lateral force mode.

faqs.question: Where can I find detailed technical specifications?
faqs.answer: Numeric system specifications are published in the Nanite brochure rather than on the product page — Inkarp can provide it on request.

faqs.question: What is the price of NaniteAFM in India?
faqs.answer: Get in touch and Inkarp will put together a quote based on the integration approach, custom stage requirements, and modes needed.

longForm.heroLead: Most AFMs decide the shape of the workflow around them — the sample comes to the instrument, cut down to fit a stage, mounted flat, brought to the lab. For quality and process control on real components, that sequence often isn't available. NaniteAFM inverts it. At under 48 × 87 × 61 mm, the scan head integrates into existing user systems or custom stages, frequently without significant modification to either. The AFM goes to the workpiece. The consequence matters more than the dimension. Large pieces stay whole. Components that can't be sectioned are measured as they are. Concave and curved surfaces are accommodated. Samples come through the analysis intact and unaltered — which for a finished part or a costly component is the difference between measuring it and destroying it. Underneath, it delivers nanoscale precision: features a few nanometres across, surface roughness below one nanometre. A scripting interface compatible with LabVIEW, Python, MATLAB, C++, and Java brings AFM control into whatever system already runs the process.

heroParagraphs: Most AFMs decide the shape of the workflow around them — the sample comes to the instrument, cut down to fit a stage, mounted flat, brought to the lab. For quality and process control on real components, that sequence often isn't available.

NaniteAFM inverts it. At under 48 × 87 × 61 mm, the scan head integrates into existing user systems or custom stages, frequently without significant modification to either. The AFM goes to the workpiece.

The consequence matters more than the dimension. Large pieces stay whole. Components that can't be sectioned are measured as they are. Concave and curved surfaces are accommodated. Samples come through the analysis intact and unaltered — which for a finished part or a costly component is the difference between measuring it and destroying it.

Underneath, it delivers nanoscale precision: features a few nanometres across, surface roughness below one nanometre. A scripting interface compatible with LabVIEW, Python, MATLAB, C++, and Java brings AFM control into whatever system already runs the process.

longForm.heroHook: AFM and SEM, on the same spot, at the same time. No sample transfer, no lost location.
longForm.heroLead: Correlating AFM and SEM data usually means moving a sample between two instruments and hoping the region of interest survives the trip. LiteScope removes that gap entirely, mounting a full atomic force microscope directly inside your SEM chamber for simultaneous, correlated imaging of the exact same spot. Correlative Probe and Electron Microscopy (CPEM) technology captures AFM and SEM data together, in situ, under identical conditions, then merges them into three-dimensional correlative images. SEM navigation finds the region of interest fast, self-sensing probes skip the laser alignment most AFMs need, and the whole scan head mounts or removes from your SEM in under five minutes.

sections.title: Product Information
sections.description: LiteScope AFM product information: CPEM technology, SEM integration, and multi-property surface characterization.
body: LiteScope mounts a complete AFM inside an SEM chamber, capturing AFM and SEM data on the same spot at the same time, under the same conditions, rather than stitching together two separate sessions.

CPEM technology merges topography, material contrast, and mechanical or electrical property data into three-dimensional correlative images, eliminating the repetitive re-locating and re-imaging that separate AFM and SEM sessions normally require.
SEM navigation locates the region of interest first, then guides the AFM tip directly to it, a fast, precise alternative to hunting for a feature blind under an AFM alone.
Self-sensing probes remove the need for optical detection or laser adjustment, a common source of setup time and drift in conventional AFM systems.
The scan head mounts to or removes from most SEM systems in under five minutes, and stays compatible with FIB, GIS, EDX, and other standard SEM accessories.
An open-hardware DSP controller, developed with the Czech Metrology Institute, lets customers modify the system directly rather than working within a closed platform.
LiteScope also runs as a standalone AFM outside the SEM chamber when that's what the work calls for.

sections.title: CPEM: True Correlative Imaging
sections.description: Traditional correlative microscopy means imaging with one instrument, moving the sample, then trying to relocate the exact same region under a second instrument, a process that eats time and introduces positional error. CPEM removes both problems at once: AFM and SEM data get captured together, on the same spot, under identical conditions, so there's no relocation step and no guessing whether the two datasets actually line up. That simultaneous capture extends across a genuinely broad property set: topography, local elasticity, hardness, magnetic domains, piezoelectric domains, conductivity, and surface potential all combine into a single three-dimensional dataset.

To validate these probes properly, researchers need more than a single detection wavelength. They need access to the fluorescence spectrum across the relevant infrared region. Photon etc. ClaIR™ is a NIR-II infrared microplate reader designed to capture full fluorescence spectra from 900 to 1600 nm in a 96-well plate format. It combines laser-based fluorescence excitation with a high-sensitivity VIS and IR spectrometer for spectral characterization of infrared-emitting probes and materials. Fluorescence measurements use 650 nm and 735 nm laser diodes, while an optional tunable light source can be connected through the integrated fiber entry. Absorbance measurements cover 500 to 1600 nm using a halogen white lamp. sections.title: Why NIR-II Detection Matters
body: Why full-spectrum NIR-II fluorescence detection matters for probe research

NIR-II fluorescence measurements require detection in a wavelength region that extends beyond conventional visible fluorescence. When a probe's emission lies in the infrared, measuring only at a selected wavelength can limit the information available about its spectral behaviour.
ClaIR™ is designed to capture fluorescence spectra from 900 to 1600 nm, allowing researchers to examine the emission profile across the NIR-II region supported by the system.

This is particularly relevant for researchers developing or characterizing NIR-II fluorescent probes, infrared-emitting materials, and nanomaterials where the spectral position and shape of the emission are important research parameters.
The system also supports absorbance measurements from 500 to 1600 nm, extending spectral characterization from the visible into the infrared.
rows: Spectral capture across the supported NIR-II range
Optional tunable light source through fiber entry
groups.note: For probe evaluation, provide the expected excitation wavelength, emission range, sample format, and whether absorbance measurement is also required. This helps determine whether the ClaIR™ configuration matches the measurement workflow.

groups.title: Flexible Excitation for NIR-II Probe Characterization
groups.description: Built-in laser excitation with optional tunable illumination
body: Excitation wavelength is an important part of fluorescence characterization. Different probes and materials may require different excitation conditions, so ClaIR™ provides two built-in laser excitation wavelengths and an option for additional tunable illumination.
The system includes 650 nm and 735 nm laser diodes for fluorescence excitation. A fiber entry provides the option to connect a tunable light source when additional excitation flexibility is required.
This configuration allows the excitation side of the measurement to be considered alongside the probe's emission characteristics.
groups.note: When requesting a configuration, provide the probe's excitation wavelength and expected emission range. This allows the available excitation and detection configuration to be evaluated together.

groups.title: Absorbance and Fluorescence in One Platform
groups.description: Measure both optical response and infrared fluorescence in a 96-well workflow
body: ClaIR™ supports absorbance and fluorescence spectroscopy, allowing researchers to work with both measurement modes in one microplate reader.

For absorbance, the system uses a halogen white lamp and covers 500 to 1600 nm. For fluorescence, the system uses 650 nm and 735 nm laser diode excitation and detects fluorescence from 900 to 1600 nm.
This combination extends the measurement workflow across visible and infrared wavelengths.

heroParagraphs: Connect micro- and macro-scale imaging with continuously tunable hyperspectral analysis.

Photon etc. GRAND-EOS™ is a global hyperspectral camera continuously tunable from 400 to 1650 nm. It combines micro and macro imaging modalities in one platform, allowing researchers and industrial users to analyze samples across different scales.
Using Photon etc.'s patented volume Bragg grating (VBG) filtering technology, GRAND-EOS™ provides non-polarized wavelength selection with high throughput and efficiency.

The system generates a hyperspectral data cube containing spatial information along the X-Y axes and spectral information along the Z-axis. Photon etc.'s global imaging technology extracts this data cube from a small number of monochromatic images without requiring image reconstruction.
GRAND-EOS™ supports reflectance, transmittance and luminescence imaging, with an adjustable field of view based on the application and sample size.

longForm.heroHook: Hyperspectral Microscopy from 400 to 1620 nm
longForm.heroLead: Capture spatial and spectral information from your sample in a single hyperspectral microscope. Photon etc. IMA™ is a hyperspectral microscope designed to acquire spatial and spectral information across the 400–1620 nm range. By combining a scientific-grade VIS, NIR and/or SWIR microscope with Photon etc.'s patented imaging filter technology, IMA™ enables detailed spectral characterization of a wide range of materials. IMA™ can acquire millions of data points in a single snapshot and rapidly map photoluminescence (PL), electroluminescence (EL), fluorescence, reflectance and transmittance. The system can be configured as either a brightfield or darkfield hyperspectral microscope, making it suitable for different sample types and imaging requirements. Unlike point-by-point scanning approaches, IMA™ uses high-throughput imaging filters to acquire hyperspectral information rapidly across the sample. IMA™ is suited to applications including advanced materials analysis, solar cell and nanomaterial research, semiconductor quality control, infrared marker studies, and hyperspectral imaging of transparent materials.

Photon etc. IMA™ is a hyperspectral microscope designed to acquire spatial and spectral information across the 400–1620 nm range. By combining a scientific-grade VIS, NIR and/or SWIR microscope with Photon etc.'s patented imaging filter technology, IMA™ enables detailed spectral characterization of a wide range of materials.
IMA™ can acquire millions of data points in a single snapshot and rapidly map photoluminescence (PL), electroluminescence (EL), fluorescence, reflectance and transmittance.
The system can be configured as either a brightfield or darkfield hyperspectral microscope, making it suitable for different sample types and imaging requirements.
Unlike point-by-point scanning approaches, IMA™ uses high-throughput imaging filters to acquire hyperspectral information rapidly across the sample.

IMA™ is suited to applications including advanced materials analysis, solar cell and nanomaterial research, semiconductor quality control, infrared marker studies, and hyperspectral imaging of transparent materials.

faqs.question: What is IR VIVO™ used for?
faqs.answer: It's a preclinical in vivo imaging system operating in the NIR-II (SWIR) spectrum, used for fluorescence-guided surgery research, vascular and lymphatic tracking, biodistribution studies, brain imaging, and multiplexed biomarker visualization in small animals.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does it operate in?
faqs.answer: 700 to 1600 nm, the NIR-II or short-wave infrared spectrum, where biological tissue becomes highly transparent to light.

faqs.question: How deep can IR VIVO™ image?
faqs.answer: Signal-to-noise sufficient for imaging is achievable to depths of 2 cm.

faqs.question: Why does NIR-II imaging see through bone and pigmented tissue?
faqs.answer: Light scattering is dramatically minimized and background autofluorescence is completely eliminated at these wavelengths, which is what allows structures like the brain through intact bone or melanoma through skin to be resolved.

faqs.question: What camera does IR VIVO™ use?
faqs.answer: An ultra-low-noise Alizé™ 1.7 InGaAs camera, deep-cooled to -60°C. Some of Photon etc.'s materials also reference a ZephIR™ 1.7 camera option — confirm the exact configuration at specification stage.

faqs.question: How many fluorescent signals can be tracked at once?
faqs.answer: Up to 10 emission channels, allowing distinct anatomical and molecular signals to be tracked simultaneously in the same animal.

faqs.question: What illumination does the system use?
faqs.answer: Laser illumination at 670, 760, 808, and 890 nm, with adjustable power density.

faqs.question: What imaging modes are available?
faqs.answer: Fluorescence, reflectance, and overlay.

faqs.question: What field of view does IR VIVO™ offer?
faqs.answer: A variable field of view from 80×64 mm, suited to a full mouse, down to 50×40 mm for an individual organ.

faqs.question: Can it monitor physiological signals without touching the animal?
faqs.answer: Yes. The fast frame rates of the InGaAs camera support contact-free cardiography and respiratory rate measurement in anesthetized or awake animals, without restraint.

faqs.question: What software controls the system?
faqs.answer: PHySpec, Photon etc.'s control software platform spanning their instrument range — confirm the specific feature scope for IR VIVO™ at configuration.

faqs.question: How much bench space does the system need?
Is there published research using IR VIVO™?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. references multiple peer-reviewed and preprint publications spanning NIR-II fluorophore development, nanoparticle imaging, tumor delineation, and vascular/lymphatic multiplexing.

sections.title: Why the NIR-II Window Matters
sections.tabSummary: What scattering and autofluorescence cost NIR-I systems
body: What scattering and autofluorescence actually cost a NIR-I system.

Every photon travelling through tissue at visible or NIR-I wavelengths scatters repeatedly before it reaches a camera, and every scatter blurs the image and shortens the useful imaging depth. On top of that, tissue itself fluoresces at those wavelengths — a background signal with nowhere to hide, sitting directly under whatever probe signal is being measured.

IR VIVO™ operates where both problems largely disappear. Across 700–1600 nm, biological tissue becomes highly transparent, scattering drops dramatically, and background autofluorescence is completely eliminated rather than merely reduced. That's the entire reason the system can resolve structures like the mouse brain through intact bone, or black melanoma through pigmented skin — targets that are, in practical terms, invisible to instruments working at shorter wavelengths, however sensitive those instruments are.

paragraphs: Running separate cohorts to track separate biomarkers costs animals, time, and introduces variability between groups that a single-animal comparison would avoid entirely. IR VIVO™'s up to 10 emission channels isolate distinct emission bandwidths across the NIR-II window, so multiple fluorescent labels can be tracked simultaneously in the same living animal.

Published work using the platform has demonstrated exactly this — lymphatic and vascular signals imaged together in the same mouse, distinguished by their different emission bandwidths within the NIR-II region. That's not two separate images overlaid afterwards; it's genuinely simultaneous acquisition across isolated channels, which is what makes real-time correlation between anatomical and molecular signals possible rather than inferred.

faqs.question: What type of camera is L-EOS™?

faqs.question: What wavelength range does L-EOS™ cover?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is available in two configurations. L-EOS 1.7 covers 900–1700 nm, while L-EOS 2.5e covers 1000–2500 nm.

faqs.question: What is the difference between L-EOS 1.7 and L-EOS 2.5e?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 uses an InGaAs sensor and covers 900–1700 nm. L-EOS 2.5e uses a T2SL sensor and covers 1000–2500 nm. They also differ in spectral resolution and spectral sampling.

faqs.question: What sensor does L-EOS 1.7 use?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 uses an InGaAs sensor, with Alizé™ 1.7 or ZephIR™ 1.7 sensor options listed by Photon etc.

faqs.question: What sensor does L-EOS 2.5e use?

faqs.question: How many spatial channels does L-EOS™ have?

faqs.question: How many spectral channels does L-EOS™ have?
faqs.answer: Both L-EOS configurations provide 640 spectral channels.

faqs.question: What is the spectral resolution of L-EOS 1.7?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 has a spectral resolution of 7.8 nm.

faqs.question: What is the spectral resolution of L-EOS 2.5e?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 2.5e has a spectral resolution of 15.3 nm.

faqs.question: What is the spectral sampling of L-EOS 1.7?
faqs.answer: The typical spectral sampling of L-EOS 1.7 is 1.3 nm/px.

faqs.question: What is the spectral sampling of L-EOS 2.5e?

faqs.question: What is the pixel size of L-EOS™?

faqs.question: Does L-EOS™ use thermoelectric cooling?

faqs.question: How cold can the L-EOS™ detector get?

longForm.heroHook: Long-Lifetime Hyperspectral SWIR Imaging for Industrial Material Analysis
longForm.heroLead: Map spectral information across materials, surfaces, and continuous processes with L-EOS™. Photon etc. L-EOS™ is a hyperspectral SWIR imaging system designed for industrial applications that require spatial and spectral information from materials and processes. It combines a scientific-grade infrared camera, thermoelectric cooling, spectrometer technology, and an industrial-ready design for demanding imaging workflows. L-EOS™ is available in two configurations covering different SWIR spectral regions: L-EOS 1.7: 900–1700 nm L-EOS 2.5e: 1000–2500 nm Both configurations provide 512 spatial channels and 640 spectral channels, with 6-pixel spatial resolution and 15 µm pixel size. The L-EOS 1.7 configuration uses an InGaAs sensor, while L-EOS 2.5e uses a T2SL sensor. Four-stage thermoelectric cooling can reach temperatures as low as -60°C or -80°C, depending on the configuration. Cooling helps reduce background noise and support high signal-to-noise performance during infrared imaging. L-EOS™ is suited to industrial workflows including material sorting, textile identification, recycling, food quality and safety, mining and geology, core scanning, search and rescue, and UAV-based applications.

sections.title: SWIR Hyperspectral Imaging for Material Identification
body: See more than an image: capture spectral information across the material
A conventional image primarily records spatial information. Hyperspectral imaging adds another layer: spectral information at each measured spatial position.
For industrial applications, this can be valuable when two materials look similar in visible light but exhibit different spectral responses in the SWIR region.
L-EOS™ combines line-based spatial acquisition with multiple spectral channels, creating a hyperspectral measurement that can be used to investigate material differences across a scene.

sections.title: Why Deep Cooling Matters in SWIR Imaging
body: Reduce detector noise for sensitive measurements
SWIR imaging applications can involve weak optical signals. Detector temperature can influence unwanted noise and therefore affect the quality of acquired images.
ZephIR™ 1.7 uses a four-stage thermoelectric cooler capable of maintaining an operating temperature as low as −80 °C.
The deep cooling is designed to support the camera's low-noise performance while avoiding the infrastructure associated with water or liquid-nitrogen cooling.

longForm.heroHook: Deep-Cooled SWIR Imaging from 900 to 2500 nm
longForm.heroLead: High-speed, deep-cooled SWIR imaging for demanding scientific experiments and industrial applications. Photon etc. ZephIR™ 2.5e is a deep-cooled short-wave infrared (SWIR) camera sensitive from 900 to 2500 nm. Its T2SL focal plane array, deep thermoelectric cooling and low-noise operation are designed to help acquire weak infrared signals with improved signal quality. The camera uses a 640 × 512 pixel sensor with 15 µm pixels and provides frame rates up to 240 fps, with ROI frame rates up to 4000 fps. ZephIR™ 2.5e uses TEC + forced-air cooling and can reach a cooling temperature of −80 °C at 20 °C ambient, without requiring water cooling or liquid-nitrogen refrigeration. For system integration, the camera supports USB 3.0 and CameraLink™, external trigger input/output, and Photon etc.'s PHySpec™ control and analysis software. Developers can also use the supplied C++ and Python SDK.

notes: When should you choose ClaIR™?

ClaIR™ is particularly relevant when the research question requires spectral information across the NIR-II region, rather than simply determining whether fluorescence is present at one selected wavelength.

sections.title: Why NIR-II Detection Matters
body: Why full-spectrum NIR-II fluorescence detection matters for probe research

NIR-II fluorescence measurements require detection in a wavelength region that extends beyond conventional visible fluorescence. When a probe's emission lies in the infrared, measuring only at a selected wavelength can limit the information available about its spectral behaviour.
ClaIR™ is designed to capture fluorescence spectra from 900 to 1600 nm, allowing researchers to examine the emission profile across the NIR-II region supported by the system.

This is particularly relevant for researchers developing or characterizing NIR-II fluorescent probes, infrared-emitting materials, and nanomaterials where the spectral position and shape of the emission are important research parameters.
The system also supports absorbance measurements from 500 to 1600 nm, extending spectral characterization from the visible into the infrared.
rows: Spectral capture across the supported NIR-II range
Optional tunable light source through fiber entry
groups.note: For probe evaluation, provide the expected excitation wavelength, emission range, sample format, and whether absorbance measurement is also required. This helps determine whether the ClaIR™ configuration matches the measurement workflow.

groups.title: Flexible Excitation for NIR-II Probe Characterization
groups.description: Built-in laser excitation with optional tunable illumination
body: Excitation wavelength is an important part of fluorescence characterization. Different probes and materials may require different excitation conditions, so ClaIR™ provides two built-in laser excitation wavelengths and an option for additional tunable illumination.
The system includes 650 nm and 735 nm laser diodes for fluorescence excitation. A fiber entry provides the option to connect a tunable light source when additional excitation flexibility is required.
This configuration allows the excitation side of the measurement to be considered alongside the probe's emission characteristics.
groups.note: When requesting a configuration, provide the probe's excitation wavelength and expected emission range. This allows the available excitation and detection configuration to be evaluated together.

groups.title: Absorbance and Fluorescence in One Platform
groups.description: Measure both optical response and infrared fluorescence in a 96-well workflow
body: ClaIR™ supports absorbance and fluorescence spectroscopy, allowing researchers to work with both measurement modes in one microplate reader.

For absorbance, the system uses a halogen white lamp and covers 500 to 1600 nm. For fluorescence, the system uses 650 nm and 735 nm laser diode excitation and detects fluorescence from 900 to 1600 nm.
This combination extends the measurement workflow across visible and infrared wavelengths.

faqs.question: What is IMA™?
faqs.answer: IMA™ is a hyperspectral microscope from Photon etc. that captures spatial and spectral information across the 400–1620 nm range.

faqs.question: What is IMA™ used for?
faqs.answer: IMA™ is used for hyperspectral characterization of advanced materials, solar cells, nanomaterials, semiconductors, infrared markers, transparent materials, crystals, polymers and other research samples.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does IMA™ cover?
faqs.answer: IMA™ provides hyperspectral coverage from 400 to 1620 nm, spanning the VIS, NIR and SWIR regions.

faqs.question: What does IMA™ measure?
faqs.answer: IMA™ can rapidly map photoluminescence, electroluminescence, fluorescence, reflectance and transmittance.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ measure photoluminescence?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ supports photoluminescence mapping and Photon etc. demonstrates the system for PL mapping of perovskite crystals.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ measure electroluminescence?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ can map electroluminescence and is positioned for applications including solar-cell and semiconductor research.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ perform fluorescence imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ supports hyperspectral fluorescence imaging.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ measure reflectance?
faqs.answer: Yes. Reflectance is one of the measurement modes supported by IMA™.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ measure transmittance?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ supports transmittance measurements for suitable samples.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ be configured as a darkfield microscope?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ can be configured as either a brightfield or darkfield hyperspectral microscope.

faqs.question: What samples can be studied using darkfield IMA™?
faqs.answer: Photon etc. identifies transparent materials such as polymers, crystals and living cells as applications for hyperspectral darkfield microscopy.

faqs.question: How many data points can IMA™ acquire?
faqs.answer: Photon etc. states that IMA™ can acquire millions of data points in a single snapshot.

faqs.question: How is IMA™ different from point-by-point hyperspectral scanning?
faqs.answer: IMA™ uses high-throughput imaging filters for rapid hyperspectral acquisition, rather than relying on standard point-by-point scanning.

faqs.question: What type of microscope does IMA™ use?
faqs.answer: IMA™ combines a scientific-grade VIS, NIR and/or SWIR microscope with Photon etc.'s patented imaging filter technology.

faqs.question: Is IMA™ suitable for solar-cell research?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. identifies solar-cell research as an application and highlights PL and EL hyperspectral analysis.

faqs.question: Is IMA™ suitable for nanomaterial research?
faqs.answer: Yes. Advanced materials and nanomaterial analysis are listed among IMA™ applications.

faqs.question: Is IMA™ suitable for semiconductor analysis?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. identifies semiconductor quality control using hyperspectral PL and EL as an IMA™ application.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ be used for infrared marker research?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. identifies research involving infrared markers in complex environments, including tissues and living cells, using hyperspectral SWIR microscopy.

faqs.question: What is the price of IMA™ in India?
faqs.answer: Pricing depends on the required optical configuration, spectral range and application requirements. Contact Inkarp for a quotation.

longForm.heroHook: Hyperspectral Microscopy from 400 to 1620 nm
longForm.heroLead: Capture spatial and spectral information from your sample in a single hyperspectral microscope. Photon etc. IMA™ is a hyperspectral microscope designed to acquire spatial and spectral information across the 400–1620 nm range. By combining a scientific-grade VIS, NIR and/or SWIR microscope with Photon etc.'s patented imaging filter technology, IMA™ enables detailed spectral characterization of a wide range of materials. IMA™ can acquire millions of data points in a single snapshot and rapidly map photoluminescence (PL), electroluminescence (EL), fluorescence, reflectance and transmittance. The system can be configured as either a brightfield or darkfield hyperspectral microscope, making it suitable for different sample types and imaging requirements. Unlike point-by-point scanning approaches, IMA™ uses high-throughput imaging filters to acquire hyperspectral information rapidly across the sample. IMA™ is suited to applications including advanced materials analysis, solar cell and nanomaterial research, semiconductor quality control, infrared marker studies, and hyperspectral imaging of transparent materials.

sections.title: How IMA™ Works
body: From a microscopic image to a hyperspectral data set
Traditional microscopy provides detailed spatial information about a sample. Hyperspectral microscopy adds spectral information to those spatial features.
IMA™ combines the two.
Sample → Microscopic imaging → Hyperspectral acquisition → Spatial + spectral data → Material characterization
Each measured region can therefore be considered in terms of both:
Where is the feature?

products.overview: Visible light and NIR-I imaging both hit the same wall: biological tissue scatters and absorbs at those wavelengths, and autofluorescence buries whatever signal makes it through. Push into the short-wave infrared — 700 to 1600 nm — and that wall mostly disappears. Tissue becomes transparent enough to image structures conventional systems simply cannot reach.

faqs.question: What is IR VIVO™ used for?
faqs.answer: It's a preclinical in vivo imaging system operating in the NIR-II (SWIR) spectrum, used for fluorescence-guided surgery research, vascular and lymphatic tracking, biodistribution studies, brain imaging, and multiplexed biomarker visualization in small animals.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does it operate in?
faqs.answer: 700 to 1600 nm, the NIR-II or short-wave infrared spectrum, where biological tissue becomes highly transparent to light.

faqs.question: How deep can IR VIVO™ image?
faqs.answer: Signal-to-noise sufficient for imaging is achievable to depths of 2 cm.

faqs.question: Why does NIR-II imaging see through bone and pigmented tissue?
faqs.answer: Light scattering is dramatically minimized and background autofluorescence is completely eliminated at these wavelengths, which is what allows structures like the brain through intact bone or melanoma through skin to be resolved.

faqs.question: What camera does IR VIVO™ use?
faqs.answer: An ultra-low-noise Alizé™ 1.7 InGaAs camera, deep-cooled to -60°C. Some of Photon etc.'s materials also reference a ZephIR™ 1.7 camera option — confirm the exact configuration at specification stage.

faqs.question: How many fluorescent signals can be tracked at once?
faqs.answer: Up to 10 emission channels, allowing distinct anatomical and molecular signals to be tracked simultaneously in the same animal.

faqs.question: What illumination does the system use?
faqs.answer: Laser illumination at 670, 760, 808, and 890 nm, with adjustable power density.

faqs.question: What imaging modes are available?
faqs.answer: Fluorescence, reflectance, and overlay.

faqs.question: What field of view does IR VIVO™ offer?
faqs.answer: A variable field of view from 80×64 mm, suited to a full mouse, down to 50×40 mm for an individual organ.

faqs.question: Can it monitor physiological signals without touching the animal?
faqs.answer: Yes. The fast frame rates of the InGaAs camera support contact-free cardiography and respiratory rate measurement in anesthetized or awake animals, without restraint.

faqs.question: What software controls the system?
faqs.answer: PHySpec, Photon etc.'s control software platform spanning their instrument range — confirm the specific feature scope for IR VIVO™ at configuration.

faqs.question: How much bench space does the system need?
Is there published research using IR VIVO™?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. references multiple peer-reviewed and preprint publications spanning NIR-II fluorophore development, nanoparticle imaging, tumor delineation, and vascular/lymphatic multiplexing.

longForm.heroHook: See the brain through intact bone. See melanoma through skin. Without opening either.
longForm.heroLead: Visible light and NIR-I imaging both hit the same wall: biological tissue scatters and absorbs at those wavelengths, and autofluorescence buries whatever signal makes it through. Push into the short-wave infrared — 700 to 1600 nm — and that wall mostly disappears. Tissue becomes transparent enough to image structures conventional systems simply cannot reach. IR VIVO™ is built entirely around that window. Photon etc.'s ultra-low-noise Alizé™ 1.7 InGaAs camera, deep-cooled to -60°C, paired with high-intensity laser illumination, delivers signal-to-noise clean enough to resolve features 2 cm deep — the mouse brain through intact skull, black melanoma through pigmented skin, vasculature no surface camera will ever show you. Up to 10 emission channels let distinct fluorescent labels be tracked simultaneously in the same animal, isolated by emission bandwidth across the NIR-II window. For oncology, neuroscience, and drug discovery teams who've hit the resolution ceiling of NIR-I systems, this is the platform built for what comes after it.

sections.title: Why the NIR-II Window Matters
sections.tabSummary: What scattering and autofluorescence cost NIR-I systems
body: What scattering and autofluorescence actually cost a NIR-I system.

Every photon travelling through tissue at visible or NIR-I wavelengths scatters repeatedly before it reaches a camera, and every scatter blurs the image and shortens the useful imaging depth. On top of that, tissue itself fluoresces at those wavelengths — a background signal with nowhere to hide, sitting directly under whatever probe signal is being measured.

IR VIVO™ operates where both problems largely disappear. Across 700–1600 nm, biological tissue becomes highly transparent, scattering drops dramatically, and background autofluorescence is completely eliminated rather than merely reduced. That's the entire reason the system can resolve structures like the mouse brain through intact bone, or black melanoma through pigmented skin — targets that are, in practical terms, invisible to instruments working at shorter wavelengths, however sensitive those instruments are.

paragraphs: Running separate cohorts to track separate biomarkers costs animals, time, and introduces variability between groups that a single-animal comparison would avoid entirely. IR VIVO™'s up to 10 emission channels isolate distinct emission bandwidths across the NIR-II window, so multiple fluorescent labels can be tracked simultaneously in the same living animal.

Published work using the platform has demonstrated exactly this — lymphatic and vascular signals imaged together in the same mouse, distinguished by their different emission bandwidths within the NIR-II region. That's not two separate images overlaid afterwards; it's genuinely simultaneous acquisition across isolated channels, which is what makes real-time correlation between anatomical and molecular signals possible rather than inferred.

faqs.question: What is L-EOS™?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is a hyperspectral SWIR imaging system from Photon etc. designed for industrial infrared imaging, material analysis, sorting, recycling, textiles, geology, food applications, and other hyperspectral workflows.

faqs.question: What type of camera is L-EOS™?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is a hyperspectral linescan camera system designed for industrial SWIR imaging applications.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does L-EOS™ cover?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is available in two configurations. L-EOS 1.7 covers 900–1700 nm, while L-EOS 2.5e covers 1000–2500 nm.

faqs.question: What is the difference between L-EOS 1.7 and L-EOS 2.5e?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 uses an InGaAs sensor and covers 900–1700 nm. L-EOS 2.5e uses a T2SL sensor and covers 1000–2500 nm. They also differ in spectral resolution and spectral sampling.

faqs.question: What sensor does L-EOS 1.7 use?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 uses an InGaAs sensor, with Alizé™ 1.7 or ZephIR™ 1.7 sensor options listed by Photon etc.

faqs.question: What sensor does L-EOS 2.5e use?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 2.5e uses a T2SL sensor, specifically the ZephIR™ 2.5e configuration listed by Photon etc.

faqs.question: How many spatial channels does L-EOS™ have?
faqs.answer: Both L-EOS configurations provide 512 spatial channels.

faqs.question: How many spectral channels does L-EOS™ have?
faqs.answer: Both L-EOS configurations provide 640 spectral channels.

faqs.question: What is the spectral resolution of L-EOS 1.7?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 has a spectral resolution of 7.8 nm.

faqs.question: What is the spectral resolution of L-EOS 2.5e?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 2.5e has a spectral resolution of 15.3 nm.

faqs.question: What is the spectral sampling of L-EOS 1.7?
faqs.answer: The typical spectral sampling of L-EOS 1.7 is 1.3 nm/px.

faqs.question: What is the spectral sampling of L-EOS 2.5e?
faqs.answer: The typical spectral sampling of L-EOS 2.5e is 2.6 nm/px.

faqs.question: What is the pixel size of L-EOS™?
faqs.answer: Both L-EOS configurations have a 15 µm pixel size.

faqs.question: Does L-EOS™ use thermoelectric cooling?
faqs.answer: Yes. L-EOS™ uses four stages of thermoelectric cooling.

faqs.question: How cold can the L-EOS™ detector get?
faqs.answer: At 20°C ambient temperature, L-EOS 1.7 can reach -60°C or -80°C, while L-EOS 2.5e can reach -80°C.

faqs.question: What is L-EOS™ used for?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is used for industrial hyperspectral imaging applications including material sorting, plastic sorting, textile analysis and recycling, food quality and safety, mining and geology, core scanning, search and rescue, and UAV applications.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used for textile analysis?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. specifically presents L-EOS™ for textile analysis and fabric identification, including applications involving complex blends and recycling.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used for plastic sorting?
faqs.answer: Yes. Plastic sorting is listed by Photon etc. as an application for L-EOS™.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used for mining and geology?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. lists mining and geology among the industrial applications for its hyperspectral imaging solutions and provides core-scanning resources associated with L-EOS™.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used for food quality and safety?
faqs.answer: Yes. Food Quality / Safety is listed among the L-EOS™ application resources.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used with UAVs?

longForm.heroHook: Long-Lifetime Hyperspectral SWIR Imaging for Industrial Material Analysis
longForm.heroLead: Map spectral information across materials, surfaces, and continuous processes with L-EOS™. Photon etc. L-EOS™ is a hyperspectral SWIR imaging system designed for industrial applications that require spatial and spectral information from materials and processes. It combines a scientific-grade infrared camera, thermoelectric cooling, spectrometer technology, and an industrial-ready design for demanding imaging workflows. L-EOS™ is available in two configurations covering different SWIR spectral regions: L-EOS 1.7: 900–1700 nm L-EOS 2.5e: 1000–2500 nm Both configurations provide 512 spatial channels and 640 spectral channels, with 6-pixel spatial resolution and 15 µm pixel size. The L-EOS 1.7 configuration uses an InGaAs sensor, while L-EOS 2.5e uses a T2SL sensor. Four-stage thermoelectric cooling can reach temperatures as low as -60°C or -80°C, depending on the configuration. Cooling helps reduce background noise and support high signal-to-noise performance during infrared imaging. L-EOS™ is suited to industrial workflows including material sorting, textile identification, recycling, food quality and safety, mining and geology, core scanning, search and rescue, and UAV-based applications.

body: See more than an image: capture spectral information across the material
A conventional image primarily records spatial information. Hyperspectral imaging adds another layer: spectral information at each measured spatial position.
For industrial applications, this can be valuable when two materials look similar in visible light but exhibit different spectral responses in the SWIR region.
L-EOS™ combines line-based spatial acquisition with multiple spectral channels, creating a hyperspectral measurement that can be used to investigate material differences across a scene.

longForm.heroHook: Deep-Cooled SWIR Imaging from 900 to 2500 nm
longForm.heroLead: High-speed, deep-cooled SWIR imaging for demanding scientific experiments and industrial applications. Photon etc. ZephIR™ 2.5e is a deep-cooled short-wave infrared (SWIR) camera sensitive from 900 to 2500 nm. Its T2SL focal plane array, deep thermoelectric cooling and low-noise operation are designed to help acquire weak infrared signals with improved signal quality. The camera uses a 640 × 512 pixel sensor with 15 µm pixels and provides frame rates up to 240 fps, with ROI frame rates up to 4000 fps. ZephIR™ 2.5e uses TEC + forced-air cooling and can reach a cooling temperature of −80 °C at 20 °C ambient, without requiring water cooling or liquid-nitrogen refrigeration. For system integration, the camera supports USB 3.0 and CameraLink™, external trigger input/output, and Photon etc.'s PHySpec™ control and analysis software. Developers can also use the supplied C++ and Python SDK.

body: Rotary evaporators, vacuum systems, spectrometers, and other analytical instrumentation are the equipment this chiller is designed around.
Benchtop doesn't mean underpowered. Two confirmed capacities, 400W and 1000W, cover meaningfully different cooling loads within a footprint that stays on the bench.
Control is straightforward. A microprocessor-based controller runs the unit, with a digital display switchable between °C and °F.
Bench space stays flexible. An optional mobile cart lets the same chiller move under the bench when the surface itself is needed for something else.
It's part of a proven line. PolyScience describes this as part of an award-winning chiller range, alongside the separate, more powerful DuraChill Portable line.
Maintenance is meant to be simple. PolyScience states straightforward operation and maintenance as a design goal for this line specifically.

sections.title: Choosing between 400W and 1000W
body: Choosing between 400W and 1000W comes down to what's actually connected to the chiller, not a general sense of "bigger is safer."

A rotary evaporator running light solvent recovery generates a different cooling demand than a vacuum system or spectrometer under continuous use. Undersizing the chiller means it struggles to hold temperature under load; oversizing it just adds cost and footprint without a real benefit. Matching capacity to the actual heat load of your connected equipment is what makes the choice between 400W and 1000W meaningful.

sections.title: What runs automatically, and what that actually prevents
body: Three systems on this chiller run without anyone checking on them, and each one prevents a specific, common failure mode.

DynamicFilter changes itself on a preprogrammed monthly schedule, removing the filter change from anyone's checklist entirely. sections.eyebrow: Controller Tiers: Temperature, Wattage and Stability
sections.title: Matching a controller type to your precision requirement
body: Each controller tier is a genuinely different product, not a rebadged version of the same hardware, and the numbers back that up.

PX reaches the same 200°C ceiling as AP and AD, but does it at 1,200 W with ±0.004°C stability, the tightest in the line. AP matches PX's temperature range at a lower 1,100 W and slightly looser ±0.005°C. AD holds the same range and wattage as AP but loosens to ±0.01°C, the trade-off for digital rather than programmable control. DX caps at 175°C with ±0.01°C stability. SD caps lower still, at 170°C, with ±0.04°C. MX is the most basic tier: 135°C ceiling, ±0.07°C stability, and no 28-liter option at all.

faqs.question: What is the Viscosity Water Bath used for?

faqs.question: Why does this bath use a glass reservoir?
faqs.answer: Capillary viscosity testing requires visually timing fluid movement through the viscometer, which a glass reservoir allows and a stainless steel one would block entirely.

sections.title: Viscosity Water Baths (17 L) at a Glance

sections.subheading: Why viscosity testing needs a different bath than general heating
body: Testing standards, not general heating, drive the design. Built specifically to support ASTM D-445 kinematic viscosity testing, with the temperature precision that standard requires.
Glass is a functional choice, not an aesthetic one. A capillary viscometer test depends on watching fluid move through the tube, which a stainless steel reservoir simply can't show.
The lid still covers the bath. Lidded viscometer openings let the tubes pass through while keeping the bath enclosed during the test.
Cooling comes built in. A tap water cooling coil is included, supporting temperature control without a separate chiller.
Two controllers, one clear choice. Advanced Digital and MX cover different levels of control sophistication, both built around the same 17-liter, glass-reservoir platform.
It's a fixed platform, not a capacity range. Every Viscosity Bath in this line is 17 liters; the only real configuration decision is the controller.
DuraTop carries over from the Circulating Baths line. The same insulating, chemical-resistant deck material, proven across PolyScience's broader range.

sections.title: Viscometer Compatibility and Visual Monitoring
body: A viscosity test is only as good as your ability to see it happen, and that's the entire reason this bath is built the way it is.

Capillary viscometers rely on visually timing fluid as it moves through a narrow tube, which a stainless steel reservoir would hide completely. The glass reservoir keeps that visible throughout, while the lidded openings hold the viscometer in the correct position without leaving the bath uncovered. Configured for popular capillary viscometer types, the bath is built to slot directly into an existing ASTM D-445 testing workflow.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the Heated Circulating Baths and the Refrigerated/Heated line?
faqs.answer: The Heated line covers ambient+10°C to +200°C without refrigeration, while the Refrigerated/Heated line adds cooling down to −40°C; choose the Heated line if your application never needs to go below ambient temperature.

faqs.question: What is the most precise controller tier available?
faqs.answer: PX, with stability to ±0.004°C at up to 1,200 W, reaching the full 200°C range.

faqs.question: How do I choose between the six controller tiers?
faqs.answer: Match your required precision and maximum temperature to the tier: PX or AP for the tightest stability at full range, AD for standard digital control, DX or SD for moderate precision at a lower temperature ceiling, and MX for the simplest, most economical option.

faqs.question: How do I find the exact part number for my application?

faqs.question: Does the MX controller support a 28-liter reservoir?

faqs.question: Is this bath suitable for flammable liquids?
faqs.answer: Yes, with an Advanced Series controller (AP or PX), which meets DIN 12876-1 Class III standards for flammable liquid use.

faqs.question: What voltage and frequency does this bath support in India?

faqs.question: What accessories are included?

body: No refrigeration system means this line covers ambient+10°C to +200°C without the cost of cooling capability you won't use if your work never goes below ambient.

Six real tiers, not six marketing labels. PX, AP, AD, DX, SD, and MX each carry their own confirmed temperature ceiling, wattage, and stability figure, not just a different badge on the same hardware.
Precision goes as tight as ±0.004°C. That's the PX controller specifically, the tightest stability figure across either PolyScience circulating bath line built so far.
Some tiers trade range for cost. MX tops out at 135°C with ±0.07°C stability and doesn't offer a 28-liter option at all, a genuinely different product for genuinely simpler applications.

DuraTop is a real material choice. A precision-molded phenolic top stays cooler at high temperatures and resists lab chemicals, not just a coating.
Safety scales with the application. Advanced Series controllers meet DIN 12876-1 Class III specifically for flammable liquid work, on top of the standard over-temperature and alarm protections.

sections.eyebrow: Controller Tiers: Temperature, Wattage and Stability
sections.title: Matching a controller type to your precision requirement
body: Each controller tier is a genuinely different product, not a rebadged version of the same hardware, and the numbers back that up.

PX reaches the same 200°C ceiling as AP and AD, but does it at 1,200 W with ±0.004°C stability, the tightest in the line. AP matches PX's temperature range at a lower 1,100 W and slightly looser ±0.005°C. AD holds the same range and wattage as AP but loosens to ±0.01°C, the trade-off for digital rather than programmable control. DX caps at 175°C with ±0.01°C stability. SD caps lower still, at 170°C, with ±0.04°C. MX is the most basic tier: 135°C ceiling, ±0.07°C stability, and no 28-liter option at all.

faqs.question: What is the Viscosity Water Bath used for?
faqs.answer: It's a temperature-controlled bath purpose-built for capillary viscometer testing under ASTM D-445, commonly used for petroleum, lubricant, and chemical viscosity measurement.

faqs.question: Why does this bath use a glass reservoir?
faqs.answer: Capillary viscosity testing requires visually timing fluid movement through the viscometer, which a glass reservoir allows and a stainless steel one would block entirely.

faqs.question: How do I choose between the AD and MX controllers?

faqs.question: How do I set up the included cooling coil?
faqs.answer: Connect the coil to a tap water supply; it provides supplemental cooling support without requiring a separate chiller unit.

faqs.question: What viscometers does this bath support?

faqs.question: What temperature range does this bath cover?
faqs.answer: Up to 200°C, with stability to ±0.01°C.

faqs.question: Does this bath come in different capacities?
faqs.answer: No. This line is offered at a fixed 17-liter capacity; the controller type is the primary configuration choice.

faqs.question: What is the difference between this and the Digital General Purpose Water Bath?
faqs.answer: The Viscosity Bath is purpose-built for ASTM D-445 testing with a glass reservoir and higher temperature range, while the General Purpose line covers everyday laboratory heating with a stainless steel reservoir up to 100°C.

sections.subheading: Why viscosity testing needs a different bath than general heating
body: Testing standards, not general heating, drive the design. Built specifically to support ASTM D-445 kinematic viscosity testing, with the temperature precision that standard requires.
Glass is a functional choice, not an aesthetic one. A capillary viscometer test depends on watching fluid move through the tube, which a stainless steel reservoir simply can't show.
The lid still covers the bath. Lidded viscometer openings let the tubes pass through while keeping the bath enclosed during the test.
Cooling comes built in. A tap water cooling coil is included, supporting temperature control without a separate chiller.
Two controllers, one clear choice. Advanced Digital and MX cover different levels of control sophistication, both built around the same 17-liter, glass-reservoir platform.
It's a fixed platform, not a capacity range. Every Viscosity Bath in this line is 17 liters; the only real configuration decision is the controller.
DuraTop carries over from the Circulating Baths line. The same insulating, chemical-resistant deck material, proven across PolyScience's broader range.

sections.title: Viscometer Compatibility and Visual Monitoring
body: A viscosity test is only as good as your ability to see it happen, and that's the entire reason this bath is built the way it is.

Capillary viscometers rely on visually timing fluid as it moves through a narrow tube, which a stainless steel reservoir would hide completely. The glass reservoir keeps that visible throughout, while the lidded openings hold the viscometer in the correct position without leaving the bath uncovered. Configured for popular capillary viscometer types, the bath is built to slot directly into an existing ASTM D-445 testing workflow.

Where the standard PRO400DS offers 14.5 inches of total length, PRO400DSEL's Extra Length stand more than doubles that to 31 inches, purpose-built for taller containers and unique glassware like large-scale carboys. body: How PRO400DSEL's speed knob, diagnostics, and containment options keep processing reliable.
Homogenization results depend on hitting a consistent RPM run after run, and staying alert to problems before they affect your sample or damage the motor.

The 3-turn speed knob adjusts RPM in increments of hundreds, rather than the coarser thousands-based adjustment found on simpler units, giving the finer control that sensitive emulsions specifically need. A bright LED display keeps that setting visible clearly throughout a run. The Dual-Power Light Indicator adds a layer of diagnostic feedback, flagging errors or problems immediately so downtime and motor overload risk both stay lower. Where aerosol containment matters, the PRO SAFETY SEAL chamber assembly fits directly onto the unit to keep aerosols contained and cross-contamination risk down.

paragraphs: Stopping to clean a probe between every sample is one of the biggest hidden time costs in manual homogenizing, and it's exactly what Multi-Prep removes from the workflow.

Self-engagement and disengagement of the Multi-Prep Probes happens automatically, meaning no manual probe handling interrupts a run once it starts. Because the system draws from a 12-pack of probes, a clean probe engages for every sample position, eliminating both cross-contamination risk and the time normally spent cleaning a single generator between runs. Built from 316 stainless steel and PTFE rather than disposable plastic, those probes hold up to tougher tissue types and frozen samples, and clean fully afterward by flaming, autoclaving, or chemical methods, ready for indefinite reuse.

sections.title: Programmability and Manual Mode
sections.tabSummary: Storing protocols and running one-off trials
body: How Multi-Prep's stored programs and manual mode fit both routine and one-off homogenizing needs.
Different labs run different protocols, and Multi-Prep is built to hold onto those differences rather than forcing everyone through a single fixed setting.

Up to 10 different homogenizing programs store directly in the system's memory, so established protocols run consistently every time without needing to be re-entered or re-calibrated. For situations that fall outside a stored program, new homogenizing trials or a quick, single-sample run, manual mode handles individual sample processing directly, without needing to build a new program first. Both modes run through the same ergonomically arranged LCD and control panel, keeping programming parameters fully visible whichever mode is active.

paragraphs: Some processes need brute force at high RPM. Others need delicate control at the low end where a heavier touch would damage a sample. PRO25D is built to deliver both precisely, not just broadly.

Digital speed control allows precise adjustment throughout the entire 0 to 30,000 RPM range, rather than snapping between fixed speed steps that might overshoot what a sensitive sample or delicate emulsion actually needs. sections.title: High-Viscosity Processing
sections.tabSummary: Handling samples up to 50,000 mPas
body: How PRO25D handles samples up to 50,000 mPas without losing performance.
Thick, viscous samples push most rotor-stator homogenizers to their limits, and that's exactly where PRO25D's 50,000 mPas rating earns its place.

Viscosity handling up to 50,000 mPas means compounds, thick suspensions, and dense formulations process on the same unit that handles thin liquid samples, without needing separate equipment for each viscosity range. That capability, combined with generator probes ranging from 5mm to 30mm in diameter, lets the probe itself be matched to how thick and how large the sample actually is. Where viscosity does reduce maximum processing capacity, adding a Deflector Head to the generator probe helps move sample material more effectively, increasing the maximum volume that can still be homogenized.

Existing PRO Quick Connect probes stay compatible with this redesigned motor unit, so current ProScientific users can upgrade without replacing probes or accessories already on hand.

paragraphs: Understanding how rotor-stator homogenization actually works explains why it handles certain samples differently than an ultrasonic probe would. The generator probe draws material directly into itself, where it passes through the narrow gap between a rotating rotor and a fixed stator, experiencing both mechanical shear from the blade action and hydraulic shear from the turbulent flow that gap creates.

The PRO Quick Connect probe system is what makes switching between applications practical rather than a maintenance chore. Coupling stays secure during operation, vibration drops compared to less precise connection systems, and cleaning between samples is straightforward since the stainless-steel probe disconnects cleanly.

paragraphs: Many homogenizing protocols aren't a single speed held for a single duration, they're a sequence: ramp up, hold, pause, adjust, repeat. PRO400PC is built to hold that entire sequence as one program rather than requiring manual re-entry at every step.

Each program stores up to 23 unique cycles, and each cycle independently defines its own speed, run time, and the pause before the next cycle begins. Programs build either directly from the unit's keypad for standalone use, or from a laptop or desktop computer over RS232 serial communication using the included PROgrammable software, useful when a protocol is complex enough to benefit from a full computer interface. Because an infinite number of programs can be created and stored, every distinct protocol a lab runs gets its own saved sequence rather than being reconstructed from notes each time.

body: How PRO400PC's data logging supports industry-standard process verification.
Knowing a homogenization run happened isn't the same as being able to prove it ran exactly as specified, and that gap is exactly what PRO400PC's data logging is built to close.

As a run proceeds, data graphs directly on the computer screen in real time, showing the process as it happens rather than only after the fact. Both the program itself and the data collected, set time and set speed measured against actual time and actual speed, can be stored and recalled later, whether for screen display or as a printed record. That level of traceable documentation is what lets PRO PC homogenizer units meet industry requirements for verification of processing and ongoing documentation maintenance.

paragraphs: Stopping to clean a probe between every sample is one of the biggest hidden time costs in manual homogenizing, and it's exactly what Multi-Prep removes from the workflow.

Self-engagement and disengagement of the Multi-Prep Probes happens automatically, meaning no manual probe handling interrupts a run once it starts. Because the system draws from a 12-pack of probes, a clean probe engages for every sample position, eliminating both cross-contamination risk and the time normally spent cleaning a single generator between runs. Built from 316 stainless steel and PTFE rather than disposable plastic, those probes hold up to tougher tissue types and frozen samples, and clean fully afterward by flaming, autoclaving, or chemical methods, ready for indefinite reuse.

sections.title: Programmability and Manual Mode
sections.tabSummary: Storing protocols and running one-off trials
body: How Multi-Prep's stored programs and manual mode fit both routine and one-off homogenizing needs.
Different labs run different protocols, and Multi-Prep is built to hold onto those differences rather than forcing everyone through a single fixed setting.

Up to 10 different homogenizing programs store directly in the system's memory, so established protocols run consistently every time without needing to be re-entered or re-calibrated. For situations that fall outside a stored program, new homogenizing trials or a quick, single-sample run, manual mode handles individual sample processing directly, without needing to build a new program first. Both modes run through the same ergonomically arranged LCD and control panel, keeping programming parameters fully visible whichever mode is active.

sections.tabSummary: Handling samples up to 50,000 mPas
body: How PRO25D handles samples up to 50,000 mPas without losing performance.
Thick, viscous samples push most rotor-stator homogenizers to their limits, and that's exactly where PRO25D's 50,000 mPas rating earns its place.

Viscosity handling up to 50,000 mPas means compounds, thick suspensions, and dense formulations process on the same unit that handles thin liquid samples, without needing separate equipment for each viscosity range. That capability, combined with generator probes ranging from 5mm to 30mm in diameter, lets the probe itself be matched to how thick and how large the sample actually is. Where viscosity does reduce maximum processing capacity, adding a Deflector Head to the generator probe helps move sample material more effectively, increasing the maximum volume that can still be homogenized.

paragraphs: Understanding how rotor-stator homogenization actually works explains why it handles certain samples differently than an ultrasonic probe would. The generator probe draws material directly into itself, where it passes through the narrow gap between a rotating rotor and a fixed stator, experiencing both mechanical shear from the blade action and hydraulic shear from the turbulent flow that gap creates.

The PRO Quick Connect probe system is what makes switching between applications practical rather than a maintenance chore. Coupling stays secure during operation, vibration drops compared to less precise connection systems, and cleaning between samples is straightforward since the stainless-steel probe disconnects cleanly.

paragraphs: Many homogenizing protocols aren't a single speed held for a single duration, they're a sequence: ramp up, hold, pause, adjust, repeat. PRO400PC is built to hold that entire sequence as one program rather than requiring manual re-entry at every step.

Each program stores up to 23 unique cycles, and each cycle independently defines its own speed, run time, and the pause before the next cycle begins. Programs build either directly from the unit's keypad for standalone use, or from a laptop or desktop computer over RS232 serial communication using the included PROgrammable software, useful when a protocol is complex enough to benefit from a full computer interface. Because an infinite number of programs can be created and stored, every distinct protocol a lab runs gets its own saved sequence rather than being reconstructed from notes each time.

body: How PRO400PC's data logging supports industry-standard process verification.
Knowing a homogenization run happened isn't the same as being able to prove it ran exactly as specified, and that gap is exactly what PRO400PC's data logging is built to close.

As a run proceeds, data graphs directly on the computer screen in real time, showing the process as it happens rather than only after the fact. Both the program itself and the data collected, set time and set speed measured against actual time and actual speed, can be stored and recalled later, whether for screen display or as a printed record. That level of traceable documentation is what lets PRO PC homogenizer units meet industry requirements for verification of processing and ongoing documentation maintenance.

faqs.question: What is the Mya 4 Reaction Station used for?
faqs.answer: It's a 4-zone automated reaction station used for process development, Design of Experiment work, scale-up, and reaction screening, with each zone independently controlled.

faqs.question: How independent are the four zones really?
faqs.answer: Genuinely independent, with up to 200°C of temperature difference tolerated between adjacent zones, thanks to high-performance insulation.

faqs.question: How do I set up two reactions at very different temperatures side by side?
faqs.answer: Assign each reaction to a separate zone and set its temperature independently; as long as the difference between adjacent zones stays within 200°C, both run without interfering with each other.

faqs.question: How do I cool a reaction without a separate chiller?
faqs.answer: Use the built-in Peltier cooling, which reaches -25°C directly from a standard tap water supply, with no separate chiller unit required.

faqs.question: What vessels does the Mya 4 support?
faqs.answer: Vials and tubes from 2 to 20 mL, round bottom flasks from 25 to 250 mL, and process reaction vessels from 50 to 400 mL.

faqs.question: Can I mix magnetic and overhead stirring across zones?
faqs.answer: Yes. Magnetic stirring is standard on every zone, and the optional Mya Compact overhead stirrer can be used on adjacent zones alongside it.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the Control Pad and PC Control Software?
faqs.answer: The Control Pad is supplied as standard for manual or automated profile operation; the optional PC Control Software adds integration and control of third-party devices like pumps, balances, and pH sensors.

faqs.question: Does the Mya 4 support 24/7 unattended operation?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is a core design intent, with automated profiles and full data-logging supporting unattended runs.

faqs.question: Can the Mya 4 export reaction data?
faqs.answer: Yes, in CSV format, from either the Control Pad or the PC Control Software.

faqs.answer: The price depends on your vessel, stirring, and control configuration. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

Four fully independent zones sit close together, yet high-performance insulation holds up to a 200°C difference between adjacent zones, so a reflux at 150°C and a cryogenic reaction at -20°C can run side by side without interfering with each other. Cooling comes from Peltier technology and tap water, reaching -25°C with no separate chiller to plumb in. sections.title: Zone Independence and Temperature Control
sections.tabSummary: What 200°C isolation and Peltier cooling actually deliver
body: Running genuinely different reactions side by side depends on the zones not talking to each other thermally, and that's the specific engineering problem Mya 4 solves.

High-performance insulation holds up to a 200°C difference between adjacent zones, so a high-temperature reflux and a low-temperature crystallization can run next to each other without either affecting the other's result. Cooling itself comes from Peltier technology reaching -25°C directly from a tap water supply, removing the need for a separate recirculating chiller entirely. Block and solution temperature are tracked separately, since what the block reads and what's actually happening in the vessel aren't quite the same thing.
