faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axiovert 5 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an inverted microscope for cell culture and research, supporting DIC, iHMC, phase contrast, brightfield, and multichannel fluorescence on one stand.

faqs.question: Does it need a computer to operate?
faqs.answer: No. In standalone configuration, an Axiocam camera and on-screen display run the system independently, saving images directly to USB.

faqs.question: How does multichannel fluorescence work?
faqs.answer: Paired with Colibri 3 LED illumination and any ZEISS microscope camera, select the channels for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, then press Snap. The system automatically adjusts exposure, acquires each channel, switches wavelengths, and delivers a single overlaid image with a scale bar embedded in the file metadata.

faqs.question: What contrast techniques are available?
faqs.answer: DIC, improved Hoffman Modulation Contrast (iHMC), phase contrast, and brightfield, in transmitted light, combined with multichannel fluorescence.

faqs.question: Can it handle large culture vessels?
faqs.answer: Yes, Axiovert 5 offers enough space for cell factories, not just standard dishes.

faqs.question: Is AI-based cell analysis available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an optional addition, AI Cell Count and AI Cell Confluency through ZEISS Labscope, pre-trained and requiring no prior AI knowledge to use.

faqs.question: What software options are available?
faqs.answer: Three configuration paths: standalone with an Axiocam and on-screen display, ZEISS Labscope for connected and multichannel fluorescence imaging, or ZEISS ZEN for advanced research-grade analysis.

faqs.question: Can the microscope be upgraded later?
faqs.answer: Yes, both hardware and software are upgradeable, so the stand can adapt as work requirements change rather than needing replacement.

faqs.question: How is Axiovert 5 different from Axiovert 5 digital?
faqs.answer: Axiovert 5 offers the widest contrast technique range (DIC, iHMC, phase contrast, brightfield, and fluorescence) with a choice of external camera and light source. Axiovert 5 digital integrates the camera and fluorescence system into a closed, all-in-one unit with one additional fluorescence channel and no external camera or light source decisions to make.

faqs.question: How is it different from Primovert?
faqs.answer: Primovert is a compact microscope built specifically to fit a laminar flow cabinet, covering brightfield and phase contrast, with fluorescence and AI analysis available on specific versions. faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axiovert 7 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an inverted microscope for routine cell culture work and multidimensional life science research, supporting live-cell imaging, fixed samples, tissue sections, and fluorescence experiments, from monolayers through to organoids.

faqs.question: Is Axiovert 7 suitable for live cell imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes. Label-free live cell culture is monitored using phase contrast, DIC, PlasDIC, or iHMC, and long-term live-cell and 3D models, including organoids and Organ-on-a-Chip systems, are supported under stable environmental conditions with automated time-lapse imaging.

faqs.question: Which contrast methods are available with Axiovert 7?
faqs.answer: Six: PH (phase contrast), FL (fluorescence), DIC, PlasDIC, iHMC, and POL (polarization).

faqs.question: Can Axiovert 7 perform multichannel fluorescence imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, multichannel fluorescence images are automatically overlaid and saved together with scale and metadata, supporting digital optical sectioning for improved resolution in X, Y, and Z.

faqs.question: What software is used with ZEISS Axiovert 7?
faqs.answer: ZEISS ZEN imaging software, enabling precise multidimensional experiments including Z-stacks, time-lapse imaging, and automated scanning for slides and multiwell plates.

faqs.question: Is Axiovert 7 expandable?
faqs.answer: Yes. The system uses modular hardware, upgradable software, and extensive interfaces, adapting from digital optical sectioning to long-term live-cell imaging as research requirements change, including in accordance with GxP guidelines.

faqs.question: Can Axiovert 7 be used for whole slide imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, the system performs panoramic scanning and whole-slide imaging of stained or immunofluorescence-labeled tissue sections for quantitative spatial analysis.

faqs.question: What types of cameras are compatible with Axiovert 7?
faqs.answer: Specific camera compatibility was not itemized on the source page reviewed. Inkarp can confirm compatible camera options directly.

faqs.question: What is the field of view?
faqs.answer: 23 mm.

faqs.question: What magnification range does it cover?
faqs.answer: 1.25x to 100x across its objective range.

faqs.question: Is the focus and stage motorized?
faqs.answer: Yes, both are motorized, enabling reproducible, automated imaging.

faqs.question: How is Axiovert 7 different from Axiovert 5?
faqs.answer: Axiovert 7 adds motorized focus and stage, polarization contrast, whole-slide scanning, multiwell plate automation, and GxP-adaptable workflows. Axiovert 5 covers broad contrast flexibility (DIC, iHMC, phase contrast, brightfield, fluorescence) with manual operation, suited to routine work without the same level of automated, high-throughput capability.

longForm.heroLead: Research doesn't stay still. A project that starts with a simple monolayer culture can end up needing time-lapse organoid imaging, whole-slide scanning, or high-throughput multiwell analysis, and the microscope shouldn't be the thing holding that progression back. Axiovert 7 covers a genuinely wide range: six contrast methods (PH, FL, DIC, PlasDIC, iHMC, POL), a 23 mm field of view, and objectives spanning 1.25x to 100x magnification. Focus, press Snap, and the system captures a sharp, reproducible image instantly, with multichannel fluorescence automatically overlaid and saved together with scale and metadata. Motorized focus and stage paired with ZEISS ZEN software enable Z-stacks, time-lapse imaging, and automated scanning across slides and multiwell plates, precisely and reproducibly, without constant hands-on adjustment. The system is built modular from the start, so digital optical sectioning, long-term live-cell imaging, and GxP-compliant workflows are additions, not replacements. What it captures: everything from label-free routine cell culture to whole-slide pathology imaging. What it automates: focus, stage movement, and multichannel fluorescence acquisition. What it grows into: GxP-compliant, modular research workflows, on the same platform.

Across a lab running dozens of samples a day, that isn't a convenience feature, it's a genuine change in how much research actually fits into a working session.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axioscan 7 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an automated digital slide scanner, used across life science research, pharma and biotech spatial biology, clinical diagnostics, and geology, digitizing microscope slides at high throughput.

faqs.question: How many slides can it scan in one run?
faqs.answer: Up to 100, depending on the configuration, with reliable 24/7 unattended operation.

faqs.question: What configurations are available?
faqs.answer: Four: Standard (Life Science Research), Spatial Biology (Pharma & Biotech), Clinical, and Geology and Materials, each with different slide formats, contrast techniques, and software integration.

faqs.question: Is Axioscan 7 certified for clinical diagnostic use?
faqs.answer: Only the Clinical configuration carries IVDR certification. The Standard, Spatial Biology, and Geology configurations are not certified for diagnostic use.

faqs.question: What contrast techniques are supported?
faqs.answer: Up to five, depending on configuration: brightfield, fluorescence, circular polarization, crossed linear polarization, and TIE (transport of intensity equation).

faqs.question: How many objectives are available?
faqs.answer: Up to 14 on Standard and Geology configurations, 3 on Spatial Biology, and 2 base objectives with 4 additional options on Clinical.

faqs.question: What software does it use?
faqs.answer: ZEN, or third-party solutions, on Standard and Geology. Spatial Biology adds SlideStream software and Mindpeak AI-based image analysis. Clinical integrates into IMS/PACS systems via ZEISS Solutions Lab and a Dicom converter.

faqs.question: Can it handle multiple staining rounds on the same tissue?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the Spatial Biology configuration, which supports coregistration of multiple staining rounds alongside Mindpeak AI-based analysis.

faqs.question: What slide formats are supported?
faqs.answer: 1x3", 2x3", and 4x3" on Standard and Geology (Geology adds GEO format specifically), 1x3" only on Spatial Biology and Clinical.

faqs.question: Is this suitable for geological or petrographic work?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Geology configuration supports GEO-format slides and pairs with the Petrography Analysis Toolbox (PetPAT) for quantitative analytics.

faqs.question: How does the Clinical configuration connect to hospital systems?
faqs.answer: Via ZEISS Solutions Lab and a Dicom converter, integrating into existing IMS and PACS infrastructure. Zeiss notes this integration path itself is not an in vitro diagnostic device.

faqs.question: Where can I find detailed technical specifications?
faqs.answer: Detailed dimensions, weight, and full objective and camera part numbers were not published on the source page reviewed. Inkarp can request the full specification sheet from Zeiss.

longForm.heroLead: A manual microscope scales with the number of hands available to operate it. Axioscan 7 doesn't. Set up a task once, and it digitizes up to 100 slides in a single automated run, with 24/7 uninterrupted operation across similar slide sets or genuinely mixed applications. It isn't one fixed instrument, it's four configurations: Standard, Spatial Biology, Clinical, and Geology, each built around different slide formats, contrast techniques, objectives, and software integration for the field it actually serves. Switch rapidly between fluorescence, brightfield, and polarization without reconfiguring hardware between runs. Image quality holds consistent across the whole batch, not just the first slide or the last. Research-grade data quality supports demanding fluorescence work, and ZEN software unlocks the deeper processing and analysis layer once scanning is done. The Clinical configuration carries IVDR certification, the only Zeiss product in this build with that specific regulatory status. What it automates: the entire slide-to-digital-image pipeline, unattended. What it configures to: the actual field, life science, pharma, clinical, or geology. body: High-performance digital slide scanning across four fields. Spatial biology at scale, life science research, clinical applications, and geology.

sections.description: Choosing between Standard, Spatial Biology, Clinical, and Geology.
body: Buying an automated slide scanner sized for a general lab, then trying to run clinical diagnostic samples or multi-round spatial biology staining through it, means fighting the hardware and software the whole way. Axioscan 7 avoids that by not being one general-purpose system, Zeiss builds four distinct configurations, each with its own slide format range, contrast technique set, objective count, and software layer.

Standard covers the broadest general research use, up to 14 objectives and the full contrast range including crossed linear polarization. Spatial Biology trades objective breadth (down to 3) for SlideStream software and Mindpeak AI, purpose-built for coregistering multiple staining rounds and running AI-based analysis at scale. Clinical narrows the slide format to 1x3" only and adds direct IMS/PACS integration, with the IVDR certification that makes diagnostic use possible. Geology keeps Standard's broad objective and contrast range but adds GEO format slide support for petrographic work.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Celldiscoverer 7 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an automated live-cell imaging platform, used for explorative high-content research, including cell biology, organoid research, developmental biology, and high-content screening.

faqs.question: Do I need to be a microscopy expert to use it?
faqs.answer: No. Insert the sample carrier and the system makes all necessary settings automatically, including calibration, focus, and aberration correction.

faqs.question: How much faster is the latest generation?
faqs.answer: Up to 9x faster widefield acquisition and up to 1.8x faster confocal acquisition, compared to the previous generation.

faqs.question: What is Autoimmersion?
faqs.answer: Fully automated water immersion supply and removal through a 50x objective, sealed with an elastic silicon membrane, supporting live-cell imaging at 37°C over several days.

faqs.question: What is Autocorr?
faqs.answer: Automatic correction ring adjustment on the objective, compensating for spherical aberration caused by different vessel bottom thickness or material.

faqs.question: Can it handle different sample carrier types?
faqs.answer: Yes, automatic sample recognition detects relevant vessel features on loading, supporting Petri dishes, chamber slides, multi-well plates, plastic or glass, thin or thick bottoms, and low- or high-skirt plates.

faqs.question: How does focus work for long time-lapse experiments?
faqs.answer: Find Focus locates the region of interest with one click; Definite Focus holds that position throughout the experiment, whether it runs seconds or several days, and automatic focus maps support multiple positions simultaneously.

faqs.question: Can it do confocal imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the optional LSM 910 and Airyscan 2 upgrade, delivering up to 1.9x resolution improvement, spectral imaging, and photomanipulation techniques like FRAP and FRET.

faqs.question: Is there protection against objective damage?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Adaptive Lens Guard prevents collisions with the sample vessel or hardware while automatically maximizing the available scanning area.

faqs.question: Can throughput be increased with automation?
faqs.answer: Yes, an optional robotic sample loader from Peak Analysis & Automation (PAA) handles all SBS multi-well plate formats for high-volume, unattended processing.

faqs.question: What software analyzes the imaging data?
faqs.answer: arivis Pro, for 2D through complex 3D and 4D dataset analysis, with arivis Cloud for neural network training and arivis Hub for parallel cloud-based processing across multiple datasets.

faqs.question: Is it reliable in a shared, multi-user lab?
faqs.answer: Yes, workflows execute reproducibly without manual recalibration between users, and predictive service analytics schedule maintenance based on actual component wear.

faqs.question: How is Celldiscoverer 7 different from Axioscan 7?
faqs.answer: Celldiscoverer 7 automates live-cell and high-content imaging, with immersion, incubation, and focus systems built for living, dynamic samples. Axioscan 7 automates digitization of fixed, prepared slides at high volume, with no equivalent need for immersion or incubation.

sections.title: Automatic Adaptation to Any Sample Carrier
sections.description: What Autocorr and automatic sample recognition actually solve.
body: High-numerical-aperture objectives, the kind live-cell imaging genuinely needs, only deliver their promised contrast and sensitivity when their optics correctly compensate for the specific vessel they're looking through. Bottom thickness varies. Material varies, plastic versus glass. Skirt height varies between plate designs. Every one of those variations introduces spherical aberration if left uncorrected, and manually adjusting a correction ring for each new vessel type is exactly the kind of expertise-gated step that slows a lab down.

Celldiscoverer 7 removes it. Automatic sample recognition detects the relevant vessel features the moment a sample loads, and Autocorr adjusts the objective's correction ring to compensate, without anyone touching a dial. The freedom that unlocks is real: Petri dishes, chamber slides, multi-well plates, plastic or glass, thin or thick vessel bottoms, low-skirt or high-skirt plates, all usable interchangeably, at full optical quality, on the same system.

sections.description: What each specialized lighting module actually solves.
body: A flat, polished microelectronic part and a translucent zebrafish embryo need genuinely different light. One reflects almost everything back specularly, hiding detail under glare. The other needs gentle, uniform illumination that doesn't scatter or overheat the sample. SteREO Discovery V8 doesn't try to solve both with one fixed light source, it offers a module for each.

CL 1500 ECO fiber-optic cold light, paired with a wide range of light guides, is built specifically for developmental biology, gentle enough for zebrafish and Drosophila embryos without heat stress. The Coaxial Reflected-Light Illuminator S goes the opposite direction, purpose-built for smooth, specular surfaces like polished metal parts and microelectronic devices, with illumination and observation optimized specifically around the PlanApo S 1.0x objective. VisiLED ring light S 40-10 DF combines brightfield and darkfield in reflected light for PCB and surface inspection, and a light manager keeps coaxial lighting brightness stable through the entire zoom range, so illumination doesn't shift as magnification changes.

sections.title: eZoom, Explained
sections.description: Why electronic lens positioning beats a mechanical curve.
body: Every stereo microscope zoom body has to move lenses precisely as magnification changes. A mechanical zoom body does this with a physical cam curve, one fixed mechanical path that every unit follows, tolerances and all. Those tolerances compound as magnification increases, which is exactly where a soft image costs the most.

eZoom replaces that physical curve with stepping motors that position each lens electronically, correcting for the actual tolerance of the individual lenses in that specific microscope rather than assuming a uniform mechanical path fits every unit. Zeiss states the result directly: doubled precision compared to a mechanical zoom body, visibly more detail captured across the zoom range. The defocus curve stays tighter to the depth-of-field envelope throughout, rather than drifting outside it as magnification climbs.

sections.title: Reproducible Zoom Positions
sections.description: Why 99% accuracy matters more than raw magnification.
body: A 345x magnification figure is only useful if you can actually get back to it. Most zoom systems drift slightly every time they're adjusted, close enough for casual observation, not precise enough for a measurement or comparison that depends on consistent conditions.

eZoom solves that directly. User-defined zoom positions are set once and recalled with more than 99% reproducibility, which means a measurement taken today at a specific magnification and a measurement taken next month at the same defined position are genuinely comparable, not approximately similar. That reproducibility comes from the same electronic lens positioning that gives eZoom its 2x precision advantage over a mechanical zoom body, stepping motors correcting for individual lens tolerance rather than following one fixed mechanical path.

A beetle, a circuit board, a bullet, a root tip pulled straight from the soil, all need to be seen whole, in three dimensions, without any preparation getting in the way. Three stands and two tube options assemble into whichever combination the work calls for, and every version ships with integrated near-vertical LED illumination as standard. High-contrast, three-dimensional viewing comes standard across all three. Add a microscope camera to the phototube, and documentation happens on the spot, no separate setup required. What it skips: slide prep, staining, coverslips, anything the specimen shouldn't need in the first place. What it configures to: classroom, biology lab, or industrial inspection bench. body: Standard stereo optics show color fringing at high magnification, a soft halo around edges that gets worse the further you zoom in. That's not a minor cosmetic issue when the work depends on distinguishing genuine material boundaries from optical artifacts. Apochromatic correction removes it, at every point across Stemi 508's zoom range.

The 8:1 zoom ratio means that correction holds from a 122 mm field of view down to the finest detail an interchangeable eyepiece and front optic combination can resolve, up to 250x. And because working distance stretches to 287 mm at the wide end, reaching that level of detail doesn't mean crowding tools, hands, or a soldering iron into a cramped gap under the objective.

sections.title: Fixed-Köhler Illumination
sections.description: Why removing an adjustment step matters in a classroom.
body: Köhler illumination is the standard for even, glare-free microscope lighting, and getting it right normally takes a trained hand: aligning the condenser, centering the field diaphragm, adjusting for each new sample. In a research lab, that is a five-minute task for someone who does it daily. In a classroom of thirty students on their first day with a microscope, it is thirty separate failure points before anyone has actually looked at a cell.

Primostar 1 removes the step entirely. The illumination arrives pre-fixed, so image quality does not depend on whether the last student to use the microscope set it up correctly. A teacher hands the microscope over already working.

longForm.heroLead: A microscope that needs a manual before the first lesson isn't ready for a classroom. Primostar 3 comes pre-configured, straight out of the box, so students and lab staff focus on what they're actually looking at, not on how to get there. It comes in three ready-made packages, each built for a specific job. Fixed-Köhler for basic education, with a large 20 mm field of view already adjusted and a set of objectives and eyepieces already in place. A teaching and routine lab package with a choice of 30-watt halogen or energy-saving LED, plus an optional fluorescence tube. And a digital classroom package built around an integrated 8.3 megapixel HD WiFi camera, for sharing live images straight to a projector or monitor. Built from solid, resistant materials, the kind that keep working smoothly after years of daily use in a busy teaching lab, with minimal maintenance along the way. What it saves you: setup time, energy cost, and the guesswork over which configuration to buy. What it adds over Primostar 1: digital connectivity, package flexibility, and optional fluorescence. faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axiolab 5 used for?
faqs.answer: It is an upright microscope built for clinical and biomedical laboratory routine work, including hematology, histology, cytopathology, and general clinical microscopy, with built-in Smart Microscopy documentation.

faqs.question: What is Smart Microscopy?
faqs.answer: A documentation system that captures a true-color, correctly scaled image with a single press of the Snap button, without needing a separate computer or software.

faqs.question: Does scaling get added automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes, every image captured includes correct scaling information automatically, no manual scale bar insertion needed.

faqs.question: Do I need a separate computer to use Axiolab 5?
faqs.answer: No, in stand-alone configuration the microscope and Axiocam camera operate independently of a computer system. Labscope and ZEN configurations add connected or research-grade options where needed.

faqs.question: What cameras does it work with?
faqs.answer: Axiocam 212 color or Axiocam 203 mono, depending on the configuration chosen.

faqs.question: Can it handle fluorescence imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, with powerful LED illumination across various wavelengths, and multichannel fluorescence support through the ZEISS Labscope configuration.

faqs.question: What makes it ergonomic?
faqs.answer: One-hand access to the Snap button, stage drive, focus, and brightness control, adjustable ergotubes, a height and torque-adaptable rackless stage, and a dual specimen holder that reduces slide changes.

faqs.question: Can it track samples by barcode?
faqs.answer: Yes, either through a barcode reader connected to the Axiocam 212 color camera, or by scanning with an iPad's built-in camera through Labscope.

faqs.question: Is a two-person shared view available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an optional co-observation bundle with a photo tube or ergo photo tube, built for real-time case review and resident training.

faqs.question: How does Eco-mode work?
faqs.answer: Axiolab 5 automatically goes to standby after 15 minutes of inactivity, saving energy without needing to be switched off manually.

faqs.question: How is Axiolab 5 different from Primostar 3?
faqs.answer: Primostar 3 is built primarily for teaching and basic routine lab work. Axiolab 5 is positioned specifically for clinical and biomedical laboratories, with Smart Microscopy documentation, dedicated ergonomic features, and co-observation options Primostar 3 doesn't offer.

faqs.question: Is there a return policy?
faqs.answer: Yes, a 60-day risk-free purchase. If it isn't the right fit, it can be returned with no questions asked.

It's not difficult work, but it interrupts every single slide, and across a full clinic day that adds up to real time lost and real focus broken.

Axiolab 5 removes the interruption. Press the ergonomic Snap button directly on the stand, and the system captures a detail-rich, true-color image, exactly as seen through the eyepieces, with correct scaling added automatically. No computer switch. No manual settings. The procedure integrates into the microscopy workflow that's already happening, rather than pausing it.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axioscope 5 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an upright microscope built for biomedical routine and research work, supporting histology, cytology, hematology, and multichannel fluorescence documentation including immunofluorescence and FISH.

faqs.question: How does the four-channel fluorescence feature work?
faqs.answer: Paired with Colibri 3 LED illumination and the Axiocam 203 mono camera, select the channels for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, then press Snap. The system automatically adjusts exposure, acquires each channel, switches wavelengths, and delivers a single overlaid image with a scale bar, without needing a PC.

faqs.question: Does brightfield documentation work the same way?
faqs.answer: Yes, focus the sample and press Snap. The captured color matches exactly what's seen through the eyepieces, with brightness and white balance adjusted automatically.

faqs.question: Is the focus motorized?
faqs.answer: No, Axioscope 5 uses manual Z focus. Motorized focus is a feature of Axioscope 7.

faqs.question: Can Axioscope 5 perform whole slide imaging?
faqs.answer: No, whole slide imaging requires Axioscope 7's motorized stage and Z-control. Axioscope 5 is built for field-of-view documentation and multichannel fluorescence rather than full slide digitization.

faqs.question: What makes Axioscope 7 different from Axioscope 5?
faqs.answer: Axioscope 7 adds a motorized stage and motorized Z-control (autofocus) for scanning and stitching entire slides into whole slide images, with ZEN software supporting full GxP compliance for regulated environments. Axioscope 5 keeps focus manual and is built for routine field-of-view documentation.

faqs.question: Is Axioscope 7 suitable for clinical diagnostics?
faqs.answer: Axioscope 7 is positioned for clinical research labs and biomedical research applications, with ZEN core software supporting GxP compliance where regulated diagnostic workflows require it.

faqs.question: What is the advantage of whole slide imaging on a motorized upright microscope?
faqs.answer: It allows an entire specimen to be digitized automatically, large tissue sections scanned with a motorized stage, focus maintained across the whole sample, and multi-position, multi-channel datasets stitched into a single high-resolution image, useful for archival, remote review, and downstream digital analysis.

faqs.question: Which Axioscope is right for my lab?
faqs.answer: If the work is routine and research documentation, including multichannel fluorescence, without needing to digitize entire slides, Axioscope 5 fits. If the lab needs to scan and archive complete specimens, particularly under regulated conditions, Axioscope 7 is the better fit.

faqs.question: What illumination does it use?
faqs.answer: 10W LED or 50W Halogen for transmitted light, and Colibri 3, Viluma 5/7, or HXP for fluorescence.

faqs.question: Can samples be tracked by barcode?
faqs.answer: Yes, either through a barcode reader connected to the Axiocam 212 color camera, or by scanning with an iPad's camera through Labscope.

faqs.question: Is a shared, two-person view available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an optional co-observation bundle with a photo tube or ergo photo tube, built for pathology case review and resident training.

faqs.question: Is there a return policy?

longForm.heroHook: Four fluorescence channels. One click. Not one PC required.
longForm.heroLead: Multichannel fluorescence used to mean a workstation, manual channel switching, and exposure settings adjusted by hand between every wavelength. Axioscope 5 collapses all of that into one press. Pair it with the Colibri 3 LED light source and the Axiocam 203 mono camera, select the channels for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, and press Snap. The system switches wavelengths, adjusts exposure automatically, acquires each channel, and hands back a single overlaid multichannel image with a scale bar already included, even without a PC connected. The same Smart Microscopy logic runs through brightfield work too. Focus, press Snap, done. Color appears in the captured image exactly as it looked through the eyepieces, brightness and white balance adjusted automatically. Ergotubes adapt eyepiece height and angle to natural posture, every essential control sits within easy reach, and the light manager adjusts illumination automatically, no manual lamp brightness dialing between samples. What it replaces: manual channel switching and PC-based fluorescence documentation. What it adds over Axiolab 5: true multichannel fluorescence, up to four channels in one click. Where it sits in the range: below Axioscope 7's motorized whole slide imaging, above routine brightfield-only microscopes.

sections.title: Four Channels, One Click
sections.description: How Colibri 3 and Smart Microscopy handle multichannel fluorescence.
body: Multichannel fluorescence imaging is normally a stop-start process: select a channel, adjust exposure, capture, switch, adjust again, capture again, then combine everything into an overlay afterward, usually on a connected computer. That's four separate manual decisions before a single usable image exists.

Axioscope 5 removes the stopping. Paired with Colibri 3 and the Axiocam 203 mono camera, select the channels needed for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, then press Snap. The system adjusts exposure time automatically, acquires the image, switches to the next channel, and repeats, on its own. What comes out the other end is a single overlaid multichannel fluorescence image, scale bar included, without needing a PC connected at all.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Smart Zoom 5 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an automated digital microscope for quality assurance, quality control, and failure analysis across industrial applications, built to be simple enough for untrained users while delivering reproducible results.

faqs.question: What is the magnification range?
faqs.answer: 10x to 2020x, across four smart objectives.

faqs.question: What happens when an objective is changed mid-inspection?
faqs.answer: The objectives are encoded, so the software automatically recognizes the change, recalibrates measurement, and returns to the correct focus and x/y position, no manual refocusing or relocation needed.

faqs.question: Does it protect the sample from accidental contact?
faqs.answer: Yes, collision detection automatically retracts the optical engine to a safe position the instant contact is detected, protecting both the sample and the user.

faqs.question: Can repeat inspections be automated?
faqs.answer: Yes, macro recording mode stores step-by-step workflows for the same sample type, letting them be repeated reproducibly without in-depth microscope knowledge.

faqs.question: What is the Best Image function?
faqs.answer: A one-click feature that generates a series of images under varying lighting and processing conditions, including HDR, noise filtering, and sharpening, so the best result can be selected for the application.

faqs.question: Can Smart Zoom 5 connect to an electron microscope?
faqs.answer: Yes, through Shuttle & Find, which relocates a defined region of interest from the digital microscope to an electron microscope using automated marker recognition, then aligns both images into an overlay.

faqs.question: What illumination options are available?
faqs.answer: A built-in, segmentable LED ring light, giving complete control over illumination, alongside coaxial brightfield and full or segmented ringlight configurations demonstrated across various applications.

faqs.question: Does tilting the microscope lose the region of interest?
faqs.answer: No, the motorized, encoded architecture keeps the focused region of interest in focus and centered even as the arm tilts up to ±45°.

faqs.question: Can reports be generated directly?
faqs.answer: Yes, images can be annotated and exported directly to Word report templates.

faqs.question: How is Smart Zoom 5 different from Zeiss's research microscopes?
faqs.answer: Smart Zoom 5 belongs to Zeiss's Industrial Quality Solutions division, built specifically for QA/QC, failure analysis, and industrial inspection with encoded, automated optics. The Research Microscopy Solutions range (Primostar, Axiovert, Stemi, SteREO Discovery) is built for biological and life science research instead.

longForm.heroLead: Changing magnification usually means losing your place, refocus, relocate, recalibrate, repeat. Smart Zoom 5 removes that entirely. Every objective is encoded, so the moment it's swapped, the software recognizes the change, corrects the measurement calibration, and returns to the exact focus and x/y position, no manual recovery step required. Four smart objectives cover a 10x to 2020x magnification range, with a built-in, segmentable LED ring light giving complete control over illumination. Collision detection retracts the optical engine automatically the instant an objective contacts the sample, protecting both in one motion. Built-in vibration dampening and optical image stabilization keep detail crisp even on a busy industrial floor. A macro recording mode captures a step-by-step inspection workflow once, then repeats it reproducibly, without needing microscope expertise from whoever runs it next. And when a defect needs a closer look under an electron microscope, Shuttle & Find relocates the exact region of interest there in the shortest possible time, no manual re-searching required. What it removes: manual refocusing, recalibration, and relocation on every objective change. What it protects: both the sample and the operator, automatically, on contact. What it connects to: an electron microscope, when the inspection needs to go further.

sections.title: Encoded Objectives, Explained
sections.description: Why swapping lenses doesn't cost setup time here.
body: Changing magnification on most microscopes means losing everything the inspection had already established, focus, calibration, and exactly where on the sample the region of interest actually was. Every swap becomes a small reset, refocus manually, recalibrate manually, hunt for the same spot manually.

Smart Zoom 5's objectives are encoded, so the system knows exactly which one is mounted at all times. Swap objectives mid-inspection, and the software recognizes the change immediately: measurement calibration adjusts automatically, focus returns to where it was, and the x/y position snaps back to the exact region of interest, ready to continue the analysis without any of the usual recovery steps.

sections.title: Shuttle & Find
sections.description: How a region of interest moves from digital to electron microscopy. Some failure analysis needs more resolution than any optical microscope can provide, and the usual bridge to an electron microscope is manual: describe the location, hope it translates, spend real time re-finding the same spot under a completely different imaging system. Shuttle & Find removes that gap. Define a region of interest on Smart Zoom 5, and the same location relocates on the electron microscope within the shortest possible time, using automated marker recognition rather than manual searching. Once found, both images align into a single overlay, giving a direct visual bridge between the optical and electron-level views of the exact same feature. faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axio Zoom V16 used for?
faqs.answer: It's a fluorescence stereo zoom microscope built for large object fields, used to image complete model organisms in fluorescence contrast, alongside routine screening and demanding multidimensional imaging.

faqs.question: What is the zoom ratio?
What numerical aperture does it achieve?
faqs.answer: NA 0.25 as the stated headline figure, reaching NA 0.5 with the Plan-NEOFLUAR Z 2.3x objective across a 1.5 mm object field, already in the medium zoom range.

faqs.question: Can it image whole organisms in fluorescence?
faqs.answer: Yes, demonstrated directly on a complete mouse embryo and a two-color Drosophila embryo, without needing to tile or stitch multiple fields.

faqs.question: What are the three zoom modes?
faqs.answer: Brightness mode (highest brightness across the zoom range, for fluorescence), Eyepiece mode (optimized for ocular observation), and Camera mode (adapted to the connected camera's performance).

faqs.question: What does the Best Mode button do?
faqs.answer: It determines the current optical state and automatically optimizes transmitted light, including an increased-contrast brightfield option, and can save and reload that configuration for future experiments.

faqs.question: What is eZoom?
faqs.answer: An electronic zoom system that replaces the mechanical zoom curve with stepping motors, correcting for individual lens tolerances and delivering doubled precision compared to a mechanical zoom body.

faqs.question: How is it controlled?
faqs.answer: Via a SyCop 3 touchscreen, consistent with the control approach used across the SteREO Discovery family.

faqs.question: How does it fit into Zeiss's wider stereo and zoom range?

faqs.question: How is it different from SteREO Discovery V20?
faqs.answer: Both use eZoom, but V16 is built specifically around fluorescence brightness and large object fields for whole-organism imaging, while V20 is built for maximum stereo magnification (up to 345x) and highly reproducible zoom positioning.

longForm.heroHook: NA 0.5, in the medium zoom range. Not the top of it. The middle.
longForm.heroLead: Numerical aperture usually climbs slowly as magnification increases, and stays modest everywhere else. Axio Zoom V16 breaks that pattern: with the Plan-NEOFLUAR Z 2.3x objective, it reaches a numerical aperture of NA 0.5 across a 1.5 mm object field, already in the medium zoom range, not stretched thin at the extreme high end. That aperture is what drives everything else. Superior fluorescence brightness in large object fields means whole model organisms, a full mouse embryo, an entire Drosophila embryo, image in fluorescence contrast without breaking the specimen into tiles first. The 16:1 zoom covers overview through fine detail on the same optical path. eZoom replaces the mechanical zoom curve with stepping motors that account for individual lens tolerance, doubling precision over a mechanical zoom body. Three selectable zoom modes, Brightness, Eyepiece, and Camera, optimize the aperture-to-resolution trade-off for whichever task is actually happening. And the Best Mode button reads the current optical state and adjusts transmitted light automatically, saved and recalled for the next experiment at the touch of the same button. What it achieves: high numerical aperture well before the top of the zoom range. What it images: complete model organisms in fluorescence, not fragments of them. What it remembers: exact illumination settings, saved and reloaded per experiment.

sections.eyebrow: Three Zoom Modes, One Purpose Each
sections.title: Three Zoom Modes, One Purpose Each
sections.description: Why the same optical path behaves differently depending on what's actually happening.
body: Every stereo zoom microscope balances the same three things against each other, brightness, depth of field, and resolution, and the ideal balance shifts depending on whether someone's looking through the eyepieces, capturing a camera image, or chasing the brightest possible fluorescence signal. Axio Zoom V16 doesn't force one fixed compromise across all three, eZoom's motorized iris diaphragm shifts the balance per mode.

Brightness mode holds the highest possible brightness across the entire zoom range, built specifically for fluorescence observation where signal strength is the whole game. Eyepiece mode favors conventional ocular observation, maximum depth of field at large fields for orientation, maximum resolution at high magnification for detail. Camera mode adapts to whatever camera is actually connected, tuning the resolution-to-depth-of-field relationship to get the most out of that specific sensor across the full range.

sections.title: Intelligent Transmitted Light
sections.description: What the Best Mode button actually automates. Manually optimizing transmitted light for a given specimen and zoom position means understanding the current optical state well enough to adjust it correctly, a skill that takes real time to build and doesn't transfer automatically to a different operator. The Best Mode button removes that requirement. Axio Zoom V16 determines the actual optical state on its own and optimizes transmitted light automatically, adding increased-contrast brightfield to the standard brightfield, darkfield, and oblique options already available. Once the setting is right for a specific application, it saves and reloads at the touch of the same button, so the next experiment starts from exactly the same optical configuration rather than being rebuilt from scratch.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axiovert 5 digital used for?
faqs.answer: It's an all-in-one inverted cell imaging system built around AI-assisted analysis, used for routine cell culture monitoring, cell counting, confluency measurement, and multichannel fluorescence documentation.

faqs.question: Does the AI need training before it can be used?
faqs.answer: No. The AI Cell Count and AI Cell Confluency modules are pre-trained and ready to use immediately, with no training or prior knowledge required from the operator.

faqs.question: How many fluorescence channels can it capture?
faqs.answer: Up to 5 channels, triggered from the same Snap button used for standard image capture.

faqs.question: What does pressing the Snap button actually do?
faqs.answer: Depending on the mode selected, it triggers a single image acquisition, multi-channel fluorescence imaging, the full AI cell counting and confluency workflow, or video recording.

faqs.question: How does AI cell counting work in practice?
faqs.answer: Examine the culture as usual, then take a picture while moving across the vessel. The image is analyzed automatically, and a result, both visual and quantitative, arrives instantly.

faqs.question: Is it suitable for labs with multiple users of different experience levels?

faqs.question: Does the closed-box design make it harder to check on cells?

faqs.question: Can it record video?
faqs.answer: Yes, video recording is one of the four outcomes triggered by the Snap button.

faqs.question: How is Axiovert 5 digital different from Primovert digital?

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axiovert 5 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an inverted microscope for cell culture and research, supporting DIC, iHMC, phase contrast, brightfield, and multichannel fluorescence on one stand.

faqs.question: Does it need a computer to operate?
faqs.answer: No. In standalone configuration, an Axiocam camera and on-screen display run the system independently, saving images directly to USB.

faqs.question: How does multichannel fluorescence work?
faqs.answer: Paired with Colibri 3 LED illumination and any ZEISS microscope camera, select the channels for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, then press Snap. The system automatically adjusts exposure, acquires each channel, switches wavelengths, and delivers a single overlaid image with a scale bar embedded in the file metadata.

faqs.question: What contrast techniques are available?
faqs.answer: DIC, improved Hoffman Modulation Contrast (iHMC), phase contrast, and brightfield, in transmitted light, combined with multichannel fluorescence.

faqs.question: Can it handle large culture vessels?
faqs.answer: Yes, Axiovert 5 offers enough space for cell factories, not just standard dishes.

faqs.question: Is AI-based cell analysis available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an optional addition, AI Cell Count and AI Cell Confluency through ZEISS Labscope, pre-trained and requiring no prior AI knowledge to use.

faqs.question: What software options are available?
faqs.answer: Three configuration paths: standalone with an Axiocam and on-screen display, ZEISS Labscope for connected and multichannel fluorescence imaging, or ZEISS ZEN for advanced research-grade analysis.

faqs.question: Can the microscope be upgraded later?
faqs.answer: Yes, both hardware and software are upgradeable, so the stand can adapt as work requirements change rather than needing replacement.

faqs.question: How is Axiovert 5 different from Axiovert 5 digital?
faqs.answer: Axiovert 5 offers the widest contrast technique range (DIC, iHMC, phase contrast, brightfield, and fluorescence) with a choice of external camera and light source. Axiovert 5 digital integrates the camera and fluorescence system into a closed, all-in-one unit with one additional fluorescence channel and no external camera or light source decisions to make.

faqs.question: How is it different from Primovert?
faqs.answer: Primovert is a compact microscope built specifically to fit a laminar flow cabinet, covering brightfield and phase contrast, with fluorescence and AI analysis available on specific versions. Axiovert 5 covers a substantially wider range of contrast techniques and fluorescence channels, suited to labs needing more imaging flexibility than a flow cabinet setup allows.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axiovert 7 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an inverted microscope for routine cell culture work and multidimensional life science research, supporting live-cell imaging, fixed samples, tissue sections, and fluorescence experiments, from monolayers through to organoids.

faqs.question: Is Axiovert 7 suitable for live cell imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes. Label-free live cell culture is monitored using phase contrast, DIC, PlasDIC, or iHMC, and long-term live-cell and 3D models, including organoids and Organ-on-a-Chip systems, are supported under stable environmental conditions with automated time-lapse imaging.

faqs.question: Which contrast methods are available with Axiovert 7?
faqs.answer: Six: PH (phase contrast), FL (fluorescence), DIC, PlasDIC, iHMC, and POL (polarization).

faqs.question: Can Axiovert 7 perform multichannel fluorescence imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, multichannel fluorescence images are automatically overlaid and saved together with scale and metadata, supporting digital optical sectioning for improved resolution in X, Y, and Z.

faqs.question: What software is used with ZEISS Axiovert 7?
faqs.answer: ZEISS ZEN imaging software, enabling precise multidimensional experiments including Z-stacks, time-lapse imaging, and automated scanning for slides and multiwell plates.

faqs.question: Is Axiovert 7 expandable?
faqs.answer: Yes. The system uses modular hardware, upgradable software, and extensive interfaces, adapting from digital optical sectioning to long-term live-cell imaging as research requirements change, including in accordance with GxP guidelines.

faqs.question: Can Axiovert 7 be used for whole slide imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, the system performs panoramic scanning and whole-slide imaging of stained or immunofluorescence-labeled tissue sections for quantitative spatial analysis.

faqs.question: What types of cameras are compatible with Axiovert 7?
faqs.answer: Specific camera compatibility was not itemized on the source page reviewed. Inkarp can confirm compatible camera options directly.

faqs.question: What is the field of view?
faqs.answer: 23 mm.

faqs.question: What magnification range does it cover?
faqs.answer: 1.25x to 100x across its objective range.

faqs.question: Is the focus and stage motorized?
faqs.answer: Yes, both are motorized, enabling reproducible, automated imaging.

faqs.question: How is Axiovert 7 different from Axiovert 5?
faqs.answer: Axiovert 7 adds motorized focus and stage, polarization contrast, whole-slide scanning, multiwell plate automation, and GxP-adaptable workflows. Axiovert 5 covers broad contrast flexibility (DIC, iHMC, phase contrast, brightfield, fluorescence) with manual operation, suited to routine work without the same level of automated, high-throughput capability.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axio Observer used for?
faqs.answer: It's an open, modular inverted microscope platform for demanding multimodal imaging of living and fixed specimens, built to be tailored precisely to the requirements of individual research programmes, from widefield through super-resolution imaging.

faqs.question: What is AI Sample Finder?
faqs.answer: An automated feature that detects the sample carrier, adjusts focus, and finds the relevant sample region without manual input, reducing time to image from minutes to just seconds.

faqs.question: Can it perform optical sectioning?
faqs.answer: Yes, with ZEISS Apotome 3, using structured illumination to remove out-of-focus light and produce high-contrast optical sections, even from thicker specimens.

faqs.question: Does it support automated water immersion?
faqs.answer: Yes, via the Autoimmersion Module, available for Axio Observer 7, which automates hands-free water immersion and removes the risk of data loss or objective damage from manual immersion errors.

faqs.question: How does it handle long time-lapse experiments?
faqs.answer: Definite Focus 3 compensates for focus drift, keeping multi-day, multi-position time-lapse experiments sharp and high-contrast throughout.

faqs.question: Can it capture multiple fluorescence channels simultaneously?
faqs.answer: Yes, using Duolink alongside ZEN imaging software, two spectrally separated channels can be captured together at high speed.

faqs.question: What light sources are available?
faqs.answer: Viluma 5 and Viluma 7 multicolor LED sources for fluorescence, and the Xylis white light LED source, which delivers reproducible output with no warm-up time across its lifespan.

faqs.question: Can it be combined with electron microscopy data?
faqs.answer: Yes, acquired images combine with electron microscopy data and other imaging modalities for correlative workflows.

faqs.question: What is ZEISS Microscopy Copilot?
faqs.answer: An AI assistant aware of the specific microscope configuration and available ZEN Toolkits, providing quick, natural-language guidance on experiment setup, automation, and post-processing.

faqs.question: How is Axio Observer different from Axiovert 7?
faqs.answer: Axiovert 7 is a fully specified, motorized platform with six confirmed contrast methods and automated whole-slide and multiwell workflows. Axio Observer is a more open platform, defined by its AI-driven automation and an extensive accessory ecosystem (Apotome 3, Autoimmersion Module, Definite Focus 3, Duolink), built to be assembled specifically around the experiment, including correlative and super-resolution imaging.

faqs.question: Which cameras is it compatible with?
faqs.answer: The full ZEISS Axiocam portfolio, selected by sensitivity, resolution, and speed to match the application.

faqs.answer: A full contrast method list, magnification range, and stand dimensions were not published on the source page reviewed. Inkarp can request the full specification sheet from Zeiss.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axioscan 7 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an automated digital slide scanner, used across life science research, pharma and biotech spatial biology, clinical diagnostics, and geology, digitizing microscope slides at high throughput.

faqs.question: How many slides can it scan in one run?
faqs.answer: Up to 100, depending on the configuration, with reliable 24/7 unattended operation.

faqs.question: What configurations are available?
faqs.answer: Four: Standard (Life Science Research), Spatial Biology (Pharma & Biotech), Clinical, and Geology and Materials, each with different slide formats, contrast techniques, and software integration.

faqs.question: Is Axioscan 7 certified for clinical diagnostic use?
faqs.answer: Only the Clinical configuration carries IVDR certification. The Standard, Spatial Biology, and Geology configurations are not certified for diagnostic use.

faqs.question: What contrast techniques are supported?
faqs.answer: Up to five, depending on configuration: brightfield, fluorescence, circular polarization, crossed linear polarization, and TIE (transport of intensity equation).

faqs.question: How many objectives are available?
faqs.answer: Up to 14 on Standard and Geology configurations, 3 on Spatial Biology, and 2 base objectives with 4 additional options on Clinical.

faqs.question: What software does it use?
faqs.answer: ZEN, or third-party solutions, on Standard and Geology. Spatial Biology adds SlideStream software and Mindpeak AI-based image analysis. Clinical integrates into IMS/PACS systems via ZEISS Solutions Lab and a Dicom converter.

faqs.question: Can it handle multiple staining rounds on the same tissue?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the Spatial Biology configuration, which supports coregistration of multiple staining rounds alongside Mindpeak AI-based analysis.

faqs.question: What slide formats are supported?
faqs.answer: 1x3", 2x3", and 4x3" on Standard and Geology (Geology adds GEO format specifically), 1x3" only on Spatial Biology and Clinical.

faqs.question: Is this suitable for geological or petrographic work?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Geology configuration supports GEO-format slides and pairs with the Petrography Analysis Toolbox (PetPAT) for quantitative analytics.

faqs.question: How does the Clinical configuration connect to hospital systems?
faqs.answer: Via ZEISS Solutions Lab and a Dicom converter, integrating into existing IMS and PACS infrastructure. Zeiss notes this integration path itself is not an in vitro diagnostic device.

sections.description: Choosing between Standard, Spatial Biology, Clinical, and Geology.
body: Buying an automated slide scanner sized for a general lab, then trying to run clinical diagnostic samples or multi-round spatial biology staining through it, means fighting the hardware and software the whole way. Axioscan 7 avoids that by not being one general-purpose system, Zeiss builds four distinct configurations, each with its own slide format range, contrast technique set, objective count, and software layer.

Standard covers the broadest general research use, up to 14 objectives and the full contrast range including crossed linear polarization. Spatial Biology trades objective breadth (down to 3) for SlideStream software and Mindpeak AI, purpose-built for coregistering multiple staining rounds and running AI-based analysis at scale. faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Celldiscoverer 7 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an automated live-cell imaging platform, used for explorative high-content research, including cell biology, organoid research, developmental biology, and high-content screening.

faqs.question: Do I need to be a microscopy expert to use it?
faqs.answer: No. Insert the sample carrier and the system makes all necessary settings automatically, including calibration, focus, and aberration correction.

faqs.question: How much faster is the latest generation?
faqs.answer: Up to 9x faster widefield acquisition and up to 1.8x faster confocal acquisition, compared to the previous generation.

faqs.question: What is Autoimmersion?
faqs.answer: Fully automated water immersion supply and removal through a 50x objective, sealed with an elastic silicon membrane, supporting live-cell imaging at 37°C over several days.

faqs.question: What is Autocorr?
faqs.answer: Automatic correction ring adjustment on the objective, compensating for spherical aberration caused by different vessel bottom thickness or material.

faqs.question: Can it handle different sample carrier types?
faqs.answer: Yes, automatic sample recognition detects relevant vessel features on loading, supporting Petri dishes, chamber slides, multi-well plates, plastic or glass, thin or thick bottoms, and low- or high-skirt plates.

faqs.question: How does focus work for long time-lapse experiments?
faqs.answer: Find Focus locates the region of interest with one click; Definite Focus holds that position throughout the experiment, whether it runs seconds or several days, and automatic focus maps support multiple positions simultaneously.

faqs.question: Can it do confocal imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the optional LSM 910 and Airyscan 2 upgrade, delivering up to 1.9x resolution improvement, spectral imaging, and photomanipulation techniques like FRAP and FRET.

faqs.question: Is there protection against objective damage?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Adaptive Lens Guard prevents collisions with the sample vessel or hardware while automatically maximizing the available scanning area.

faqs.question: Can throughput be increased with automation?
faqs.answer: Yes, an optional robotic sample loader from Peak Analysis & Automation (PAA) handles all SBS multi-well plate formats for high-volume, unattended processing.

faqs.question: What software analyzes the imaging data?
faqs.answer: arivis Pro, for 2D through complex 3D and 4D dataset analysis, with arivis Cloud for neural network training and arivis Hub for parallel cloud-based processing across multiple datasets.

faqs.question: Is it reliable in a shared, multi-user lab?
faqs.answer: Yes, workflows execute reproducibly without manual recalibration between users, and predictive service analytics schedule maintenance based on actual component wear.

faqs.question: How is Celldiscoverer 7 different from Axioscan 7?
faqs.answer: Celldiscoverer 7 automates live-cell and high-content imaging, with immersion, incubation, and focus systems built for living, dynamic samples. Axioscan 7 automates digitization of fixed, prepared slides at high volume, with no equivalent need for immersion or incubation.

Insert a sample carrier, and the system handles calibration, focus, and aberration correction automatically, no microscopy expertise required to get research-grade results. Autoimmersion delivers water immersion automatically through a 50x objective, and Autocorr adjusts the objective's correction ring on its own to compensate for spherical aberration across different vessel types, Petri dishes, chamber slides, multi-well plates, plastic or glass, thin or thick bottoms, all recognized automatically on load. Adaptive Lens Guard protects the objective from collisions while maximizing usable scanning area. Find Focus and Definite Focus locate and hold the region of interest across seconds or multiple days. Add LSM 910 with Airyscan 2, and the same platform delivers confocal 3D imaging with up to 1.9x resolution improvement, on the same automated stand. What it removes: the need to become a microscopy expert before getting reliable data. What it adapts to: the actual sample carrier, automatically, on every load. sections.title: Automatic Adaptation to Any Sample Carrier
sections.description: What Autocorr and automatic sample recognition actually solve.
body: High-numerical-aperture objectives, the kind live-cell imaging genuinely needs, only deliver their promised contrast and sensitivity when their optics correctly compensate for the specific vessel they're looking through. Bottom thickness varies. Material varies, plastic versus glass. Skirt height varies between plate designs. Every one of those variations introduces spherical aberration if left uncorrected, and manually adjusting a correction ring for each new vessel type is exactly the kind of expertise-gated step that slows a lab down.

Celldiscoverer 7 removes it. Automatic sample recognition detects the relevant vessel features the moment a sample loads, and Autocorr adjusts the objective's correction ring to compensate, without anyone touching a dial. The freedom that unlocks is real: Petri dishes, chamber slides, multi-well plates, plastic or glass, thin or thick vessel bottoms, low-skirt or high-skirt plates, all usable interchangeably, at full optical quality, on the same system.

faqs.question: What does "modular" actually mean here?

faqs.question: Can a camera be attached?

sections.title: Illumination Built for the Surface
sections.description: What each specialized lighting module actually solves.
body: A flat, polished microelectronic part and a translucent zebrafish embryo need genuinely different light. One reflects almost everything back specularly, hiding detail under glare. The other needs gentle, uniform illumination that doesn't scatter or overheat the sample. SteREO Discovery V8 doesn't try to solve both with one fixed light source, it offers a module for each.

CL 1500 ECO fiber-optic cold light, paired with a wide range of light guides, is built specifically for developmental biology, gentle enough for zebrafish and Drosophila embryos without heat stress. The Coaxial Reflected-Light Illuminator S goes the opposite direction, purpose-built for smooth, specular surfaces like polished metal parts and microelectronic devices, with illumination and observation optimized specifically around the PlanApo S 1.0x objective. VisiLED ring light S 40-10 DF combines brightfield and darkfield in reflected light for PCB and surface inspection, and a light manager keeps coaxial lighting brightness stable through the entire zoom range, so illumination doesn't shift as magnification changes.

sections.title: eZoom, Explained
sections.description: Why electronic lens positioning beats a mechanical curve.
body: Every stereo microscope zoom body has to move lenses precisely as magnification changes. A mechanical zoom body does this with a physical cam curve, one fixed mechanical path that every unit follows, tolerances and all. Those tolerances compound as magnification increases, which is exactly where a soft image costs the most.

eZoom replaces that physical curve with stepping motors that position each lens electronically, correcting for the actual tolerance of the individual lenses in that specific microscope rather than assuming a uniform mechanical path fits every unit. Zeiss states the result directly: doubled precision compared to a mechanical zoom body, visibly more detail captured across the zoom range. The defocus curve stays tighter to the depth-of-field envelope throughout, rather than drifting outside it as magnification climbs.

faqs.question: How reproducible are the zoom positions?

faqs.question: How is that reproducibility achieved?
faqs.answer: eZoom replaces the mechanical zoom curve with stepping motors that position lenses electronically, correcting for individual lens tolerances rather than following a fixed mechanical path.

faqs.question: What is SYCOP?

faqs.question: How does V20 fit into the wider SteREO system?

faqs.answer: Both use motorized eZoom and SYCOP control, but V20 extends the zoom ratio to 20:1 (versus V12's 12:1), reaching up to 345x total magnification and 1000 LP/mm resolution, with a specifically quantified reproducibility figure of more than 99%.

body: A 345x magnification figure is only useful if you can actually get back to it. Most zoom systems drift slightly every time they're adjusted, close enough for casual observation, not precise enough for a measurement or comparison that depends on consistent conditions.

eZoom solves that directly. User-defined zoom positions are set once and recalled with more than 99% reproducibility, which means a measurement taken today at a specific magnification and a measurement taken next month at the same defined position are genuinely comparable, not approximately similar. That reproducibility comes from the same electronic lens positioning that gives eZoom its 2x precision advantage over a mechanical zoom body, stepping motors correcting for individual lens tolerance rather than following one fixed mechanical path.

sections.description: What color accuracy and range actually mean at the eyepiece.
body: Standard stereo optics show color fringing at high magnification, a soft halo around edges that gets worse the further you zoom in. That's not a minor cosmetic issue when the work depends on distinguishing genuine material boundaries from optical artifacts. Apochromatic correction removes it, at every point across Stemi 508's zoom range.

The 8:1 zoom ratio means that correction holds from a 122 mm field of view down to the finest detail an interchangeable eyepiece and front optic combination can resolve, up to 250x. And because working distance stretches to 287 mm at the wide end, reaching that level of detail doesn't mean crowding tools, hands, or a soldering iron into a cramped gap under the objective.

sections.description: Why removing an adjustment step matters in a classroom.
body: Köhler illumination is the standard for even, glare-free microscope lighting, and getting it right normally takes a trained hand: aligning the condenser, centering the field diaphragm, adjusting for each new sample. In a research lab, that is a five-minute task for someone who does it daily. In a classroom of thirty students on their first day with a microscope, it is thirty separate failure points before anyone has actually looked at a cell.

Primostar 1 removes the step entirely. The illumination arrives pre-fixed, so image quality does not depend on whether the last student to use the microscope set it up correctly. A teacher hands the microscope over already working.

longForm.heroLead: A microscope that needs a manual before the first lesson isn't ready for a classroom. It comes in three ready-made packages, each built for a specific job. Fixed-Köhler for basic education, with a large 20 mm field of view already adjusted and a set of objectives and eyepieces already in place. A teaching and routine lab package with a choice of 30-watt halogen or energy-saving LED, plus an optional fluorescence tube. Built from solid, resistant materials, the kind that keep working smoothly after years of daily use in a busy teaching lab, with minimal maintenance along the way. What it saves you: setup time, energy cost, and the guesswork over which configuration to buy. What it adds over Primostar 1: digital connectivity, package flexibility, and optional fluorescence. body: Buying a microscope usually means choosing between a long list of individual options, illumination, objectives, contrast method, camera, and hoping the combination actually works together. Primostar 3 skips that. Zeiss builds three complete packages, each matched to a specific job, and the choice comes down to what the microscope is actually for.

The Fixed-Köhler package is built for basic teaching: a large 20 mm field of view already adjusted, objectives and eyepieces already fitted, energy-saving LED illumination. Nothing to configure. The teaching and routine package goes further, a choice between 30-watt halogen or LED, a range of contrasting techniques, and the option to add fluorescence later. The digital classroom package puts an 8.3 megapixel WiFi camera at the center, built specifically for sharing live images across a room or a video call.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axiolab 5 used for?
faqs.answer: It is an upright microscope built for clinical and biomedical laboratory routine work, including hematology, histology, cytopathology, and general clinical microscopy, with built-in Smart Microscopy documentation.

faqs.question: What is Smart Microscopy?
faqs.answer: A documentation system that captures a true-color, correctly scaled image with a single press of the Snap button, without needing a separate computer or software.

faqs.question: Does scaling get added automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes, every image captured includes correct scaling information automatically, no manual scale bar insertion needed.

faqs.question: Do I need a separate computer to use Axiolab 5?
faqs.answer: No, in stand-alone configuration the microscope and Axiocam camera operate independently of a computer system. Labscope and ZEN configurations add connected or research-grade options where needed.

faqs.question: What cameras does it work with?
faqs.answer: Axiocam 212 color or Axiocam 203 mono, depending on the configuration chosen.

faqs.question: Can it handle fluorescence imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, with powerful LED illumination across various wavelengths, and multichannel fluorescence support through the ZEISS Labscope configuration.

faqs.question: What makes it ergonomic?
faqs.answer: One-hand access to the Snap button, stage drive, focus, and brightness control, adjustable ergotubes, a height and torque-adaptable rackless stage, and a dual specimen holder that reduces slide changes.

faqs.question: Can it track samples by barcode?
faqs.answer: Yes, either through a barcode reader connected to the Axiocam 212 color camera, or by scanning with an iPad's built-in camera through Labscope.

faqs.question: Is a two-person shared view available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an optional co-observation bundle with a photo tube or ergo photo tube, built for real-time case review and resident training.

faqs.question: How does Eco-mode work?
faqs.answer: Axiolab 5 automatically goes to standby after 15 minutes of inactivity, saving energy without needing to be switched off manually.

faqs.question: How is Axiolab 5 different from Primostar 3?
faqs.answer: Primostar 3 is built primarily for teaching and basic routine lab work. Axiolab 5 is positioned specifically for clinical and biomedical laboratories, with Smart Microscopy documentation, dedicated ergonomic features, and co-observation options Primostar 3 doesn't offer.

sections.title: Smart Microscopy
sections.description: How one button removes the entire computer-switching routine.
body: Anyone who has documented a slide manually knows the sequence: place the sample, focus, switch to the computer, adjust white balance, set exposure time and gain, capture, insert a scale bar, switch back to the eyepieces. It's not difficult work, but it interrupts every single slide, and across a full clinic day that adds up to real time lost and real focus broken.

Axiolab 5 removes the interruption. Press the ergonomic Snap button directly on the stand, and the system captures a detail-rich, true-color image, exactly as seen through the eyepieces, with correct scaling added automatically. No computer switch. No manual settings. The procedure integrates into the microscopy workflow that's already happening, rather than pausing it.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axioscope 5 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an upright microscope built for biomedical routine and research work, supporting histology, cytology, hematology, and multichannel fluorescence documentation including immunofluorescence and FISH.

faqs.question: How does the four-channel fluorescence feature work?
faqs.answer: Paired with Colibri 3 LED illumination and the Axiocam 203 mono camera, select the channels for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, then press Snap. The system automatically adjusts exposure, acquires each channel, switches wavelengths, and delivers a single overlaid image with a scale bar, without needing a PC.

faqs.question: Does brightfield documentation work the same way?
faqs.answer: Yes, focus the sample and press Snap. The captured color matches exactly what's seen through the eyepieces, with brightness and white balance adjusted automatically.

faqs.question: Is the focus motorized?
faqs.answer: No, Axioscope 5 uses manual Z focus. Motorized focus is a feature of Axioscope 7.

faqs.question: Can Axioscope 5 perform whole slide imaging?
faqs.answer: No, whole slide imaging requires Axioscope 7's motorized stage and Z-control. Axioscope 5 is built for field-of-view documentation and multichannel fluorescence rather than full slide digitization.

faqs.question: What makes Axioscope 7 different from Axioscope 5?
faqs.answer: Axioscope 7 adds a motorized stage and motorized Z-control (autofocus) for scanning and stitching entire slides into whole slide images, with ZEN software supporting full GxP compliance for regulated environments. Axioscope 5 keeps focus manual and is built for routine field-of-view documentation.

faqs.question: Is Axioscope 7 suitable for clinical diagnostics?
faqs.answer: Axioscope 7 is positioned for clinical research labs and biomedical research applications, with ZEN core software supporting GxP compliance where regulated diagnostic workflows require it.

faqs.question: What is the advantage of whole slide imaging on a motorized upright microscope?
faqs.answer: It allows an entire specimen to be digitized automatically, large tissue sections scanned with a motorized stage, focus maintained across the whole sample, and multi-position, multi-channel datasets stitched into a single high-resolution image, useful for archival, remote review, and downstream digital analysis.

faqs.question: Which Axioscope is right for my lab?
faqs.answer: If the work is routine and research documentation, including multichannel fluorescence, without needing to digitize entire slides, Axioscope 5 fits. If the lab needs to scan and archive complete specimens, particularly under regulated conditions, Axioscope 7 is the better fit.

faqs.question: What illumination does it use?
faqs.answer: 10W LED or 50W Halogen for transmitted light, and Colibri 3, Viluma 5/7, or HXP for fluorescence.

faqs.question: Can samples be tracked by barcode?
faqs.answer: Yes, either through a barcode reader connected to the Axiocam 212 color camera, or by scanning with an iPad's camera through Labscope.

faqs.question: Is a shared, two-person view available?
faqs.answer: Yes, as an optional co-observation bundle with a photo tube or ergo photo tube, built for pathology case review and resident training.

faqs.question: Is there a return policy?
faqs.answer: Yes, a 60-day risk-free purchase. If it isn't the right fit, it can be returned with no questions asked.

longForm.heroHook: Four fluorescence channels. One click. Not one PC required.
longForm.heroLead: Multichannel fluorescence used to mean a workstation, manual channel switching, and exposure settings adjusted by hand between every wavelength. Axioscope 5 collapses all of that into one press. Pair it with the Colibri 3 LED light source and the Axiocam 203 mono camera, select the channels for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, and press Snap. The system switches wavelengths, adjusts exposure automatically, acquires each channel, and hands back a single overlaid multichannel image with a scale bar already included, even without a PC connected. The same Smart Microscopy logic runs through brightfield work too. Focus, press Snap, done. Color appears in the captured image exactly as it looked through the eyepieces, brightness and white balance adjusted automatically. Ergotubes adapt eyepiece height and angle to natural posture, every essential control sits within easy reach, and the light manager adjusts illumination automatically, no manual lamp brightness dialing between samples. What it replaces: manual channel switching and PC-based fluorescence documentation. What it adds over Axiolab 5: true multichannel fluorescence, up to four channels in one click. Where it sits in the range: below Axioscope 7's motorized whole slide imaging, above routine brightfield-only microscopes.

sections.title: Four Channels, One Click
sections.description: How Colibri 3 and Smart Microscopy handle multichannel fluorescence.
body: Multichannel fluorescence imaging is normally a stop-start process: select a channel, adjust exposure, capture, switch, adjust again, capture again, then combine everything into an overlay afterward, usually on a connected computer. That's four separate manual decisions before a single usable image exists.

Axioscope 5 removes the stopping. Paired with Colibri 3 and the Axiocam 203 mono camera, select the channels needed for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, then press Snap. The system adjusts exposure time automatically, acquires the image, switches to the next channel, and repeats, on its own. What comes out the other end is a single overlaid multichannel fluorescence image, scale bar included, without needing a PC connected at all.

sections.title: Axioscope 5 or Axioscope 7
sections.description: The real difference, straight from Zeiss's own side-by-side comparison. Choosing between these two comes down to one question: does the work need whole slide imaging, or does it stop at routine and research-grade fluorescence and brightfield documentation? The practical takeaway: Axioscope 7's motorized stage and Z-control exist specifically to scan and stitch entire slides into high-resolution whole slide images, with ZEN software supporting full GxP compliance where regulated environments require it. If that's not the goal, Axioscope 5's manual focus and Labscope-based workflow cover routine and research fluorescence work at a lower cost and simpler operation.
